Title: Police reveal new details in case of missing women linked to Philadelphia home
Article_Text:
5 women 'appear to be deceased' in images recovered from Philadelphia home: Police
Investigators are combing through more than 1 million digital images and videos.
Images and videos recovered from a home in Philadelphia show five women who "appear to be deceased," though no bodies have been recovered and the massive investigation into the missing women is ongoing, police on Thursday.
The case began in June when Eugene Horsch, 44, was arrested. At the time, guns and narcotics were recovered, and Horsch allegedly had an ID impersonating law enforcement, Philadelphia Police Deputy Commissioner Frank Vanore said at a news conference.
In a search at Horsch's home, authorities discovered chemicals and five urns believed to hold human ashes, Vanore said. One urn is believed to contain Horsch's father's remains, another is believed to be a relative, and another is believed to be a friend, officials said, adding that the remaining two are unidentified.
In the search, investigators also recovered over 1 million digital images and videos, including women "posed in different positions" in the house, Vanore said.
Among the images were two missing women: 27-year-old Gabrielle Amarando and 26-year-old Maribel Fresses, Vanore said. Photos dated 2017 show the women lying unconscious in the house, Vanore said.
Philadelphia police said Thursday that "in later images," Amarando and Fresses "appeared to be deceased." The women are still missing, police said.
Another recovered video dated 2017 shows Hersch's father, RC Horsch -- who has since died -- with a woman, and both were nude, Vanore said.
In the video, the woman used drugs, was "given money by Mr. Horsch and then affixed to the bed with handcuffs by him," Vanore said.
"... He puts a zip tie around her neck, and she becomes unconscious," and she appeared to be "lifeless," Vanore said.
Authorities are also looking into two other unconscious women seen in the images and videos: a 25-year-old woman and a woman who has not been identified, police said.
Vanore said police are respecting the wishes of the families and not releasing the names of the woman seen in the video with RC Horsch and the 25-year-old woman.
Police said Thursday there is a total of five women "who appear to be deceased" in the photos and videos, including Fresses and Amarando.
"Investigators continue working to identify the Jane Doe, locate individuals depicted in the recovered material, and corroborate what is shown in the digital evidence," police said in a statement.
Philadelphia Police Commissioner Kevin Bethel stressed on Wednesday that authorities will "dictate the pace" of the massive investigation. Officials said they have "more than 1 million individual digital evidence items requiring review" and about "30% of that review has been completed."
Authorities said they've identified 58 people in the images reviewed so far; some people have been interviewed and investigators said they're working to speak with the others.
There's no current threat to the community, the chief said.

Title: County explores $50M partnership to repair 28 aging bridges
Article_Text:
POTTSVILLE — Repairs for nearly half of Schuylkill County’s bridges could be on the path to getting fast-tracked.
At the Sept. 16 commissioners meeting, a proposal was made to address the needs for 28 of the 62 county-owned bridges over the next five years. Representatives from engineering and financial firms presented a plan to bundle the bridge projects into a single public-private partnership under Pennsylvania’s Act 88 of 2012.
The plan involves 23 full bridge replacements, three rehabilitations and two complete bridge removals. Tim Benner of the Allentown-based CDR Maguire Engineering said the top priorities are the “worst of the worst” structures that have been given a poor grade in biennial inspections. The targeted bridges are in Ashland, Tremont, Girardville, Auburn and St. Clair boroughs, and Butler, Barry, Washington, Walker, Rush, East Union, Hegins, Hubley, North Union, Pine Grove, West Penn, Union and Upper Mahantongo townships.
“As structures deteriorate over time, you get into that load posting range,” Benner said, describing the threshold when legal weight-limit signs need to be placed on a bridge. “Once bridges get load posted, you can’t get trucks across, and that means you can’t get fire trucks across, EMS, school buses, the deliveries — whether that’s fuel, oil, coal, gas, things like that. … So there’s a real need to address that.”
Benner added that the new structures will be designed to last at least 80 years, that replaced bridges would be expanded to meet current safety standards, and that at least eight narrow bottleneck bridges would be widened to a minimum of 24 feet.
Scott Kramer of the Lancaster-based firm Raymond James noted that the plan is also intended to protect taxpayers from inflation tied to construction costs. He estimated total project costs at $50.8 million, which would be financed through tax-exempt “certificates of participation” issued by a newly created municipal authority.
Considering that the county can only afford to replace one or two bridges a year, all three commissioners were supportive and enthusiastic about exploring the project. Chairman Larry Padora praised the project’s “economy of scale” and said that holding the debt off the general obligation books protects the county’s bond rating.
“It’s just something, I think it’s good for the county,” he said, hinting that the board could vote on the proposal at next Wednesday’s meeting.
Commissioner Gary Hess asked if the county could still pursue state and federal grant funding for ongoing maintenance on the remaining bridges if it entered the public-private partnership, and Kramer said yes.
According to presentation documents, construction costs are estimated at $985 per square foot for replacements, $870 per square foot for rehabilitations and $400 per square foot for removals, covering over 53,000 square-feet of bridge deck area. Kramer projected that tackling 28 bridges simultaneously leverages bulk purchasing power and hedges against inflation, saving taxpayers roughly $320,000 per bridge — or $9 million total. If approved, the project team plans to submit the candidate bridge list to the state P3 board for preliminary review later this month.
Official stands by mail-in ballot processing policy
With the Nov. 3 election approaching, a few local voters expressed concerns that a mail-in ballot could be discarded over minor clerical errors without adequately informing the voter. Under current procedures, Schuylkill County does not notify voters before election day if their mail-in return envelope is missing a signature or date.
Jessica Simkulet, a judge of election for West Brunswick Township South, said that the policy is unfair to seniors, working parents and residents with disabilities.
“To receive a phone call on election day saying your ballot will not be counted and the only option you have is to report to your polling place by 8 p.m., disability be damned, is totally unacceptable,” she said. “If other counties in Pennsylvania can find a way to help their residents vote with convenience and confidence, why can’t we?”
In response, Election Bureau Director Al Gricowski confirmed that while some Pennsylvania counties choose to contact voters directly to cure ballots, Schuylkill County sticks to state statutory procedures. Officials noted that out of roughly 5,500 mail-in ballots cast in the primary election, only 15 (0.01%) were set aside due to missing signatures or dates.
Pottsville resident Lisa Von Ahn suggested the county’s election bureau immediately log outer envelopes with missing signatures or dates into the Pennsylvania SURE system, which she argued would give voters ample time to fix mistakes or arrange to vote provisionally.
Gricowski said that while staff log obvious defects into the system during the bulk intake, full pre-canvassing and formal inspection do not legally begin until 7 a.m. on election day, per state law.
“I think we could do better,” Von Ahn commented after leaving the meeting.

Title: Rupee to headline South Jersey Caribbean Festival - The Caribbean Camera
Article_Text:
The South Jersey Caribbean Festival will return to Camden Waterfront on Saturday, Sept. 26, after severe weather forced organizers to postpone the annual celebration twice, according to Kylla Herbert, president of the South Jersey Caribbean Cultural and Development Organization.
Herbert said heavy thundershowers on Saturday, July 18 and Aug. 22 disrupted plans for the festival, which is held at Wiggins Park in Camden, New Jersey. The rescheduled event will run from 2:00 p.m. to 8:00 p.m. and will remain free to the public.
Barbadian born Soca star Rupee is scheduled to headline the 26th Annual South Jersey Caribbean Festival. The singer is expected to perform several of his best known songs, including “Tempted to Touch,” “Jump,” and “What Happens in the Party.”
“Rupee has been a major presence in Caribbean and international music for more than 25 years,” Herbert said. She described his appearance as a major attraction, noting that “Tempted to Touch” helped introduce Soca music to audiences internationally.
The musical lineup will also include Alex Kwabena Colon and the Garifuna collective from Belize, Klymaxx Band from Antigua, Orchestra LA 95 from Puerto Rico, Niger Ali from Jamaica, Monet Esbee from the Bahamas and the Philadelphia Pan Stars Steel Orchestra from Trinidad and Tobago, among others.
Herbert said the festival is designed as a family friendly celebration featuring Caribbean music, food, arts, heritage and traditions. Cultural presentations, live performances, community vendors, arts and crafts, and activities for children will form part of the program.
“For 26 years, the festival has remained committed to being a free cultural event,” Herbert said, adding that organizers want Caribbean culture to remain accessible regardless of a family’s financial circumstances. She said sponsorships and donations help make the event possible.
Wiggins Park will provide a backdrop overlooking the Philadelphia skyline as visitors gather to celebrate the region’s Caribbean heritage. Herbert said people representing numerous islands and territories traditionally attend, creating an event that brings together different generations and communities.
“The South Jersey Caribbean Festival has become one of the region’s longstanding celebrations of Caribbean culture,” Herbert said. What began as an effort to promote cultural awareness and unity has developed into an annual gathering for Caribbean families, supporters and visitors from New Jersey, Pennsylvania, Delaware and beyond.

Title: 'We're Here To Help' Local Team Marks 15 Years Of Disaster Relief
Article_Text:
When disaster strikes, most people watch the aftermath unfold from afar, but for 15 years, Work Loving God, a group of volunteers, have dedicated their time on almost 30 missions – providing relief where they can to people who have been through natural disasters.
The group began in 2011, when a group of East Tennesseans and Fulton County residents met in the tornado recovery mission fields, according to their official pamphlet. Since then, they have averaged around three trips per year. Now, they gear up for their next trip in
Oct. 18 to the 24, Work Loving God will drive to North Carolina, transporting around 10,000 pounds of equipment and hearts dedicated to the cause with them, according to Michael Binder, member of the group.
From tornados, hurricanes and floods, WLG answers the call, helping build and repair homes after natural disasters. They take what is given to them and pour it back out, with 97% percent of all funds going directly to mission trips.
The group continues to return to North Carolina not because they like the scenery, or the warmth, but because it’s an area that has been forgotten in the media, Binder explained.
“The thing that’s unique about Hurricane Helene is it occurred in an area that was not in the flood zone,” Binder said. “The federal government has flood maps and if you’re not in the flood zone, you can’t buy flood insurance.”
Consequently, some people who lose their homes might not receive insurance coverage. The only way they can be made whole is either through their own savings or donations, according to Binder.
Although WLG was formed in 2011, Binder’s involvement in disaster relief began years earlier. Binder said some of the most memorable moments have come not from the physical work, but from the relationships formed along the way.
For instance, he reflected on one of his first trips in 2005 to Mississippi after Hurricane Katrina where he met a man who worked 40 years to save up for retirement. The man’s plan was to then travel the country with his wife. She passed away one month later. The man was stuck at a crossroads when he decided to join the mission.
“He said ‘You will never meet finer people in your life. God bless people in the world,” Binder recounted.
Another story comes from a past trip to Western North Carolina, where the group repaired the foundation of a house that had been buried for a year and a half after Hurricane Helene. For the homeowner, the arrival of the team meant finally having someone show up after three people told her they would help, but never came back. In disbelief, she approached Binder.
“She looked at me and she asked, ‘Is this really happening? Are you really gonna fix my house?’” Binder said. “I said I know I can fix your house… Ma’am there’s 20 people here, and we’re here to help.”
Help they did. Before leaving, the team had completed the project, jacking up and straightening out the house’s foundation.
Based out of Morrisstown, Tenn., WLG consists of individuals from Mississippi, Tennessee, Kentucky and Pennsylvania, according to Binder.
The local members will host an Ice Cream Social Friday, Sept. 18 at McConnellsburg United Presbyterian Church, and they’re inviting the community in to hear about what they do.
“The whole community is invited to hear about this wonderful work that we’re doing. It’s the most powerful thing I do,” Binder said.
The gathering will take place at 7 p.m., featuring testimonials from people who have been on these trips. The upcoming trip is also open to community members who want to volunteer. Binder encourages both open minds and open hearts when it comes to deciding.
“The thing I hear all the time is ‘I’m not a carpenter. I can’t do this or I can’t do that,’” Binder said. “If all you do is come on the trip and help with cleanup, meal preparation or sit and spend time with people. We don’t call the people we help victims. We call them survivors. People have to tell their story 70 times before they heal.”
As the Pennsylvania team prepares for another trip to North Carolina, Binder hopes others will feel the same calling he and so many others have; whether that means picking up a hammer, preparing a meal, or offering a listening ear, the whole community is invited to learn more on Friday.

Title: Liam Neeson's R-Rated Sci-Fi Horror Movie Tears Through Epic Streaming Milestone
Article_Text:
Adam Bentz is a senior news writer at ScreenRant, where he has authored nearly 5,000 articles, including features and lists. He studied creative writing and English with a concentration in screenwriting at Southern New Hampshire University and interned as a writer/journalist for The Borgen Project, an influential organization that fights global poverty.
However, one of his proudest achievements is editing a Leonardo DiCaprio freakout compilation that has over 150K views on YouTube. Adam also fancies himself an amateur film critic on his personal website.
Though Liam Neeson's 40-year career spans several genres, he has starred in several sci-fi films, most famously playing Jedi Master Qui-Gon Jinn in Star Wars: Episode I – The Phantom Menace (1999) before going on to star in Battleship (2012), Men in Black: International (2019), and more. Although his horror resume is much shorter, one of his new movies that mashes up the two genres has just surpassed an epic streaming milestone.
That sci-fi horror movie is Cold Storage. Directed by Jonny Campbell, with a script written by David Koepp based on his own 2019 novel, it stars Liam Neeson as a former bioterrorism agent who is called back into action alongside two young employees when a highly dangerous fungus escapes from a secret laboratory. Georgina Campbell (Barbarian) and Joe Keery (Stranger Things) also star.

QUESTION 1 / 8THE START
01
Liam John Neeson was born on June 7, 1952 in County Antrim, Northern Ireland — and grew up Catholic in a largely Protestant town during the early years of the Troubles. As a teenager he won an Ulster Youth heavyweight boxing title (and broke his nose more than once doing it) before drifting into amateur theatre. Name the town.
✓ Correct! Ballymena. Neeson was raised on Corlea Gardens to Bernard, a school caretaker, and Katherine, a cook. He attended All Saints Primary and St. Patrick's Boys' Academy, and trained at the All Saints Boxing Club, where he won an Ulster Youth title at 17. He briefly studied physics and computer science at Queen's University Belfast before drifting into the Lyric Players' Theatre — a circuitous start to a Hollywood career.
✗ Wrong town. The answer is Ballymena, in County Antrim. Belfast is where he later studied at Queen's University. Derry/Londonderry and Armagh are other Northern Irish cities he had no early link to. Ballymena's hard-working, predominantly Protestant character — Neeson grew up as one of the only Catholics on his street — informed his early sense of being an outsider, something he's said in interviews shaped his acting choices.
QUESTION 2 / 8THE OSCAR
02
Neeson's breakthrough Hollywood role came in 1993 as the title figure in Steven Spielberg's Holocaust drama — a charming, womanising German industrialist and Nazi Party member who saved roughly 1,200 Jews from extermination by employing them at his enamelware factory in Krakow. The role earned Neeson his only Best Actor Oscar nomination to date. Name the character.
✓ Correct! Oskar Schindler. Spielberg's first choices included Warren Beatty and Harrison Ford; Neeson got the call after Spielberg saw him in Anna Christie on Broadway. The film won seven Oscars including Best Picture; Neeson lost Best Actor to Tom Hanks for Philadelphia. Schindler's List remains the project Neeson cites in interviews as the role that altered his career trajectory and his sense of what film could do.
✗ Wrong man on the list. The answer is Oskar Schindler. Itzhak Stern, his Jewish accountant and conscience, is played by Ben Kingsley. Amon Goeth, the murderous SS commandant of Plaszow, is Ralph Fiennes — in the role that broke him into Hollywood. Poldek Pfefferberg is the real-life survivor whose lobbying convinced novelist Thomas Keneally to write the source book in the first place.
QUESTION 3 / 8THE PREQUEL
03
Six years after Schindler's List, Neeson played the wise, slightly-rebellious Jedi Master who discovers a young Anakin Skywalker on Tatooine and is run through by Darth Maul during a triple-saber duel on Naboo in The Phantom Menace (1999). George Lucas wrote the part as the audience's emotional anchor in a crowded prequel cast. Name the character.
✓ Correct! Qui-Gon Jinn. Lucas cast Neeson specifically for his gravitas, saying he needed someone who could carry the kind of authority Alec Guinness had brought to Obi-Wan in 1977. Neeson has reprised the voice in The Clone Wars, Star Wars Rebels, Tales of the Jedi and Obi-Wan Kenobi (2022) — making him one of the few prequel-era actors with steady ongoing Lucasfilm work.
✗ Wrong Jedi. The answer is Qui-Gon Jinn. Obi-Wan Kenobi (Qui-Gon's apprentice in the prequels) is Ewan McGregor. Mace Windu is Samuel L. Jackson. Count Dooku, who turns up in Attack of the Clones and Revenge of the Sith, is Christopher Lee. Neeson is Qui-Gon — killed off at the end of Episode I but voice-resurrected across half a dozen later projects.
QUESTION 4 / 8THE PHONE
04
In Taken (2008) — the Luc Besson-produced, Pierre Morel-directed EuroCorp thriller that turned 56-year-old Neeson into a late-career action star — Bryan Mills warns his daughter's kidnappers over the phone that he has “a particular set of skills” acquired over a long career. What was Bryan Mills' former job?
✓ Correct! CIA operative — what Bryan Mills calls a “preventer” in the phone-call monologue itself: “I was an operative for the government — a preventer. I prevented bad things from happening.” Taken cost about $25M to make and grossed nearly $230M worldwide, and it almost single-handedly invented a sub-genre — aging-actor-as-action-hero — that gave Neeson a string of follow-ups (Unknown, Non-Stop, Run All Night, The Commuter).
✗ Wrong skill set. The answer is CIA operative. Bryan Mills calls himself a “preventer” in the same scene as the famous monologue. He's not Marine or FBI or Mossad — he's ex-CIA, retired to LA to be closer to his daughter Kim (played by Maggie Grace). Neeson reportedly took the part thinking it would be a small French production no one would see; instead it kicked off a 15-year action-thriller career arc.
QUESTION 5 / 8THE WIFE
05
Neeson met his wife on the 1993 Broadway revival of Eugene O'Neill's Anna Christie, in which she played the title role and he played her sailor lover. They married in 1994 and had two sons, Micheál and Daniel. She died in March 2009 from an epidural hematoma after a beginner-slope skiing accident at Mont Tremblant, Quebec. She came from one of British theatre's great acting dynasties. Name her.
✓ Correct! Natasha Richardson. Daughter of Vanessa Redgrave and director Tony Richardson, sister of Joely Richardson, niece of Lynn Redgrave. She won a Tony in 1998 for Cabaret. The Mont Tremblant accident initially seemed minor — she walked away laughing — but she developed a fatal brain bleed hours later and died March 18, 2009 at 45. Neeson has called her death the central catastrophe of his life and credits returning to work on The Next Three Days and The A-Team as what kept him moving through it.
✗ Wrong Redgrave. The answer is Natasha Richardson, his wife of 15 years. Vanessa Redgrave is her mother — and Neeson's mother-in-law, who he remained close to. Joely Richardson is her sister, also an actress. Helen Mirren is unrelated to the family. Natasha and Liam met on Anna Christie in 1993 and were married for 15 years until her death from the skiing accident in 2009.
QUESTION 6 / 8THE LION
06
Across The Chronicles of Narnia film trilogy (2005's The Lion, the Witch and the Wardrobe, 2008's Prince Caspian, 2010's The Voyage of the Dawn Treader), Neeson lent his deep, gravelly baritone to a CGI character — the Christ-figure lion ruler of Narnia. The first film's director, Andrew Adamson, cast him because the voice had to feel both kingly and tender. Name the character.
✓ Correct! Aslan, the great lion. The Narnia casting drew complaints from some C.S. Lewis purists when Neeson commented in 2010 that Aslan was “an all-encompassing spiritual figure” comparable to Buddha and Mohammed as well as Christ — Lewis's stepson Douglas Gresham publicly disagreed. Reepicheep, the swashbuckling mouse in the second and third films, is voiced first by Eddie Izzard and then by Simon Pegg. Mr. Tumnus the faun is James McAvoy.
✗ Wrong Narnian. The answer is Aslan. Reepicheep, the chivalrous swordsman mouse, is Eddie Izzard (Caspian) then Simon Pegg (Dawn Treader). Mr. Tumnus, the faun who befriends Lucy, is James McAvoy. The White Stag is the magical animal whose chase ends the first film. Aslan is Neeson — one of his most-loved family-friendly roles, and the only character he plays purely with his voice.
QUESTION 7 / 8THE WOLVES
07
In Joe Carnahan's bleak 2011 survival drama, Neeson plays an oil-rig wolf-hunter named John Ottway who survives a plane crash in the Alaskan wilderness and is gradually picked off, with the rest of his crew, by a pack of timber wolves. The closing scene shows him taping broken bottles to his fist and squaring up against the alpha. Name the film.
✓ Correct! The Grey. Carnahan and Neeson shot in -40°C conditions in Smithers, British Columbia. Neeson has said it's the closest he's come to a film that mirrors his own grief over Natasha's death — Ottway opens the movie writing a suicide letter to a wife the audience eventually learns has died. The famous final scene cuts to black before the fight resolves; a brief post-credits stinger shows the alpha wolf wounded, suggesting Ottway lands at least one blow.
✗ Wrong cold-weather Neeson. The answer is The Grey (2011). Cold Pursuit (2019) is the snowplough-driver-turned-vigilante remake of Norwegian film In Order of Disappearance. A Walk Among the Tombstones (2014) is the Lawrence Block adaptation set in NYC. Run All Night (2015) is the third Jaume Collet-Serra collaboration. The Grey is the wolves-and-Alaska one — arguably his most acclaimed late-career performance.
QUESTION 8 / 8THE COMEBACK
08
In 1990 — three years before Schindler's List — Neeson took his first major Hollywood lead as a disfigured scientist in Sam Raimi's first studio film: a Universal-released comic-book pastiche about a chemist who develops synthetic skin and uses it to impersonate his enemies. Critics now read it as Raimi's audition reel for the studios that would eventually hand him Spider-Man. Name it.
✓ Correct! Darkman. Raimi conceived it after failing to secure rights to The Shadow or Batman; he wrote his own pulp hero from scratch. The film made $49M off an $8M budget, spawned two direct-to-video sequels (without Neeson), and is now widely cited as the bridge between the Evil Dead Sam Raimi and the Spider-Man Sam Raimi. Frances McDormand co-stars as Neeson's girlfriend, the role that put her in the Coen-adjacent New York indie scene that led to Fargo.
✗ Wrong masked man. The answer is Darkman. The Shadow (1994, Alec Baldwin) and The Phantom (1996, Billy Zane) are the other early-90s pulp-hero attempts trying to ride Tim Burton's Batman wave. The Rocketeer (1991, Bill Campbell) is the Disney one. Darkman, with Neeson under a heavy bandage-and-burn make-up, is Raimi's original creation — and Neeson's first lead role in a Hollywood film.
The Verdict · Particular Set of SkillsYour Neeson Standing
☎️
/ 8
Ballymena boxer — or did you peak at Taken 2?
Now, Cold Storage has crossed two months (61 days) in the Top 10 overall movies and TV shows on MGM+ in the United States. As of today, September 16, Cold Storage is No. 7, ranking above SAS Rogue Heroes, World War Z, Insidious, and below A Tale of Two Cities, From, The Westies, The Shawshank Redemption, Deep Water, Project Hail Mary, and Cold Storage.
Before its sustained streaming success, Cold Storage was released in the United States on February 13 and suffered a slow theatrical run, grossing just over $4 million at the box office against an estimated production budget of approximately $10 million. Even so, Cold Storage reviews were positive, resulting in an 81% Rotten Tomatoes score, with critics calling it a clever yet familiar B-movie homage that serves up over-the-top performances, gooey gore, and tongue-in-cheek sci-fi humor with infectious energy.
Cold Storage also has a 75% audience score on Rotten Tomatoes.
The Film Remains A Unique One For Neeson
Cold Storage remains a rare outing for Liam Neeson, as he has starred in only a few notable horror movies throughout his career. His first was The Haunting in 1999, based on the 1959 novel The Haunting of Hill House by Shirley Jackson, which was later adapted into Mike Flanagan's 2018 miniseries. Neeson returned to horror a decade later for After.Life (2009) alongside genre regulars Christina Ricci and Justin Long.
With its mix of sci-fi and horror, Cold Storage gives Liam Neeson another chance to show off a side of his acting that fans rarely get to see.

Title: Why The Honeycrisp Apple Put Minnesota On The Map
Article_Text:
The Honeycrisp Apple Has a Pretty Incredible Minnesota Story
Minnesota may be better known for our lakes, loons, and legendary winters, but there’s another fall tradition where the North Star State has a surprisingly big claim to fame. One of America’s most beloved apples was developed right here in Minnesota, and its story is pretty darn sweet.
Much like watching the Vikings play football (or, in my case, the Packers), or putting something hearty like a pot roast in the crock pot, heading to an apple orchard during the autumn season is a yearly tradition for many of us here in the Land of 10,000 Lakes.
Minnesota Apple Orchards Make Fall a Beloved Tradition
If you're going to take part in this autumnal rite of passage, there are a lot of choices here in the North Star State. According to the United States Department of Agriculture's (USDA) Natural Resources Conservation Service, there are roughly 115–140 retail apple orchards operating across the state.
ALSO INTERESTING: Two MN and WI Oktoberfest Celebrations Named Some of the Best in the Entire Country
How Much Apple Production Does Minnesota Have?
Apple picking and apple sales are a big business here in the Bold North. Apples are a $14 million industry in the North Star State, according to the University of Minnesota, with commercial apple orchards currently operating in 78 of our 87 counties. All those orchards produce roughly 16 million pounds of fruit annually, the USDA says.
And while several other states produce way more apples than we do-- like Wisconsin, for instance, which produces nearly 39 million pounds every year-- Minnesota is a legitimate apple state. But we're particularly well known for cold-hardy varieties, including one very popular apple which was invented (or, more accurately, developed) right here, at the University of Minnesota.
Honeycrisp Was Developed at the University of Minnesota
That variety is, of course, the Honeycrisp. And Minnesota's Honeycrisp connection is huge. The Honeycrisp variety was developed at the University of Minnesota and released in 1991. That's helped give Minnesota an outsized reputation in the apple world, seeing as states like Washington, New York, Pennsylvania, and Michigan all grow way more apples than we do.
Plus, some of Minnesota's orchards have been highlighted as being some of the best in the country. Last year, USA Today's 10 Best Apple Orchard List nominated Pleasant Valley Orchard near Taylors Falls, Minnesota, as one of the top 10 orchards in the U.S.
So the next time you bite into an explosively crisp apple this fall, remember Minnesota's connection to one of the most popular varieties available. Another cool (literally!) tradition that many Minnesotans like to take part in during the fall season is checking out a corn maze. Luckily, our fair state has more than its share to satisfy your corn curiosity, as well. Keep scrolling to check out some of the best in Minnesota this autumn.

Title: Mississippi Honors Artistic Excellence With Five 2027 ﻿ ﻿Governor's Arts Awards Recipients
Article_Text:
The Mississippi Arts Commission (MAC), in partnership with the Governor’s Office, is pleased to announce the recipients of the 2027 Governor’s Arts Awards.
The 2027 recipients and awards are as follows:
Alvin Shelby, Lifetime Achievement
Doy D. Gorton, Excellence in Photography
Duwane Pendarvis, Excellence in Dance
Square Books, Arts in Community
Wright Thompson, Excellence in Literature
“Our recipients this year showcase the wide range of excellence in our artists and arts community in Mississippi, and we are privileged to honor them by sharing their stories,” said Lewis. “Their work has taken them from Mississippi to the world and back, extending to the top of ESPN, on tour with Sesame Street Live, to the White House, into the classroom, and through the pages of many books. We are eager to begin sharing their stories with you as we celebrate their contributions to the cultural landscape of our great state and our nation.”
The Governor’s Arts Awards are the highest award a living artist can receive in Mississippi. The awards recognize individuals and organizations for outstanding work in their artistic disciplines, arts-based community development, and/or arts patronage. This year, the awards celebrate 39 years of honoring artistic excellence in the state. MAC partners annually with the Governor’s Office to host the Governor’s Arts Award. The collaboration cultivates the important partnership between the arts and government.
The 2027 recipients will be recognized at the award ceremony on Thursday, February 11, 2027, at The Westin Jackson. A public reception will take place at 4:30 p.m., followed by the ceremony at 6 p.m., at The Westin Jackson. A one-hour program featuring all five recipients will air in Spring of 2027 on Mississippi Public Broadcasting.
About the Recipients
Alvin Shelby – Lifetime Achievement
Natchez, MS
Alvin Shelby is a music educator, music director, and performer with more than 40 years of experience, 35 of which he spent teaching at Cathedral Catholic School in Natchez, MS. Shelby has inspired numerous students who have gone on to pursue musical careers. He specializes in traditional inspirational music, but also enjoys writing and performing music for children, film, and jazz. He has worked with many great talents, including Lemmie Battles of the Chicago Mass Choir, Dr. Margaret Douroux of Los Angeles, CA, Dr. Princella Lee of Chicago, Elton John, Benjamin Cone, Tricia Walker, David Curry, the Mississippi Mass Choir, and many others. He has performed around the world, and his work has appeared in numerous television and film productions. He has also been band leader and musical director for many recording sessions, including Holy Family Gospel Choir in Natchez, MS, the award-winning program Southern Road to Freedom, and many others.
Doy D. Gorton – Excellence in Photography
Greenville, MS (currently residing in Carbondale, IL)
Doy D. Gorton is a photojournalist who worked as Chief Photographer of the Philadelphia Inquirer and Washington Photographer for the New York Times, covering the White House and Capitol Hill. Gorton attended the University of Mississippi, where he became engaged with the Southern Civil Rights Movement through Fannie Lou Hamer and John Lewis. He was the only white Mississippian on the staff of the Student Nonviolent Coordinating Committee (SNCC). During his time in SNCC, he decided to become a photographer. In addition to his journalistic work, Gorton shot the image used on the 1990 Fleetwood Mac album cover for “Behind the Mask” and was the photographer for “A River Runs Through It,” among other Hollywood and commercial projects.
Duwane Pendarvis – Excellence in Dance
Jackson, MS
Born in Jackson, Mississippi, Duwane Pendarvis is an accomplished dancer and educator whose career spans 50-plus years with performance experience in Concert Dance, European Tours, Festivals, Musical Theatre, and Television. Pendarvis embraced professional dance after earning a four-year music scholarship at Tougaloo College, training with renowned figures such as Gus Giordano and Joel Hall. He became a Principal Dancer and Assistant Director with the Joel Hall Dancers, touring nationally and internationally, and later gained experience with the Alvin Ailey American Dance Center and many others. For 30 years, the Joel Hall Dancers were his home. Pendarvis has choreographed, taught, and led programs in Chicago, Los Angeles, and his home state of Mississippi, including serving as Artistic Director of Joel Hall II and Resident Choreographer for Montage Theatre of Dance. In 2021, he launched Duwane Pendarvis & Company Dance Theatre.
Square Books – Arts in Community
Oxford, MS
Founded in 1979 by Richard and Lisa Howorth, Square Books is a general bookstore located on the historic town square in Oxford, Mississippi, home of William Faulkner and the University of Mississippi. With four stores and over 10,000 square feet on the square, all readers will find something to their liking. Square Books hosts over 150 author events per year and has many signed and collectible books, a very strong literary fiction section, and Southern fiction and history. The second floor of Square Books has a coffee bar so browsers can enjoy a cup and, when the weather is fair, relax on the balcony overlooking the courthouse.
Wright Thompson – Excellence in Literature
Clarksdale, MS
Wright Thompson is a senior writer for ESPN. His work has been anthologized in Best American Sports Writing more than anyone in history. He is the author of three bestsellers: “The Cost of These Dreams,” “Pappyland,” and “The Barn,” which was named Time Magazine’s non-fiction book of the year. He has won the Dan Jenkins Medal for Excellence in Sports Writing and the Ernie Pyle Award for international reporting (he’s been in war zones in Iraq and Ukraine). He has won two Emmy Awards for reporting, including one from Kyiv during the war. He is the executive producer and creator of “TrueSouth” on the SEC Network, the Emmy Award winning series that celebrates the South. His hero is Willie Morris. He is also a fifth-generation farmer in Bolivar County and a proud Mississippi resident. When asked why he lives here, when he works remotely, he often quotes Eudora Welty: “Because it’s home.”
MAC seeks sponsorship support annually to produce the Governor’s Arts Awards. If you are interested in sponsoring the awards this year to help honor these exceptional recipients, please contact communications@arts.ms.gov or visit arts.ms.gov/gaa.

Title: Robert Kraft says Ed Sheeran asked him to commit $2 million to Palestinian aid amid Macklemore controversy
Article_Text:
Robert Kraft says Ed Sheeran asked him to commit $2 million to Palestinian aid amid Macklemore controversy
The New England Patriots owner said Sheeran spoke to him about the donation before Macklemore invited him to match $1 million in net earnings that he pledged from the tour.
Macklemore on Wednesday pledged to donate the "entire $1 million" of his net earnings from Ed Sheeran's Loop Tour to Palestinian relief organizations, days after he was dropped from the tour over his pro-Palestinian comments.
He also invited New England Patriots owner Robert Kraft, who said Macklemore wouldn't be welcome at Gillette Stadium for the tour's scheduled performances at the end of September, to match his donation. Within hours, Kraft released a statement saying Sheeran had already asked him to match his $2 million donation to humanitarian aid in the region.
Their statements come amid a growing controversy following Macklemore's removal that has seen all of Sheeran's supporting acts quit the tour. Sheeran is set to play in Philadelphia this weekend.
Sheeran broke his silence about Macklemore's removal from the tour on Tuesday, saying it wasn't his decision but the promoter's. Macklemore's contract for the tour was with the promoter, Sheeran said.
Here's how the controversy began — and how it continues to unfold.
Sept. 4-5: Macklemore's performances at MetLife Stadium
Earlier this month, Macklemore performed as Sheeran's opening act at MetLife Stadium in New Jersey, where he made pro-Palestinian comments and performed his protest song "Hind's Hall."
The song was written after protests in support of Palestine occurred on college campuses across the U.S. in 2024, and is named after Hind Rajab, a 5-year-old Palestinian girl who was killed by Israeli troops in Gaza. Israel's military acknowledged in August that its troops had opened fire on the car carrying Hind and her family and said it had opened a criminal investigation into the killing.
"A big part of the reason why I wanted to do this tour in the first place is so I could stand up in stadiums like this and say two words that are very near and dear to my heart: 'Free Palestine,'" Macklemore said onstage earlier this month.
His comments drew criticism from pro-Israel groups including the Israeli-American Council, which started a petition to have the Grammy-winning artist dropped from the tour.
Macklemore was scheduled to perform at eight of Sheeran's 10 remaining shows on the Loop Tour, with Philadelphia being the next stop. After that, Gillette Stadium in Foxborough, Mass., is scheduled for performances on Sept. 25 and 26.
Sept. 14: Macklemore gets dropped from Loop Tour
In a lengthy social media post on Monday, Macklemore said, "Ed Sheeran and his team have made the decision to remove me from The Loop Tour." He described having difficult conversations with Sheeran, whom he considers "a brother."
Macklemore said Sheeran told him that Kraft, whose Kraft Group owns Gillette Stadium, didn't want Macklemore performing at the stadium over his pro-Palestinian comments. Sheeran also told Macklemore that Kraft had appealed to other stadium owners to issue him an ultimatum: "If Macklemore stays on the tour, you will not be allowed to play in our venues," according to the post.
Macklemore acknowledged that Sheeran was put in a difficult position.
The promoter, Messina Touring Group, confirmed in a statement to Rolling Stone that Macklemore won't perform on his remaining support dates because multiple venues wouldn't allow concerts to proceed with the rapper on the lineup.
Sept. 14: Robert Kraft responds
Kraft issued a statement to the media, saying that Gillette Stadium is responsible for providing a welcoming environment for all guests attending events at the venue.
"Based on Macklemore's recent actions, material shared from the stage during Ed Sheeran's shows in New Jersey, and a broader history of antisemitic rhetoric and imagery that we believe has been deeply offensive and hurtful to the Jewish community, we determined that his participation in the September 25th and 26th concerts at Gillette Stadium would cross that line," Kraft said in the statement.
"I agree with Macklemore. Too many lives have been lost and there has been too much suffering, but only sharing selective information and ignoring the actions of Hamas is not honest and only advances more divisiveness and hate," Kraft added.
Sept. 15: Ed Sheeran breaks his silence
As the controversy played out, Sheeran remained publicly silent. On Sept. 15, the pop star released a statement on social media, writing, "I am appalled by the conflict between Israel and Palestine. The suffering and pain caused on both sides is a human tragedy. There are too many wars across the world causing immeasurable pain, none of which should be tolerated."
Sheeran then explained that he preferred to remain publicly neutral on political issues and that Macklemore's removal wasn't his decision.
"Macklemore coming off tour was the promoter's decision, it was not mine. Macklemore's contract for the tour was with the promoter, not me," he wrote.
"I would never let down the fans who had made plans, nor would I abandon the touring crew and the other support acts and musicians who rely on me for work and to make a living," Sheeran wrote.
Sept. 15: Sheeran's backing band and supporting acts pull out of the tour
Sheeran's own backing band, Beoga — which had been performing several songs around the middle of each set — announced on social media that they would be departing the Loop Tour in light of Macklemore's dismissal.
"We believe in dialogue as a means of progressing the plight of the Palestinian people. … We are Irish people who understand colonialism. As founding members of the Irish Artists for Palestine movement, we are committed activists for justice and will continue to be."
Irish singer-songwriter Aaron Rowe announced in an Instagram post that he had dropped out as an opener on the tour.
"I don't take the decision lightly. Ed has been a friend to me and has changed my life, I could never thank him enough for this," the Irish musician wrote.
"But as Irish people," Rowe continued, "we know all too well about genocide, forced famine and violent occupation. I cannot stand by and allow billionaires to use their position of power to silence the rightful voices of those who speak up against Israeli genocide and who highlight the savage murder of children."
Danish pop band Lukas Graham also announced on Tuesday their withdrawal as a supporting act for Sheeran's tour.
Singer-songwriter Finneas also announced on Instagram that he was pulling out of the South American portion of the tour. "Artists must not be silenced when they speak up for the oppressed," he wrote. "I have decided to withdraw my upcoming tour dates with Ed Sheeran. I stand with Palestine and its people."
Sept. 16: Macklemore pledges $1 million to Palestinian relief groups. Kraft responds.
On Wednesday afternoon, the rapper wrote in a post on Instagram, "I will be donating the entire $1 million of my net earnings from Ed Sheeran's Loop Tour to six organizations working directly to support the Palestinian people."
He then encouraged Kraft to match his donation. "Whatever we disagree about, perhaps we can agree on this: Palestinian lives are worth protecting."
Macklemore added, "Writing a check is one of the least costly forms of solidarity available to me. I am doing it because I can, and because these organizations are doing the work while much of the world debates it."
Within hours of Macklemore's pledge, Kraft issued his own statement, saying, "I have dedicated much of my life to building bridges between all people. I believe deeply that all lives are worth protecting. Earlier today, before Macklemore challenged me to match his donation, Ed called me and asked me to commit $2 million to match his donation to aid in the region to fight this humanitarian crisis. Ed now plans to reach out to other venue owners and our goal is to continue to work together to build bridges.
"In addition, I'd like the people who are speaking in support of the Palestinian people to know that for decades, I have supported efforts that create opportunity for Palestinians and have brought young Palestinians and Israelis together to build businesses, create jobs, and forge relationships."
Sept. 17: Ticket sales collapse
Resale prices for the remaining Loop Tour dates began falling sharply. TickPick data cited by Forbes showed the cheapest ticket for Saturday's Philadelphia show at $51 on Friday morning, down from $100 on Tuesday. By Friday afternoon, StubHub listings had dropped to as low as $42.
Sept. 19: Sheeran returns to the stage in Philadelphia
Sheeran was scheduled to take the stage Saturday night at Lincoln Financial Field in Philadelphia, marking the first Loop Tour show since Macklemore's removal. The concert was pushed back from 5:30 p.m. to 8 p.m. ET after the openers dropped out, according to Ticketmaster. Music industry sources told TMZ Sheeran was prepared to perform solo, without his backing band.
A coalition of pro-Palestinian groups planned to rally outside the stadium at 4:30 p.m. Saturday. Speakers were set to include representatives from Writers Against the War on Gaza, the Boycott Cooknsolo Coalition and Shut Down Day & Zimmermann, according to a statement.
Sheeran had not commented publicly since Tuesday.

Title: Trump: Biden's FBI destroyed, altered Butler assassination attempt information – World Tribune: U.S. Politics and Culture, Geostrategy, China, North Korea, Corporate Watch, Media Watch
Article_Text:
Analysis by WorldTribune Staff, September 16, 2026 Non-AI Real World News
President Donald Trump said the Biden era FBI destroyed or altered key investigative information in the attempt on his life by would-be assassin Thomas Crooks at the July 2024 rally in Butler, Pennsylvania.
That, to quote the favorite word of Internet news headline writers, is a “bombshell.”
But what is wrong with this picture?
Why is America hearing this information from the president of the United States who was the target of this and several other assassination attempts? Is he the only U.S. Government official with burning curiosity about failed attempts on the life a U.S. president?
Are not Bob Woodward and Carl Bernstein still among the living? Why no leaks to CNN or the New York Times?
The president wrote in a post to Truth Social:
“Everybody knows the Crooked Joe Biden FBI didn’t do what they should have with respect to the Lunatic who shot me in Butler, PA. By the time I got into Office, on January 20th, most of the information was missing, altered, corrupted, or gone.
“New info was just found! Why wasn’t it seen long ago? This was all a Democrat Plot, to get me out of the Election, that failed.
“Dirty Cop Christopher Wray should pay a price for the way he handled this assassination attempt, and certainly for the things he said. GOD BLESS AMERICA — MAKE AMERICA GREAT AGAIN! President DONALD J. TRUMP.”
The FBI said during its 2024 investigation that it had not identified any co-conspirators or anyone with advance knowledge of Crooks’s attack.
Trump’s comments followed new reporting by the New York Post based on federal records provided to Senate Judiciary Committee Chairman Chuck Grassley as part of his investigation into the Butler shooting.
The records reportedly provide new details about Crooks’s growing interest in firearms and long-distance shooting before the assassination attempt.
“The trove of files includes FBI interviews with Thomas’ father, Matthew, who revealed he ‘never really had a father/son bond’ with the gunman, and that his stoic son rarely expressed strong emotions, hardly laughed and was very difficult to read,” The Post’s report said.
When he initially showed interest in firarms, during the pandemic, Thomas was a “terrible” shot — “he could not hit the paper [target],” his father told investigators, estimating it took 4-5 years of practice before he could even do that.
“Eventually, with practice, Thomas became a better marksman, coming home with range targets showing off to his dad how well he did with a target placed over 100 yards away,” the federal records obtained by The Post show.
After he questioned his son about why he was “going out so far,” Thomas explained, “he wanted to see how far he could shoot with rudimentary sights.”
He found he was able to shoot even further distances after he bought a prism sight, eventually becoming “very knowledgeable” about how to measure and zero-in on a target, and knew exactly how many clicks it would take to change the specific angle on the sight.
As Thomas’s interest in guns grew, he started buying large numbers of Amazon packages, including “parts, tools and items to increase the capacity of his rifle,” his father said.
Thomas sused the pseudonym “Bob Dole” for his delivery address, a bit of misguided paranoia he picked up after his father’s Citizens Bank checking account was hacked and several fraudulent BetMGM charges were made on his account.
Crooks’s father said he frequently caught Thomas talking to himself, a quirk that “became more noticeable over the years.”
Thomas “never showed interest in girls.” He “repeatedly denied” being gay over the years, his father said.
Crooks’s father mentioned the family was “racking” their brains trying to figure out why Thomas decided to make an attempt on Trump’s life, killing one rally-goer and severely injuring two others in the process.
Thomas “never showed any signs indicating something was wrong,” his father told investigators.
Also included in the documents provided by Grassley and obtained by The Post was one indicating an “anonymous donor” paid for the cremation of Crooks just days after the assassination attempt.
“Anonymous donor paid for cremation,” reads a note at the end of a summary of an interview the gunman’s father, Matthew, conducted with federal investigators.
The information appears to have been gleaned from a lawyer for the family, according to the document.
If he can’t get answers, who can? That is a major problem. pic.twitter.com/BOzQvHrUYC
— Liz Harrington (@realLizUSA) September 15, 2026

Title: Promac Group's Brandon Rainville eyes site on Route 5S in Florida | Business
Article_Text:
Travis Mitchell, of Environmental Design Partnership, presents conceptual plans for a 20,000-square-foot warehouse and office space with an equipment yard tentatively planned by Promac on Route 5S in the town of Florida on Monday, Sept. 14, 2026.
TOWN OF FLORIDA — A distributor of quarry, mining, landfill and waste management equipment plans to open its next dealership yard with maintenance facilities on Route 5S in the town of Florida.
Brandon Rainville, owner of Promac Group, said the company specializes in screening, crushing, hydraulic breakers, conveying, shredding, mixing and recycling equipment imported from global manufacturers such as Sandvik, Edge Innovate, Keestrack and Portafill.
“Most of it's manufactured overseas. We bring it in, do pre-delivery. It's a low-volume [business],” Rainville said.
Promac services North Carolina to Montreal from distribution sites in Middletown and Trainer, Pa. It just bought another facility in North Carolina. The tentative plan in Florida "fills the gap in this general area,” Rainville said.
Promac bought the approximately 28.5-acre property on Route 5S across from Cleveland Avenue four years ago for $307,308, Montgomery County property records show.
Travis Mitchell, managing partner of Environmental Design Partnership, briefed the Florida Planning Board on Monday on conceptual plans for a 20,000-square-foot warehouse and office space with an equipment yard at the site.
The use is allowed at the site in the town’s industrial business park zoning district. It would be served by on-site water and septic. Existing vegetation would provide screening around the property.
Rainville said the site would mostly operate during normal weekday business hours with around seven to 10 employees to start. He estimated it would receive around five heavy load deliveries a week. Smaller shipments delivered by carriers like UPS and FedEx may be more frequent.
“There'll be a parts business to support the equipment,” Rainville said.
The operations, Rainville said, will produce little noise at the site bordered at the rear by the state Thruway and next door to land targeted for solar development by Solar Energy Partners. There aren’t any nearby homes.
Planning officials didn’t have any qualms with the conceptual plans, giving their blessing to the project engineer to proceed to full design work subject to future board review.
“I don't foresee any huge issues with this project,” board Chair Stephen Viele said, noting the applicants would need to secure local and state permits as part of the approval process.
Mitchell indicated the full plans will likely be submitted within a couple of months. Rainville is targeting construction beginning as early as next spring.

Title: UNDERCOVER VIDEO: 'Shady as f**k' scheme paid people to vote for Talarico in 'roundabout way,' Soros PAC leader caught admitting
Article_Text:
L-R: Bill Clark/CQ-Roll Call Inc./Getty Images; Simon Dawson/Bloomberg/Getty Images

UNDERCOVER VIDEO: 'Shady as f**k' scheme paid people to vote for Talarico in 'roundabout way,' Soros PAC leader caught admitting
September 16, 2026
The committee manager smiles as he says Republicans would be very upset if they knew about the apparent scheme.
The head of a Texas political action committee has been caught on an undercover video apparently admitting how his group was able to pay voters indirectly to vote for the group's candidate for the U.S. Senate.
The undercover video, shared Wednesday, was recorded by Townhall and appeared to show Texas Majority PAC organizing manager Sky McAdams explaining how the scheme worked.
'If I was a Republican, I would be pissed. I would be like, that’s shady as f**k.'
"We are paying people $25 to attend a one-hour Zoom class to learn why voting is important and why the Republicans are causing all of these bad things," McAdams says, according to the video. "So it’s, like, a roundabout way of paying people for their votes, essentially. Which is interesting."
While paying voters directly would be illegal, McAdams seemed to admit that his program is "essentially" doing that indirectly.
"You can’t pay someone to vote for someone," McAdams continues, according to the video. "You can’t be like, ‘Here’s $25. Go vote for me.’ You can say, ‘Attend a one-hour class and you can receive $25.’ And then the class just talks about, like, the importance of it. It’s a little gray."
On the video, McAdams smiles and adds, "If I was a Republican, I would be pissed. I would be like, that’s shady as f**k."
The scheme is called a "paid relational program" that is run through software named "Rally" and operated by a company called "Relentless."
Texas Majority PAC was under investigation for allegedly funding state Democrats who fled Texas in order to block a vote on congressional redistricting. The group is funded in part by billionaire leftist George Soros.
Townhall posted the edited video on social media, where it was widely circulated.
RELATED: James Talarico shamelessly politicizes Amazon worker's tragic death to attack capitalism
In response to the video, Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton, Talarico's Republican opponent, said, "Absolutely outrageous! James Talarico's team just admitted they are trying to bribe people for votes. Texans aren't for sale, no matter how much James Talarico thinks they are."
A Texas Majority PAC spokesperson told Blaze News that McAdams had misrepresented the program and has since been fired.
"Participants in the program are being paid for grassroots organizing work," the spokesman added in a statement. "The way it was described by one rogue employee is factually incorrect, not how we operate, and they were immediately fired."
Blaze News' requests for comment from Relentless and the Talarico campaign were not returned in time for publication.
Relentless claims on its website that it netted "47,533 Democratic votes" in other campaigns in Arizona, Georgia, Michigan, North Carolina, and Pennsylvania in 2024.
The Texas Majority PAC said in financial disclosures that it had spent $500,000 on services from Relentless. Townhall noted hypothetically that at $25 per vote, that sum could net about 20,000 ballots.
AG Paxton also oversaw the investigation into Texas Majority PAC.

Title: Trump faces rare Truth Social criticism for defending data centers
Article_Text:
President Trump posted on Truth Social this week that artificial intelligence and the data centers that power it “will be the Greatest Economic Development Engine in History — Bigger than Oil, Gold, Diamonds, or even the Internet.”
Many of the commenters on his AI posts disagreed.
In hundreds of replies to Trump’s Truth Social posts this week, commenters criticized his enthusiasm, offering a social media snapshot that mirrors recent polling, which shows that Republicans are increasingly concerned about the technology. The New York Times analyzed thousands of comments on Trump’s posts to create a snapshot of what his most loyal supporters are thinking about his pro-AI stance.
Truth Social, which Trump created in 2022, has a user base that is relatively small compared with other social networks, with about 6 million users. But it remains a vital social space for Trump’s most ardent supporters, who typically create an enthusiastic echo chamber for the president’s ideas and rarely register opposition in big numbers.
Overall, the number of comments disparaging AI and data centers outnumbered those supporting the technology by nearly 4 to 1, the analysis showed. Many of the comments criticizing the president came from users whose profiles suggested they were otherwise staunch Trump supporters and members of his MAGA movement. Hundreds of other comments included only images or memes, which were not analyzed, or did not directly address data centers or AI.
The Times used an AI tool to help classify the sentiment of the posts and each user’s profile.
Some of the pushback on Truth Social has focused on the intrusion that data centers impose on rural areas, where more Republicans tend to live than Democrats. Data centers are massive installations that are increasingly being built in rural areas, particularly in the South. A few users suggested Trump build a data center at Mar-a-Lago, his Florida estate, to get a better taste of the disruption. One commenter criticized data centers and AI as tools of mass surveillance.
The explosive pushback is the latest sign that AI and data centers have become a thorny issue for Republicans this midterm season — a rare topic in the campaign that has united the majority of Americans in common concern.
A poll published Tuesday by the Times and Siena University found that a majority of likely voters oppose building data centers, but that Republicans, while divided on the issue, were still more open to them than Democrats or independents. The poll found that 49 percent of Republicans supported such construction while 47 percent opposed it. Three quarters of Democrats and 60 percent of independents opposed them.
Polling from Pew Research Center in November also showed that concern over AI more generally has grown since 2021, rising to half of all Republicans in 2025, up from 45 percent in 2021.
“It really doesn’t play well to his base because a lot of those folks are probably worried about AI taking their jobs,” said Raymond La Raja, a professor of political science at the University of Massachusetts Amherst, who has also conducted polling on the issue.
La Raja added that even if Trump’s base agreed with the president’s stance on AI, that support may quickly erode. “If things start to unravel with AI and we start seeing major social disruptions, you’re going to see him do a quick reversal,” he said.
The growing concern over data centers has prompted some politicians, including many Republicans, to push back on their development in tight midterm races.
The issue has become a top concern in Pennsylvania’s governor race, where Josh Shapiro, the Democratic incumbent, and Stacy Garrity, his Republican challenger, have battled over who opposes data centers more. Shapiro signed an executive order seeking stricter guardrails for their development, while Garrity has vowed to pause such developments if elected.
A fresh wave of concern burst into public view last week when a researcher at Anthropic, an AI company, quit over fears that the technology was advancing at a dangerous pace.
Trump responded Monday, posting on Truth Social that guardrails were not needed for AI because the United States was led by a “STRONG AND SMART (High IQ!) PRESIDENT.” By midday, he posted that AI was “the Golden Goose” and should not be killed. Then, in the early afternoon, he posted that fears about AI “taking over the World, destroying Humanity, and all other things bad” were nothing more than “a HOAX” — similar, he said, to two impeachment efforts against him and the federal investigation into his campaign’s interactions with Russia in 2016.
His comments drew immediate pushback.
Even some supporters who saw the logic of Trump’s support feared what would happen after he left office, giving other leaders control over AI’s future.
The pushback resembles what happened after Trump started a war with Iran this year and then posted about it online. Many users stormed the replies, disparaging his actions and expressing remorse about having once supported him as “the peace president.”
This article originally appeared in The New York Times.

Title: Man connected to missing Washington, DC, woman faces new gun charges in Beaver County
Article_Text:
The father of a 10-year-old boy whose mother has been missing from the Washington, D.C., area for nearly two weeks was in court Wednesday afternoon after police arrested him in Brighton Township on a parole violation Saturday morning.
Russell Ashford was supposed to have a hearing to be transported back to the D.C. area, but just 30 minutes before the hearing, Pennsylvania State Police filed charges against him for illegal gun possession.
Ashford is the father of a 10-year-old boy, whose mom, Antoinette Forbes, has been missing for almost two weeks.
Ashford was convicted five years ago for assaulting Forbes, punching her more than a dozen times.
“This was the underlying charge that prohibited him from possessing a firearm,” Beaver County District Attorney Nate Bible said.
He was arrested Saturday in Brighton Township for violating parole on that case. He wasn’t allowed to leave the state. The DA said license plate readers tracked him from D.C. back to Western Pennsylvania.
During their investigation, police said a local woman called them on Tuesday after Channel 11’s reporting on Ashford’s arrest Monday.
Police said she and Ashford had been dating on and off for three years. She hadn’t seen him since July but spoke to him last Wednesday.
She knew he had older children but was “shocked” to learn about his 10-year-old son. She also told police she didn’t know about the assault charges against him.
Police said the woman said in June 2025, he was moving out of his apartment at Bridgewater Crossing and going to D.C. She said he brought guns to her home. She said she didn’t think anything of it, because Ashford told her he was retired from either the FBI or the CIA.
Police took seven of Ashford’s guns from that woman’s home: Two pistols, two shotguns and three rifles.
Now, this case has to be tried in Beaver County before Ashford can be transported to the D.C. area on the probation violation charge.
“He’ll probably be in the Beaver County Jail for the foreseeable future,” Bible said.
Ashford has not been charged in Forbes’ disappearance.
Her family and friends aren’t giving up hope that she’s found safe.
“We’re focused right now on just continuing to call on the public for help in checking cameras and spreading her picture as far and wide as we can because it’s going to be, you know, somebody, you know, seeing it who has something that can help,” said longtime friend Holly Wetzel.
Ashford is scheduled back in court on September 28 for a preliminary hearing on the gun charges.
Friends and family have launched a GoFundMe campaign to help in the search for Antoinette Forbes.

Title: Hawks coach Justin Tatum opens up on sacrifices and fatherhood | Southern Highland News
Article_Text:
As Australians celebrated their fathers earlier this month, Illawarra Hawks head coach Justin Tatum was in Bendigo for the pre-season NBL Blitz, almost 17,000 kilometres away from his three children.
Subscribe now for unlimited access.
or signup to continue reading
Tatum knows being away from his kids and family is a big sacrifice he has to make to follow his dream.
And while he loves his job and the city of Wollongong and surrounding suburbs, and considers his Hawks players and staff as family, there isn't a day that goes by when he doesn't think about his children and family back home.
The 47-year-old hasn't admitted this publicly, but Tatum considered quitting the Hawks after guiding them to a championship title to return home to the US and be with his son Jayson Tatum, after the Boston Celtics star tore his Achilles tendon.
More on that later.
Tatum spoke to the Illawarra Mercury this week before the Hawks tip off their NBL27 campaign in New Zealand on Sunday against the Breakers, on a range of issues outside of basketball, from fatherhood and missing his family to his recent comments about African American fathers of NBA players, which drew the ire of the NBA.
In Jayson Tatum's own words, his father was and is the biggest basketball influence in his career.
The man Hawks fans and players call JT was a basketball coach who wanted his son to follow in his footsteps.
Tatum was his son's first coach and the one who pushed him to greatness.
But Tatum feels that the NBA often highlighted a "single mother" narrative while overlooking the role many fathers have played in their children's success.
Speaking on The Ultimate Dads Unplugged podcast, Tatum reflected on his own experiences during the 2017 NBA Draft, where he was seated next to Jayson's mother, Brandy Cole, during interviews but felt largely ignored.
"I've seen it when it started with the draft. Mom got interviewed, and sitting right next to her, nothing was asked of me.
"We know what it took for us to get our kids there, and if stuff like this is going to break me, then I don't need to be around. It is messed up, but I know my son, how much he cares and loves me, and he knows what we've been through. As long as that matters, I'm good," Tatum said on the podcast.
Why Tatum offered to quit Hawk
The Hawks coach has continued to be there for all his kids, including Boston Celtics star Tatum, in the immediate aftermath of his Achilles injury.
ESPN reporter Marc Spears reported that the Hawks coach, who was coaching in Indonesia after Illawarra's NBL championship win, also offered to quit coaching and be with his son in his time of need.
It took a phone call from Tatum to help his son get on track with his rehab.
"They cried on the phone together, and Jayson was asking him, 'Why me, Dad? Why me? Why does this have to happen to me?'. And he said, 'Son, this is God's will. You're young; you're gonna get through this," Spears, who spoke to Tatum at the time, said.
"He asked Jayson, 'Do I need to come home? I'll leave Asia right now and go home right now.' And Jayson said, 'No, Dad, stay there and coach, ' the NBA Hall of Fame reporter said.
Less than a week out from the start of the NBL27 season, Tatum was hoping to put those comments about the NBA to bed, but was happy to clarify his stance to the Mercury.
'Not belittling single mothers'
"I just gave an example of an incident where I felt that I was isolated at one time. I mean, whatever the NBA feels that they do with isolating dads or the media or the public feels that the NBA is not doing enough for dads. That's not my concern," Tatum said.
"I was just asked about a specific situation where I felt that they could have done better.
"I've been a big supporter of my son and continue to be.
"The only person that they felt they should have acknowledged was his mom when we were sitting right next to each other.
"And so I just kind of wanted to tell that story.
"At the end of the day, I felt the media could have done better by acknowledging both parents.
"When the system didn't do it, it is what it is. My son is still doing what he's doing, and I'm still supporting him because I don't want to be a negative part.
"I don't want him to have to answer anything negative about his family background that he has nothing to bring up.
"Everything got misconstrued in some ways, but there was a lot of support in a lot of ways as well.
"I don't have any disregard or no comment about what the NBA may or may not be doing with dads.
"I had a certain situation where I felt the NBA could have done better, and that's it.
"I don't want my son to have to answer questions about it at media day in a couple of weeks because that was 10 years ago.
"I'm not trying to belittle single mothers. I'm not trying to say single fathers are the best.
"I just told my story. That's it."
The cost of on-court success
The charismatic Illawarra Hawks championship-winning head coach's concern this week was about best preparing his team for Sunday's NBL season-opener in New Zealand.
But the NBL 2024-25 Coach of the Year also took time to reflect on his life on and off the court here in Wollongong since arriving as an assistant to Jacob Jackomas in April 2023.
Tatum took over the reins following Jackomas' sacking in November after a 2-7 start to the season.
After guiding the Hawks to a fairy-tale finals campaign, the American shed the interim tag in February 2024 when he signed a three-year deal to be the foundation club's new head coach.
His first full season in charge was a history-making one for the Hawks and Tatum, who guided Illawarra to just its second title in 47 years.
Emotional toll
Off the court, Tatum was missing his family, especially in the early days.
"I never imagined being away from home would affect me so much. But it did, especially in the early days in 2023," Tatum said.
"It was tough because I'd been around my family for so long, and not having them or being able to see them or interact with them had some wear and tear on me.
"As a son to my mom, having kids, and something that you normally do with them every day was taken away because a job brought me over here.
"But over the years being out here, it has gotten better. It's still tough, my first month or so being out here, but when basketball picks up, and I kind of get into a regimen, it improves."
"But there's not a day I don't think that I wish I could be home or wish I could pick my daughter up or take her to school or go see my grandsons or my son's game.
"It crosses my mind every day, but I know the support that they give me, and I also know I had to get used to being out here.
"It's always a difficult task every day, but it's something I got accustomed to."
It takes a village
Tatum credits his own upbringing and the village of people he relies on for how he raises his own children.
Tatum was only 19 when his first child, Jayson, was born.
"I wasn't the most financially well-off. I wasn't the most experienced dad, because you can't be at age 19 having a kid," he said.
"A lot of things that I knew I took out of my daily life or what my mom taught me.
"It does take a village, and dads have got a role to play in that.
"My mom was extremely helpful.
"I had a ton of family when my grandma was alive. I also had aunts and uncles; everybody was a part of that journey.
"I'm the father of the kids, but at the end of the day, I couldn't do that without the village I had, because they were very supportive of me having a kid at a young age.
"Instead of abandoning me or being disappointed, they were supportive.
"That was something that made it easier for me in life to do the same thing for my kids."

Title: Macklemore donates 1m dollars from Ed Sheeran tour to Palestinian charities
Article_Text:
Macklemore donates 1m dollars from Ed Sheeran tour to Palestinian charities
US rapper Macklemore has donated his entire net earnings from Ed Sheeran’s Loop Tour – one million US dollars (£747,328) – to charities supporting Palestinian people.
The donation comes after the musician was dropped as a supporting act over comments he made about Gaza.
Since then, all of Sheeran’s Loop Tour supporting acts, including Irish singer Aaron Rowe, Grammy award-winning musician Finneas, who is Billie Eilish’s brother, and Danish singer Lukas Graham, as well as his backing band Beoga, have dropped out of the remaining dates.
In a post shared on Instagram on Wednesday, Macklemore, real name Ben Haggerty, said: “With everything that has happened over the last 48 hours, I want to bring the conversation back to where it belongs: to the Palestinian people who are still being killed, still living under military occupation, and still fighting for their freedom.
“I will be donating the entire 1 million (dollars) of my net earings from Ed Sheeran’s Loop Tour to six organisations working directly to support the Palestinian people.”
On Monday, the rapper claimed that Robert Kraft, whose Kraft Group owns the Gillette Stadium that they were due to play in, had contacted Sheeran and told him they would not be able to play unless he was removed from the tour.
He invited the US businessman to match his donations adding that “whatever we disagree about, perhaps we can agree on this: Palestinian lives are worth protecting. A Palestinian life is no less valuable than any other life on this earth”.
He said: “Aid alone cannot address the conditions that make it necessary. This is a manmade injustice and I believe it requires immediate political change.
“Palestinians have lived for decades without basic rights and should not have to wait another day to be free. This is where my focus will remain.”
The rapper donated to the Palestine Children’s Relief Fund (PCRF), HEAL Palestine, Gaza Soup Kitchen, Medical Aid for Palestinians, UNRWA USA and American Near East Refugee Aid.
On Tuesday, Sheeran said on social media that Macklemore’s departure from the tour was the promoter’s decision and not his.
He said “upcoming tour dates had communicated that they would pull the shows if he was still supporting”, and added that Kraft, was among them.
Sheeran added: “I am not complicit. I have my personal views on this devastating conflict.”
The Shape Of You singer said he was “appalled by the conflict between Israel and Palestine”, and added he respected Macklemore “as an artist”.
In a previous statement shared by Kraft, the businessman said his decision to ban the US rapper following his comments onstage were due to a “broader history of antisemitic rhetoric and imagery that we believe has been deeply offensive and hurtful to the Jewish community”.
Sheeran’s next performance is scheduled for September 19 at the Lincoln Financial Field in Philadelphia, where Graham and Rowe had been due to open for him.
He has 17 dates still left on the tour across North and South America, with the final show scheduled for December 11 in Mexico City.
