Title: Gas prices debate continues in Congress. Can Washington lower costs?
Article_Text:
Gas prices debate continues in Congress. Can Washington lower costs?
Lawmakers in Washington are trading blame with officials from President Donald Trump’s administration as gas prices have continued to rise since the United States and Israel launched joint military strikes against Iran.
The average price of a gallon of regular gas in the U.S. on Wednesday, Sept. 16, was $4.36, according to AAA. That’s up from an average of $4.22 one week ago on Sept. 9, and $3.16 one year ago on Sept. 16, 2025, the group said. The average price of diesel fuel on Wednesday, Sept. 10, was $6.31, according to AAA.
Oil prices have spiked amid continued escalation in the war between the United States and Iran. Futures for Brent crude oil, the international benchmark, reached about $106 per barrel on Wednesday, Sept. 16. Futures for November delivery of West Texas Intermediate, the U.S. benchmark, were trading at around $103 per barrel.
Patrick De Haan, Head of Petroleum Analysis at GasBuddy, said in post on X that gas and diesel prices are both expected to continue rising as the Iran war continues.
“We may set a new 2026 high for average gas prices by the weekend,” he wrote. “Currently $4.371/gal and climbing, previous high $4.566/gal. diesel average at $6.315/gal and climbing, could hit $6.50/gal in the next 48 hours.”
With that in mind, the USA TODAY Cars team took a look at what lawmakers and Trump administration officials were saying about the current gas prices and what Washington could realistically do to lower prices.
What are lawmakers saying about high gas prices?
Democrats in Congress have pummeled the Trump administration over high gas prices since the administration launched the war with Iran, which resulted in the closure of the Strait of Hormuz, the channel through which most gas from the region previously flowed.
Maxine Waters, a California Democrat, said in a hearing of the U.S. House of Representatives House Financial Services Committee on Tuesday, Sept. 16: “Americans and small businesses feel the pain of your reckless economic policy. They’re paying sky-high prices for beef, gas, electronics and really everything around the kitchen table.”
Brad Sherman, another California Democrat, said: “The war has driven up gas prices and has driven up interest rates. Last year, I urged the administration to fill our Strategic Petroleum Reserve. They did not. As a result, we’ve not been able to respond to the Strait of Hormuz problem as effectively as we could.”
“Since the war started, gas prices are up 52%. Yes or no, are you aware of that?” Rep. Ayanna Pressley, a Democrat from Massachusetts, asked U.S. Treasury Scott Bessent in the same hearing.
“I think that’s not a good number,” Bessent replied, then added: “They’re lower than they were during the Biden administration.”
How has President Trump previously tried to lower gas prices?
In July, the White House touted the launch of 25 Freedom Fuel gas stations in the northeast United States, all selling fuel at $3.47 a gallon, to great fanfare. But the stations were concentrated in Pennsylvania and New Jersey, and they appeared to have little impact on prices at the pump in those states. The average price of gas in Pennsylvania on Sept. 10 was $4.45 per gallon, and the average price at the pump in New Jersey on Sept. 10 was $4.36.
Trump has also previously pressured gas retailers to lower prices at the pump, accusing them of price gouging at a time when oil barrel prices were starting to fall.
Trump has additionally been pushing Congress to pass legislation that would allow sales of higher-ethanol gasoline as U.S. lawmakers grapple with rising gas prices that have upset many Americans in an election year.
In an updated 2026 budget request sent to Congress on June 24, the White House requested a new law that would codify “the permanent, year-round sale” of E15 gas, which is gasoline blended with 15% ethanol. Doing so, the White House said, would amount to “an urgent and needed policy change that would expand consumer choice, support domestic fuel production, and provide additional flexibility in fuel markets.”
De Haan said in a blog post that gas prices are likely to remain elevated as long as there is an ongoing military conflict in the Middle East.
“While most of the country transitions to cheaper winter-blend gasoline this week, the scale of ongoing geopolitical escalations makes meaningful price relief unlikely in the near term,” De Haan wrote. “Motorists should brace for continued volatility ahead.”
What causes regional differences in gas prices?
Average gas prices in the U.S. on Sept. 16 ranged from $3.75 in Indiana to $6.04 in California, according to AAA.
Regional differences in gas prices can be explained by several factors, according to the U.S. Energy Information Administration. The agency listed the following reasons for regional gas price differences:
- Differences in state and local gas taxes
- Distance from supply
- Supply disruptions
- Retail competition and operating costs
- Environmental programs
“Retail gasoline prices tend to be higher the further gasoline must be transported to the point of sale because transportation costs are higher,” the agency said.

Title: Surgeon general nominee won't renounce RFK Jr. vaccine decisions – Roll Call
Article_Text:
Surgeon general nominee won’t renounce RFK Jr. vaccine decisions
Confirmation hearing of Nicole Saphier delves into measles, flavored vapes
Surgeon general nominee Nicole Saphier, seeking to be confirmed as the nation’s top health educator and spokesperson, on Wednesday declined to fully distance herself from the Trump administration’s changes to the childhood vaccine schedule when pressed by a prominent Republican.
During a hearing of the Senate Health, Education, Labor and Pensions Committee, outgoing Chairman Bill Cassidy, R-La., attempted to get Saphier on the record that the measles, mumps and rubella vaccine does not cause autism and that a universal recommendation for a hepatitis B vaccine at birth should remain in place.
Saphier would not openly refute the stances of Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. or President Donald Trump, both of whom have suggested a link between autism and the MMR vaccine.
The discussion occurred at the outset of a hearing to consider Saphier’s nomination. Also appearing were Chris Klomp, who’s nominated to be deputy HHS secretary, and Timothy Westlake, up for assistant HHS secretary for Mental Health and Substance Use.
Saphier attracted the heaviest questioning from senators, many of whom grilled her on whether she would knowingly spread misinformation if Kennedy asked her to do so.
“Well, humbly, I don’t know what causes autism, but I have not seen repeatable evidence that will suggest it causes autism,” Saphier said when Cassidy asked her if she believed that the MMR vaccine is a cause.
Cassidy interrupted Saphier to say her answer gave “too much wiggle room” and asked her to be more specific because nominees can “use wiggle room to do things that are quite contrary.”
Saphier told him that she did not believe the vaccines to be lethal, as Trump once suggested, and would recommend the shots, but she appreciated that some parents are skeptical of the vaccine and the Trump administration is trying to appeal to these people.
“I’m not sure that you reach people who are vaccine-hesitant by feeding into their own truths,” Cassidy responded. “The way to dispel confusion is not to sell more confusion.”
As for the hepatitis B vaccine, the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention’s vaccine panel in December voted to drop the universal recommendation that babies receive it at birth after Kennedy cast doubt on the validity of the shot. Cassidy, a longtime liver doctor who treated hepatitis, is a strong proponent.
A judge temporarily blocked the panel’s recommendations in March, including the change to the hepatitis B vaccine.
“I support universal hepatitis B vaccination,” Saphier told Cassidy. But she would not go as far as saying that Kennedy should keep the recommendation in place, much to Cassidy’s chagrin.
Vaping
When Sen. Susan Collins, R-Maine, asked Saphier about flavored vaping, the nominee again had to contend with the Trump administration versus conventional medical wisdom.
“As a physician, I don’t want anyone smoking anything. The lungs are very sensitive and they don’t regenerate,” Saphier said. She added that “if flavor [vapes] can entice an adult to quit smoking cigarettes, then maybe it’s something to be considered.”
In May, the Food and Drug Administration authorized four new fruit- and menthol-flavored vapes. Former FDA Commissioner Marty Makary deeply disagreed with the decision and resigned from his post soon after it was made. Rich Danker, a top HHS spokesperson, also resigned in protest of the vaping decision.
Sen. Tim Kaine, D-Va., said he was very disappointed in the administration’s shuttering of the CDC’s smoking cessation office. Sen. Lisa Murkowski, R-Alaska, added that Saphier’s past work as a social media influencer could help make her an effective anti-smoking spokesperson for the nation.
“I am as anti-smoking, anti-tobacco as you could imagine anyone to be,” Saphier responded.
Measles
Saphier’s appearance resembled Klomp’s at the Senate Finance Committee on Tuesday, where he toed the line between portraying himself as a trustworthy, policy-focused nominee while declining to fully distance himself from Kennedy’s vaccine policies.
In questioning Klomp on Wednesday, Cassidy pointed to four measles deaths in Pennsylvania. The CDC has yet to update its website to reflect these deaths, as Kennedy and Pennsylvania officials have feuded over whether they were a result of measles or other causes.
Cassidy said there’s a perception that the agency is “trying to dance around the sensitivities of [Kennedy] as opposed to being straightforward with the American people.”
Klomp said if confirmed, HHS would “address the operational shortcomings and create a clear definition of measles-related death.”

Title: Charlie Kirk's family alleges security failures contributed to his death
Article_Text:
The notice said: “Through a series of stunning failures and reckless decisions, the [Utah officials] created a foreseeable danger to Charlie.”
Sharon Turner, a spokeswoman for Utah Valley University (UVU), said the school was aware of the notice of claim, adding: “UVU addresses legal matters consistent with our established processes. Our focus remains on supporting our campus community.”
UVU said shortly after Kirk’s killing that it would seek an outside review of the event and the school’s response, but it had not yet released findings. Turner said officials expected the review to be completed soon.
UVU president Jon Anderson, who took over the position after Kirk’s death, recently told the Salt Lake Tribune: “When we get the report, it will be very comprehensive. And it’s just taken time to get it to that point.”
The notice of claim from Kirk’s family, sent to the Utah Attorney General’s Office last week, says authorities did not adequately prepare for Kirk’s visit to the state-funded university, despite his high profile and the violence against other political figures in recent years. 
They “did not conduct a meaningful risk assessment” before approving the outdoor event, the notice alleges, and UVU police did not have a written security plan for it.
The UVU police chief, Jeffrey Long, asked the university’s then-president to assign more than six officers – a fourth of the campus police force – to the event but was denied, according to the document.
It said: “Indeed, the UVU Parties’ planning was so deficient that when Mr Kirk was shot first responders were not available and Mr Kirk was transported to Timpanogos Regional Hospital in a private vehicle, not an ambulance.”
Kirk’s family representatives also say the importance of rooftop security should have been especially clear given that President Donald Trump – a friend and ally of Kirk – was injured by a rooftop shooter the year before. Trump was shot at a campaign rally in Pennsylvania.
Tools such as drones and real-time monitoring of CCTV footage could have helped prevent the shooting as well, the notice of claim said, noting that video footage presented in the criminal case showed the shooter running across the roof.
The Kirk family’s move to preserve their right to a lawsuit comes around the first anniversary of Kirk’s death. A judge recently ruled that the alleged shooter, Tyler James Robinson, will stand trial on charges that could carry the death penalty. A trial date has not been set.
Members of Kirk’s family, including his widow, Erika Kirk, have been attending hearings in Robinson’s case, and their representatives have emphasised the importance of a speedy trial.

Title: Cornell military community climbs to honor the 25th anniversary of 9/11 attacks
Article_Text:
News directly from Cornell's colleges and centers
Cornell military community climbs to honor the 25th anniversary of 9/11 attacks
By Grace DePaull
At 5:40 a.m., the steady sound of footsteps cut across the quiet of Cornell’s campus, a persistent rhythm that echoed through Schoellkopf Stadium in the hours just before sunrise. Under the glow of stadium lights, feet climbed concrete steps as sweat glistened on the faces of more than 200 cadets, veterans, staff and community members who had gathered on September 11 for a 9/11 memorial workout.
Held annually, the workout is organized by Cornell Reserve Officer Training Corps (ROTC) and honors the first responders who lost their lives during the attacks on the World Trade Center. In remembrance, participants moved through a 40-minute circuit of both stair climbs and strength exercises.
Among those taking part was Katherine McComas, vice provost for engagement and land-grant affairs and a professor in the Department of Communication. McComas oversees and supports Cornell’s ROTC programs and joined the workout for her second year.
“It gives you a burn in your legs,” McComas said. “And that burn is a privilege. It’s a privilege to feel the pain and not be in the same situation as those on September 11 but rather be alongside people who are coming together to remember and recognize that ultimate sacrifice.”
McComas’s connection to the military is personal. Her father served in Army ROTC at the University of Colorado, an experience that shaped his life and instilled in McComas a lasting connection to military and public service.
Over the past year, she has made a point of stepping outside her usual role to experience the environments, traditions and challenges that shape the students she supports. McComas visited military installations including Fort Knox, the Philadelphia Naval Yard and Joint Base McGuire-Dix-Lakehurst to deepen her understanding of the military community and better support Cornell's ROTC programs.
“I think it’s important to show that you’re willing to engage in the experiences that we’re asking our students to do,” McComas said. “For me, the workout is another opportunity to say, ‘I see you, I recognize you and we’re here today to do this together — as a community.’”
For many of the students participating in the workout, September 11, 2001, is history rather than a lived memory. For others, the events of that day are intertwined with their own military service or the experiences of those who served alongside them.
For Tony Roach, director of administration at the Meinig School of Biomedical Engineering and U.S. Navy veteran, the workout is one way those generations can come together.
“Sharing knowledge and experiences with the ROTC midshipmen and cadets before they go off into their service and lead is so important when it comes to passing the torch,” said Roach, who retired from active duty in 2022 but has remained active in Cornell’s military community as a member of the Veterans Colleague Network Group, an advisor to the Graduate Student Military Community and the Cornell Veterans House Community Fellow. “Most veterans really miss the camaraderie that comes with their military service. So, having the opportunity to recreate some of that connection is what I really value and what brings me joy."
Roach has been involved with the memorial workout for all seven years he has been at the university, first helping organize the event as the commanding officer of the Navy ROTC unit and now participating as a veteran and member of the Cornell community. Over those years, he has seen firsthand how deeply military service is woven into the fabric of the university.
“The veteran community here at Cornell is fantastic,” Roach said. “If you look back at the history of Cornell and when it was founded, there’s a connection to the military and veterans that I really had no understanding of when I first arrived. It’s really fantastic how deep and rich the history of this community is here at Cornell. It’s something I really value.”
By the time the workout concluded at 7:15 a.m., the steady rhythm of footsteps began to fade as participants moved into a cooldown, catching their breath and reflecting on the morning.
To close the memorial, Nathan Li ’27, Cornell ROTC Tri-Service Brigade commander, presented McComas with a folded American flag that had been flown over Barton Hall in recognition of her continued support of Cornell’s military community. The ceremony ended with the group joining together in one final shout: “Never forget,” echoing through the stadium.

Title: 2026 General Election: Key Voting Dates for Frederick County and Other Area Voters
Article_Text:
Voters across the region have several important dates to keep in mind ahead of the November 3, 2026, General Election.
Maryland
In Frederick, Washington, Carroll and Montgomery counties, the regular voter registration deadline is October 13. Voters who miss that deadline can still register and vote in person during early voting or on Election Day.
Early voting will be held October 22 through October 29, with early voting centers open from 7 a.m. to 8 p.m. Eligible voters who register during early voting must provide documentation showing their Maryland residence.
For mail-in voting, the deadline to request a ballot to be mailed or faxed is October 27. The deadline to request a ballot for print-at-home delivery is October 30. Completed mail-in ballots must be postmarked by November 3 or deposited at an approved drop box or local election board by 8 p.m. on Election Day.
Pennsylvania
In Adams and Franklin counties, the voter registration deadline is October 19. The deadline to apply for a mail-in or absentee ballot is 5 p.m. October 27. Completed ballots must be received by the county election office by 8 p.m. November 3. Pennsylvania voters can also apply for and complete a mail ballot in person at their county election office before Election Day. There is no early voting mechanism currently in place in Pennsylvania.
West Virginia
For voters in Berkeley and Jefferson counties, the voter registration deadline is October 13. Early voting runs October 21 through October 31. The deadline to apply for an absentee ballot is October 28, and absentee ballots generally must be hand-delivered to the County Clerk by November 2.
Virginia
In Loudoun County, early voting is scheduled to begin September 18 and continues through October 31. The voter registration and absentee-ballot application deadline is October 23. Virginia also permits eligible voters who miss the registration deadline to register and cast a provisional ballot through Election Day.
The General Election is Tuesday, November 3.

Title: A Hospitality Expert's Tips for Hosting Cozy Fall Gatherings
Article_Text:
Fall is hospitality expert Ruth McKeaney’s favorite time to entertain—and her historic home, a lovingly restored former dairy farm, makes the perfect backdrop. Gatherings are candlelit and dotted with pumpkins and gourds, and they last well into the evening.
It’s no surprise: Hillside Farm is the kind of place that makes you want to stay a while. But you don’t need a picturesque property to make guests feel welcome. Ruth’s timeless entertaining advice can help you offer that same cozy feeling for any autumn gathering you have planned.
Below, read on for Ruth’s tips to create a laid-back autumnal vibe inside and out.
Easy Fall Hosting Tips
- Look to the past: When decorating, take cues from a home’s history. In Ruth’s barn, baskets of firewood and wheelbarrows do double duty.
- Keep it casual: To immediately put guests at ease, be strategic with styling—no fussy tablescapes or perfect pumpkin stacks required!
- Just add flowers: Balance pumpkin arrangements by incorporating planters holding seasonal blooms—think asters, azaleas, or mums.
Fall Decor Ideas
Create an inviting vignette.
Experimenting with gourds of different shapes and sizes, from tall squash to round white pumpkins, ups visual interest. It adds “life, beauty, and gratitude to a home,” says Ruth. Design a perfect spot for portraits or selfies by situating it near a seating area.
Mix materials.
Sheepskin rugs draped on benches, cowhide underfoot—Ruth loves playing with texture in the barn’s dining area. “It warms up the space,” she says.
Provide places to chat.
Smaller seating areas can encourage guests to break into intimate groups. The home’s library is an ode to the West, where Ruth grew up.
Go with simple centerpieces.
Vases containing tall branches can create focal points on tabletops. Forage nearby for options. “Decorate with what the season gives you: squash, branches, linen, wool, and candlelight,” advises Ruth, author of Hungry for Home: A Year Together at Hillside Farm. “Nature has already chosen the perfect color palette.”
Feature treasured pieces.
When Ruth entertains, she loves to mix and match her ever-growing assortment of serveware, including heirlooms and estate sale finds. Pitchers become vases, antique teacups hold herbs or desserts, and mismatched glasses invite conversation.
This feature appears in the September/October 2026 issue of Good Housekeeping.
Monique Valeris is the home design director for Good Housekeeping, where she oversees the brand's home decorating coverage across print and digital. Prior to joining GH in 2020, she was the digital editor at Elle Decor. In her current role, she explores everything from design trends and home tours to lifestyle product recommendations, including writing her monthly column, "What's in My Cart."

Title: Republican senator faults Trump vaccine policy for measles deaths as panel weighs health nominees
Article_Text:
The Senate health committee’s Republican chairman on Wednesday blamed the approach toward vaccines taken by President Donald Trump’s administration for recent measles deaths in Pennsylvania and pressed the president’s pick for surgeon general to state plainly that vaccines do not cause autism.
Sen. Bill Cassidy, a Louisiana physician who chairs the panel, delivered the critical opening statement as the nation grapples with its worst measles outbreak in more than 35 years. Cassidy said three people in Pennsylvania have died of measles, with a fourth death under review, because of misinformation and misguided policies.
“To suffer from any disease is awful, but to suffer one which is avoidable, that’s even worse,” Cassidy said.
The committee weighed Trump’s nominations of Chris Klomp for deputy secretary of Health and Human Services, Dr. Nicole Saphier for surgeon general and Dr. Timothy Westlake to lead the Substance Abuse and Mental Health Services Administration. Cassidy said the country needs health leaders “who make decisions based on science, not politics or ideology.”
Cassidy directed his sharpest warning toward Saphier, repeatedly pressing her to say the measles-mumps-rubella vaccine does not cause autism. Saphier initially hedged, saying she had “not seen reputable evidence” that vaccines cause autism.
“That’s a little bit of an equivocation,” Cassidy said, warning that others had used such “wiggle room” to later act against scientific evidence.
Saphier eventually said she did not believe the MMR shot was lethal, calling it “our greatest tool for combating measles,” and said, “I do not believe childhood vaccines cause autism.”
U.S. Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. has long pushed a debunked link between vaccines and autism, contrary to scientific evidence, which Trump has also embraced.
Cassidy also pressed Saphier on the long-recommended hepatitis B vaccine at birth, which Kennedy wants to stop. Saphier called universal birth dosing “tried and true” but stopped short of saying it should be recommended.
Cassidy said vaccines are “overwhelmingly safe and effective, and they do not cause autism.” He also criticized a Trump executive order breaking up the childhood vaccine schedule for requiring more shots and making children less safe.
SENATOR GROWS MORE CRITICAL
Cassidy has become more openly critical of Kennedy’s efforts to overhaul U.S. vaccine policy despite casting the deciding vote confirming the health secretary to the post with full knowledge of Kennedy’s history of public anti-vaccine activism.
Cassidy is not up for reelection after losing his Republican primary in May. Trump targeted Cassidy and endorsed a rival over the senator’s 2021 vote to convict Trump at his second impeachment trial, making it politically easier for Cassidy to be defiant.
“CDC apparently is working on a definition of death by measles. Someone said we haven’t had to work on that for decades because no one has died from measles, and now we have people dying from measles. That’s going to be a terrible legacy for this administration,” Cassidy said.
HEALTH AGENCIES FACE LEADERSHIP GAP
Saphier, a radiologist and former Fox News contributor, is Trump’s third surgeon general pick, after wellness influencer Casey Means stalled in the Senate and Trump withdrew Dr. Janette Nesheiwat’s nomination over questions about her credentials. The United States has had no surgeon general since January 2025.
Klomp, a former health tech executive, has run much of HHS day-to-day, rising from Medicare director to chief counselor for Kennedy at the agency. The Finance Committee held his formal nomination hearing on Tuesday. Wednesday’s session is a courtesy hearing.
He drew the smoothest reception, with even his toughest Democratic questioners framing disagreements as areas for cooperation. Saphier faced the sharpest scrutiny, including from Cassidy over vaccines and Democrats on abortion. Westlake clashed with Democratic Senator Maggie Hassan over fentanyl test strips.
No Republican signaled a no vote, leaving all three on track to advance.
The hearing addressed the backlog of health vacancies across the administration. The Senate confirmed Dr. Erica Schwartz to lead the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention on August 5, while the Food and Drug Administration has lacked a permanent leader since May.
(Reporting by Ahmed Aboulenein Editing by Bill Berkrot and Will Dunham)

Title: Five Missing Women Linked To Major Investigation At Philadelphia Home
Article_Text:
Five missing women have now been connected to a growing investigation focused on a home in the Olney neighborhood of Philadelphia. Authorities say the case, which began after a suspicious car was found on Independence Mall on June 19, is centered on 44-year-old Eugene Horsch. Horsch’s residence on West Chew Avenue has been under close examination since June, and the investigation has drawn in federal agents and Philadelphia police detectives.
Among the five missing women is Nicole Fusaro, who disappeared in 2018 at age 27. Her cousin, Jonathan Halloran-Koren, told reporters that their family has been meeting with detectives. "Nicole was a beautiful, kindhearted woman who deserved so much better than what happened to her. She will forever be loved and missed by her family and friends," Halloran-Koren told WPVI.
Other women linked to the case include Gabrielle Amarando, who vanished in 2012 at age 22; Maribel Fresses, missing since 2018 at age 27; Blair Tonzelli, who disappeared in 2023 at age 35; and Amy McHale, last seen in 2016 at age 44. According to police, images and videos recovered from the property reportedly show Amarando and Fresses appearing to be deceased, though their bodies have not been found.
When Horsch was arrested, police say he was with a woman carrying an identification card belonging to Tonzelli. The woman allegedly told officers that Horsch had given her the ID. After the arrest, investigators found chemicals, drugs, firearms, and ballistic evidence at the home, as well as a 55-gallon drum connected to water lines and an underground pipe. Both are being tested for evidence, but police have not released further details due to the ongoing nature of the case.
The investigation has also turned up a handwritten note referencing serial killer Ted Bundy and methods for disposing of trash. Additionally, video evidence allegedly shows Horsch’s late father, Raymond Horsch, strangling a woman to death. That woman has not been publicly identified.
The Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI) has increased its involvement, with agents working to authenticate more than one million images recovered from the property. Eugene Horsch remains in federal custody on firearms charges, including possession of a weapon with an obliterated serial number and fake U.S. Drug Enforcement Administration and Federal Bureau of Investigation credentials. Police Commissioner Kevin Bethel has stated that a case update could come as early as this week, but no news conference date has been set.

Title: Treylon Burks depth chart plunge makes Commanders' stance clear before Week 2
Article_Text:
When Treylon Burks was listed as a starting wide receiver on the Washington Commanders' depth chart before Week 1 against the Philadelphia Eagles, many thought this could be the big opportunity he'd been waiting for. Just a few days later, that proved otherwise.
Instead of starting, Burks was a healthy scratch at Lincoln Financial Field. And he was listed behind Terry McLaurin on the Week 2 depth chart, not as the starting slot receiver.
Make of that what you will, but it's clear the coaching staff may not rate Burks as highly as fans believed earlier in the summer.
Treylon Burks' fortunes with the Commanders have taken a shift ffor the worse
Of course, depth charts don't mean much at this stage. One look at Burks' recent fortunes would tell you that. But being a healthy scratch with others preferred ahead of him for such a key game spoke volumes.
Burks is a squad piece and nothing more for now. And when his time does eventually come, it could be a do-or-die scenario.
This isn't what Burks had in mind when he signed a new deal with the Commanders this offseason. He was encouraged by his projected role within new offensive coordinator David Blough's scheme, and getting another shot gave the Arkansas product some much-needed stability after things fell flat with the Tennessee Titans.
That might still happen. But it's clear that Burks is already facing an uphill battle to stay relevant.
The Commanders have Terry McLaurin and Stefon Diggs as their top receiver duo. Rookie third-round pick Antonio Williams flashed immense potential on his NFL debut, and he is the No. 3 option after just one game. Jaylin Lane was the starting kick and punt returner, and Dyami Brown also got some time on the field after being preferred over Burks and Luke McCaffrey.
This was a harsh reality check for Burks. If there was ever a time to raise his effort and finally make the most of his outstanding physical attributes, it's now.
Treylon Burks cannot afford to become an afterthought with the Commanders
Anything less, and another new contract might not be forthcoming when the 2027 offseason arrives.
It's early days. A lot can happen in the coming months. All it will take is an injury, underperformance, and perhaps even a favorable matchup to get Burks back in the mix. And when that moment arrives, he must seize it.
Burks cannot afford to become an afterthought. The athletic gifts are there, but something is preventing the Commanders from giving him more responsibility. They have improved options in the passing game, but this is the sort of player who should be getting opportunities.
Therefore, it's a confidence issue. And it works both ways.
If Blough trusted him, Burks would be involved. It's not there right now, and the player just hasn't generated the momentum required. Until that changes, he might be watching from the sidelines a lot more.
This is a far cry from the optimism around Burks from just a few short days ago.
And the challenge facing the 2022 first-round selection cannot be overstated.
The Commanders are not running a charity. Everyone has to earn their playing time, from the franchise cornerstones to the depth pieces and everything in between. Competition for spots has increased, and the pressure is building to right last season's wrong.
Anyone going through the motions won't be involved. Burks is working hard, but recent events suggest he's pretty far down the food chain.
When, or if, that changes anytime soon might also be out of his hands.

Title: Commanders must feel validated by Von Miller's goose egg in Cowboys debut
Article_Text:
When the Washington Commanders opted not to bring edge rusher Von Miller back this offseason, they probably didn't expect him to land in the NFC East with the Dallas Cowboys. But after the veteran's debut goose egg, general manager Adam Peters should feel vindicated.
Miller played 11 snaps against the New York Giants on Sunday Night Football. He didn't register a stat at all as the Cowboys took a humbling loss at MetLife Stadium to start the campaign.
Nobody was expecting miracles from Miller. But such a lackluster output when he was so eager to make an immediate contribution for the Cowboys cannot be seen as anything other than disappointing.
Von Miller's regression is why Commanders didn't offer him another deal
The Commanders brought Miller in last season, and he finished as the team's sack leader as injuries decimated the defense. The future Pro Football Hall of Famer wanted to return, but Peters had other ideas. After taking his time before choosing a destination, he settled on Dallas, believing the squad could go deep into the playoffs.
Based on their opening-day efforts, those ambitions seem far off.
Miller didn't make a tackle. He didn't generate quarterback pressure. He isn't the dominant performer of old, but he wasn't the only Cowboys defender to fall flat with the national primetime audience watching.
Sound familiar?
The former Texas A&M game-wrecker chose the Commanders because he thought they were close to winning it all after reaching the NFC Championship Game. That didn't happen, and unless Dallas makes major improvements, Miller will have backed the wrong horse for the second straight year.
It's only Week 1. Anomalies happen as teams adjust to competitive games again, and opening weekend brings more shocks than any other. But for Miller and the Cowboys' defense, this inept showing mirrored the unit that dropped to laughable depths in 2025.
Commanders will be looking to limit Von Miller's influence in Week 2
The Commanders will be cracking a wry smile at Dallas' misfortune. Their new-look pass-rushing room caused havoc against the Philadelphia Eagles, and even though the result didn't go Washington's way, the explosiveness, creativity, and aggression under Daronte Jones were night and day compared to last season.
As for Miller? He'll look to make a bigger impression this weekend. And he shouldn't lack motivation.
Miller comes up against his ex-employers when Washington visits AT&T Stadium in what's quickly become a must-win game for two bitter division rivals.
Both lost in Week 1. Both cannot afford to start 0-2. And both have enormous personal pride on the line.
There will be revenge on Miller's mind. He left the Commanders on good terms, but he also felt bitterness that his pleas for a new contract went unanswered.
He'll be looking to make Peters pay for going in this direction. But despite the obvious concerns about the offensive line, Washington shouldn't have too much to worry about.
Miller had a debut to forget in Dallas. He's a little older, a little slower, and a little less responsive after the snap. But he will know the strengths and weaknesses of every Washington lineman in his path this weekend.
And if a 37-year-old Miller ends up torching the Commanders during whatever time he's on the field, they have much bigger problems than we thought.

Title: Trump's Wars, Both Real And Trade, Are Now Hiking Americans' Borrowing Costs, Too
Article_Text:
Trump’s Wars, Both Real And Trade, Are Now Hiking Americans’ Borrowing Costs, Too
WASHINGTON — President Donald Trump’s trade war against the planet and his real war against Iran have stoked higher inflation over the past year and have now increased borrowing costs for Americans, too.
Kevin Warsh, Trump’s handpicked Federal Reserve chair, cited “geopolitical” factors multiple times in his explanation for the central bank’s decision to raise interest rates by a quarter point, the first rate hike since 2023.
Politics: Trump Says He's Nominating Kevin Warsh To Lead The Federal Reserve
“The plain fact is that inflation is too high, and has been for too long. This summer’s inflation readings do not tell me that underlying trends have meaningfully improved,” Warsh said at a press conference Wednesday.
Warsh would not, when asked, comment on either Trump’s Iran war or his various import taxes on Canada and other nations.
“Part of the independence of the Federal Reserve is we stay in our lane. Independence is a two-way street. We let people that do trade policy and fiscal policy stay in their lane, too. That’s how we can stand up here and call them the way we see them,” he said, seeming to nod at likely criticism from Trump.
Trump, though, does not respect the independence of other institutions, particularly the Federal Reserve. He even threatened recently to cut off trade with some other countries entirely if the Fed did not do as he wanted and lower rates.
Politics: Tucker Carlson: Orders To Keep Epstein Files Under Wraps Came Straight From Trump
By late Wednesday afternoon, Trump had only posted a demand that the interest rate be lowered to 1% or less — the Fed’s new target is 3.75% to 4% — but did not attack the board or Warsh personally. “LOWER THE INTEREST RATES FOR THE UNITED STATES OF AMERICA, AND FAST!” Trump wrote two hours after the Fed’s announcement.
And two hours after that, he told reporters traveling with him to a campaign rally in North Carolina that he does not blame Warsh for the rate hike, but the others on the board.
“He’s got a hostile board,” he said. “They’re raising that only for political reasons, and that’s a raise against Trump.”
Trump also suggested he had collaborated with Warsh beforehand and gave him permission to vote with the others.
Politics: Trump’s War Already Costing Americans Tens Of Billions And It’s Getting Worse
“I told Kevin, I said, ‘You might as well vote with the board because it’s just not going to matter,’” he said.
Advertisement
The president, however, is a habitual liar, and it cannot be determined if he ever had any such discussion with Warsh.
Warsh had previously declined to comment on his previous conversations with Trump. “I don’t have anything for you on discussions with the president,” he said.
Like this article? Keep independent journalism alive. Support HuffPost.
Economists broadly have attributed rising inflation since Trump retook power to his global trade war, which increased prices on a broad range of goods, and to his decision to attack Iran, which spiked prices for crude oil, gasoline, diesel and jet fuel.
The new rate hike of a quarter point will increase rates on consumer loans and credit cards, making Americans pay more in a new way. Trump’s foreign policy and his dramatic increase of the federal deficit and debt have already made mortgage rates higher by increasing the rates paid by government bonds.
Politics: Kennedy Tells Anti-Vaccine Activists They Have A Friend In Trump's White House
On a nearly daily basis, Trump lies that he inherited high inflation from his predecessor Joe Biden, but, in fact, high post-pandemic inflation rates had fallen to 3% by the time Trump retook office in January 2025.
The inflation rate continued to decrease for the first few months of Trump’s term but then reversed course and began rising again after Trump announced his tariffs against the rest of the world that April. A year later, inflation — led primarily by higher prices for both crude oil and refined fuels — increased some more after Trump unilaterally began a war against Iran on Feb. 28.
If Trump does start attacking Warsh, it will not be the first time he has gone after a Fed chair he himself elevated.
In November 2017, Trump chose Jerome Powell as the new chair of the Federal Reserve, praising him as perfect for the job. “He’s strong, he’s committed, he’s smart,” he said as he announced his nomination in the White House Rose Garden. “I am confident that Jay has the wisdom and leadership to guide our economy through any challenges that our great economy may face.”
Politics: Trump’s ‘Golden Age’ Of Tariffs Has Been Great — If You Like Higher Prices
Powell was confirmed by the Senate three months later, and not long after that, Trump was already angry at him for raising interest rates. “I think the Fed is making a mistake. They are so tight. I think the Fed has gone crazy,” he told reporters, unprompted, after getting off Air Force One in Erie, Pennsylvania, en route to a campaign rally.
Trump began going after Powell in personal terms after retaking office last year for not lowering rates quickly enough. He and his allies even ginned up investigations against him in an attempt to remove him as chair before his second term as chair expired.
In response, Powell decided to remain as a governor on the Fed board through the end of his term next January, rather than leave at the end of his chairmanship in May, as departing chairs have traditionally done.

Title: Evidence pulled from DC mother's home as her ex faces new gun charges in Pennsylvania
Article_Text:
Evidence pulled from DC mother’s home as her ex faces new gun charges in Pennsylvania
WASHINGTON (7News) — Nearly two weeks after D.C. mother Antoinette Forbes disappeared, new developments unfolded in two states as investigators continue searching for answers about what happened to her.
A source close to the investigation tells 7News a homicide detective is now leading the investigation into Forbes’ disappearance.
On Tuesday, 7News cameras captured forensic investigators spending hours inside Forbes’ home in the 3200 block of Nebraska Avenue, Northwest. Investigators were seen carrying multiple brown paper bags and other items out of the home and loading them into a van.
RELATED | Ex of missing DC mom faces extradition hearing in Pennsylvania
Police have not said what was inside the bags, what investigators removed from the home, or whether any of the items collected are considered evidence.
The involvement of a homicide detective does not mean police have determined Forbes is dead. Metropolitan Police Department (MPD) has not publicly announced the case as a homicide investigation and has not publicly named a suspect or person of interest.
A friend of Forbes, Holly, told 7News she was encouraged to see investigators continuing to work the case.
“To be honest, I’m grateful for all the work that the authorities are doing to continue to work this case and leave no stone unturned so that we can find Antoinette and find out what has happened,” she said.
Former D.C. homicide detective Kenneth Jarels said that the circumstances surrounding Forbes’ disappearance would immediately stand out to investigators.
Two cellphones were left behind, along with her keys and wallet. Her car remained at the home, her dog was still inside, and a friend who went to check on her found the door unlocked. Jarels called those details, particularly when considered together, “red flags.”
Jarels cautioned that he does not know enough about the investigation to call the home a crime scene. But he said forensic investigators working inside a secured home could be looking for a wide range of information, including evidence not visible to the naked eye, documents and other material that could help establish what happened.
What happened before Forbes disappeared
MPD said Forbes, 53, was last seen around 3 p.m. on Friday, Sept. 4, in the 3200 block of Nebraska Avenue Northwest near Foxhall Road.
But her family said there was contact with her after that.
Forbes’ sister, Aileen Forbes, told 7News she spoke with her over FaceTime Saturday morning. The sisters laughed and discussed future plans, and Aileen said nothing seemed unusual. A friend also told 7News Forbes responded to a text message that morning.
On Sunday, Aileen said she texted her sister after learning Forbes had COVID, but this time she received no response. She said that was highly unusual.
A friend later went to Forbes’ home to check on her. The friend found the door unlocked. Forbes’ keys, wallet, purse, and two cellphones were inside. Her dog was there, and her car was still in the driveway. The friend then contacted police.
Aileen has described her sister as a devoted mother and accomplished professional whose disappearance is completely out of character.
“She is a solid mother. She is a brilliant professional. And for her to be missing, we can’t comprehend it,” Aileen told 7News.
The family has continued asking anyone who may have seen Forbes or noticed anything unusual to contact investigators.
Russell Ashford faces new charges in Pennsylvania
A separate development Tuesday involved Russell Ashford, Forbes’ former partner and the father of her 10-year-old son.
Ashford was scheduled to appear in Beaver County, Pennsylvania, for an extradition hearing as Maryland seeks to bring him back on a Montgomery County probation violation warrant.
That extradition hearing never happened.
Instead, Pennsylvania authorities filed seven new felony counts of possession of a prohibited firearm against Ashford.
According to the Pennsylvania criminal complaint, investigators said seven firearms were found tied to Ashford: two pistols, two shotguns and three rifles.
Police allege Ashford stored the guns at a girlfriend’s home in May. The woman told investigators she did not know Ashford was prohibited from possessing firearms.
Ashford said nothing during his brief court appearance.
A judge said the Pennsylvania charges will be handled before Ashford is extradited to Maryland. Ashford was expected to have a preliminary arraignment at the jail, followed by a preliminary hearing within approximately 10 days.
Ashford has not been charged in connection with Forbes’ disappearance.
The 2021 assault involving Forbes
The firearm prohibition cited by Pennsylvania authorities traces back to a 2021 first-degree assault case in Montgomery County involving Forbes.
Maryland court records show Ashford was charged with first-degree assault stemming from an incident on June 10, 2021. He pleaded guilty on Dec. 14, 2021.
Court records reviewed by 7News describe a brutal assault that left Forbes with multiple fractures to her face, damage to her right eye, a concussion and an injury to her hand. Records indicate their young son was present during the incident.
Ashford was originally sentenced in April 2022 to 15 years, with all but nine months suspended, followed by five years of supervised probation.
The Maryland docket also shows an order requiring Ashford to surrender firearms was entered on April 25, 2022.
In a separate family court case filed shortly after the assault, a Montgomery County judge awarded Forbes emergency sole legal and physical custody of their child and ordered Ashford to have no contact with Forbes or the child until further order of the court.
Forbes’ friends said they did not know about the violence at the time.
“We know, and I’m sure most people have seen the coverage now, of the past assaults, and that was brutal,” Holly told 7News. “Her friends and her family did not know about that.”
She said learning about it after Forbes disappeared has been painful.
“It is sad now to know that she was kind of carrying that by herself and didn’t feel like she could burden her friends or family with that.”
A change in Ashford’s Maryland court record this summer
Maryland court records also show Ashford’s case returned before Judge David Lease for a reconsideration hearing on July 9, 2026.
The current docket lists the disposition as “probation before judgment” effective July 9 and separately lists the outcome as “Probation Modified.”
The Pennsylvania criminal complaint filed this week nevertheless alleges Ashford was prohibited from possessing the seven firearms.
Why Maryland wants Ashford back
Ashford had been held in Beaver County on a Montgomery County probation violation warrant.
Beaver County District Attorney Nate Bible previously told 7News that Ashford’s supervision had been transferred to Pennsylvania while Maryland retained jurisdiction over his case.
Bible said his understanding was that the alleged violation involved Ashford leaving Pennsylvania and traveling into Maryland or the D.C. area.
Bible also told 7News that license plate readers helped investigators track Ashford’s vehicle. He said that while Ashford was being taken into custody, authorities in Pennsylvania were assisting law enforcement from D.C. and Maryland with investigative steps, including search warrants.
The new Pennsylvania gun case now means those charges will move forward before the extradition process resumes.
No charge in Forbes’ disappearance
Despite the court developments involving Ashford and the history between him and Forbes, authorities have not charged Ashford with any crime connected to Forbes’ disappearance.
MPD has also not publicly identified him as a suspect or person of interest.
Holly told 7News she and the other friends of Forbes are trying not to speculate about the investigation.
“We’re keeping an eye on it, but I don’t want to comment on that or speculate on anything related to that,” she said. “I will leave that to the courts and the authorities to handle that.”
Forbes’ friends said their focus remains on finding her.
“I think we all just want to know what happened to our friend,” Holly said.
Anyone with information about Forbes’ whereabouts or her disappearance is asked to call D.C. police at 202-727-9099 or text a tip to 50411.

Title: 2026 NFL Week 2: Dallas Cowboys vs. Washington Commanders
Article_Text:
Welcome to Week 2 of the Dallas Cowboys season.
For the first, and hopefully last, time the Cowboys are looking to bounce back from a loss. This past Sunday was a humbling experience for the Cowboys as they had an enormous amount of positivity heading into the season opener, but football is a meritocracy and the New York Giants earned the right to win that game.
This week the Cowboys will have to out work and out earn another division rival in the Washington Commanders. Like Dallas, Washington lost in Week 1 to a division rival in the Philadelphia Eagles. This means that the loser of this game is going to be sitting at 0-2 overall and within the NFC East.
Dak Prescott, CeeDee Lamb, George Pickens, Javonte Williams and the rest of Brian Schottenheimer’s “GOTI” offense are going to have to be more consistent if they want to change the team’s fortunes.
What’s more is that the defense is going to need more than Caleb Downs to shine. Quinnen Williams, Donovan Ezeriuaku, DaRon Bland, and specifically Christian Parker are going to have to make sure last week was an aberration.
This post will serve as our story stream for the week. All articles related to the game will cycle through.
Here we go.

- How to fix the Cowboys Sunday night defensive disasterThe Dallas Cowboys’ defense on Sunday night was an absolute sieve. Article_Text:
The Suburban League is the driving force behind a move that, if successful, would separate public and private schools for postseason tournaments.
Meeting with members of the Ohio Prep Sportswriters Association in Southwestern Ohio on Sept. 15, OHSAA executive director Doug Ute confirmed the Suburban League from Northeast Ohio is circulating a petition around the state in an attempt to get a referendum vote on the 2027 ballot to separate public and private schools.
The report was first made by WCPO-TV 9’s Mike Dyer.
In an exclusive interview with The News-Herald, Nordonia athletic director Rob Eckenrode explained the stance of the 16-team Suburban League in its quest to have member schools of the OHSAA vote on whether public and private schools should have separate postseason tournaments.
“I would say it’s very difficult for a public school that has to rely on kids from a smaller entity or community,” Eckenrode said. “We take the kids who walk through our doors and do the best we can with those students. We don’t have the opportunity to bring them in from, say, a seven-county area.
“Let’s put it on the ballot and see what happens. The last time was in the 2007-2008 timeframe and the measure failed fairly close from what I remember. Twenty years later? Maybe it’s time to look at it again.”
Though public-private separation has been a hot-button topic for decades, the last two times OHSAA member schools voted on it were in 1978 and 1993.
For a measure to be put up for referendum vote by the OHSAA’s member schools, a petition must:
• Get five signatures from within each of the state’s five OHSAA districts — Central, Northeast, Northwest, Southwest and Southeast.
• Receive 75 signatures total from high school principals around the state in those five OHSAA districts; and
• File the petition by December with the aforementioned signatures.
If that criterion is met, a referendum vote of the state’s 818 member schools — 656 of which are public and 162 of which are non-public schools — could be held in May 2027. The earliest a change could happen is for the 2028-29 school year, according to Ute in the WCPO report.
“So far it’s been fairly positively received,” Eckenrode said. “We’ve followed the OHSAA processes. It’s nothing about removing private schools from the OHSAA. It’s working within the existing system. Public and private schools will still be able to participate in the regular season, but in playoff time, no matter what the sport you’d have a public school division and a private school division.”
Alabama’s high school athletic association voted to separate public and private schools for postseason playoffs starting the fall of 2026. Pennsylvania’s state house this spring advanced legislation that would allow its athletic association to separate into different postseason tournaments as well.
Eckenrode said “it’s nothing personal with private schools” and that “it’s entirely about giving public schools the opportunity, or evening the opportunity, to win a state championship.”
He reiterated that it’s not his nor the Suburban League’s decision to make, but rather the principals around the state in the referendum voting — if, he said, enough signatures are gained to put it on the ballot for member schools to vote upon.
“In our area, there are super teams that have been formed,” Eckenrode said. “It’s difficult for a public school to compete against a team that’s made up from kids from seven different counties. When you have a small community going against kids from Cuyahoga, Lake, Medina, Summit, Geauga, Lorain all going to the same school, I mean, it’s tough. It’s tough.”
In discussing the topic at Princeton High School on Sept. 15 with member of the OPSMA, Ute said the OHSAA is not taking a position on the petition being circulated by the Suburban League, which consists of Aurora, Barberton, Brecksville, Copley, Hudson, Kenston, Mayfield, Medina, Medina Highland, Nordonia, North Royalton, Revere, Solon, Stow-Munroe Falls, Twinsburg and Wadsworth.
“We get this kind of conversation every year,” Ute told WCPO. “The league in Northeast Ohio that has some pretty passionate people about the split between private and public. We’ll make it clear: It’s not to remove anyone from our association. It’s just to separate the tournaments.
“You can’t just look at who is winning a state tournament,” said Ute to WCPO. “I think you really got to look at that regional level and things like that. We have data on every year from every sport on the competitive balance piece on private and public. And so that’s the kind of information we want to get out if they meet the Dec. 1 deadline.”
OHSAA spokesperson Tim Stried told The News-Herald the petition being circulated by the Suburban League, “itself is not the vote, which would take place next May if they get enough signatures. If the vote becomes imminent, the OHSAA will release more information and explain what separate tournaments would mean, including potential unintended consequences.”

Title: House votes for a third time to end the Iran war as conflict drags on
Article_Text:
WASHINGTON -- For a third time, the U.S. House has voted to end the war in Iran, approving a war powers resolution that would halt President Donald Trump's ability to continue military action without congressional approval.
The roll call late Tuesday, 220-204, was similar to earlier efforts this summer, with a few more Republicans joining all Democrats voting to bring an end to the conflict. None of the resolutions have made it to the president's desk, where Trump would almost certainly veto the measure.
"Remember when Donald Trump said that this war would last just a few weeks?" said Rep. Seth Moulton, D-Mass., who served as a Marine during the Iraq War and pushed the resolution forward.
He said it's time for Congress to "actually ask tough questions, as the Constitution directs us to do, rather than be subservient to another warmongering administration."
Republican Rep. Brian Mast of Florida, the chairman of the House Foreign Affairs Committee, questioned which military resources Democrats would want to remove from the region where he said Iran remains a threat.
Mast said Trump is against "forever wars, and that is what he is ending" -- the decades of hostilities from Iran.
"They are a continuous ongoing threat to the United States," Mast said. "Enough is enough."
The action is likely the last House vote on the Iran war ahead of the midterm elections, where the conflict overseas is playing a substantial role in the political campaigns. The war that Trump launched Feb. 28 has dragged, with on-again, off-again deadly missile strikes being exchanged and causing havoc in the region for nearly seven months.
Lawmakers are heading home at the end of the week to campaign nearly full-time, with less than 50 days to go before the elections that will determine control of Congress as Democrats try to wrest power from Republicans.
Voters are confronting high prices, particularly for gas at the pumps, as the conflict disrupts the flow of oil resources through the vital Strait of Hormuz.
The Congressional Budget Office said Tuesday the war has cost more than $38 billion, as of Aug. 1, and is projected to be costing between $2 billion and $3 billion monthly, depending on the intensity of the fighting. The budget office projected inflation will be 0.5 percentage points higher than expected heading into 2027 due to the war.
Trump had promised not to involve the U.S. in foreign wars when he won a second term in the White House.
In the previous House actions, four Republicans voted to halt the war in Iran, but that number rose to seven in Tuesday's war powers vote, including GOP lawmakers from battleground Iowa, Rep. Zachary Nunn and Rep. Mariannette Miller-Meeks, and retiring Rep. Nancy Mace of South Carolina.
They joined GOP Reps. Tom Barrett of Michigan, Warren Davidson of Ohio, Brian Fitzpatrick of Pennsylvania and Rep. Thomas Massie of Kentucky voting in favor of the war powers resolution, with all Democrats.
Congress has tried repeatedly to alter the trajectory of the war against Iran, but efforts to limit the Trump administration's military action remain a longshot so long as the president is able to fend off or veto the measures.
The House first approved a war powers resolution in June, and followed up with another one in July, all seeking to halt U.S. action in Iran. The Senate on its 10th try also approved a war powers resolution to end the conflict, but GOP senators quickly reversed course the next day after Trump berated them during a closed-door lunch.
While the Constitution gives Congress the authority to declare war, it also gives the president authority as the commander in chief to engage in some military actions. The War Powers Act, created in the aftermath of the Vietnam conflict, sought to put a more specific time limit on the president's power, requiring congressional approval for sustained military actions after 60 or 90 days.
House Speaker Mike Johnson acknowledged at a press conference Tuesday the need to bring gas prices down.
But the Republican speaker said he believes the Iran conflict is entering a "new phase" as allies step up to help stabilize the region. When that happens, he said, "you're going to see, as the president said, anytime gas prices will go down again, the cost of groceries will as well."
Johnson said Trump expects the shift after the election, and the speaker added, "I'd love it to happen today."

Disney+ and Hulu: Adventure Time: Side Quests (Season 2) Finn and Jake are back for more adventure and even more side quests across the wild, wonderful land of Ooo. Wrestling toads, facing baby gladiators, and getting tangled up in one too many magic spells, it's clear no side quest is too strange, too small, or too dangerous to take on. Season 2 of Adventure Time: Side Quests keeps its heart in the same place as before with two best friends, endless trouble, and a whole lot of butt-kicking along the way, proving that in the land of Ooo, even the smallest of detours can lead to the biggest adventures! Disney+ and Hulu: Africa Earth's Wild Home National Geographic's Africa Earth's Wild Home, is a seven-part event series that brings African wildlife and landscapes to the screen like never before, using the latest technology to tell the most extraordinary stories from the continent and cutting-edge CGI to unearth the deep history and forces that shaped Africa's natural worlds. Presented by Rolex, Africa Earth's Wild Home launches an ambitious multiyear franchise that will document our planet continent by continent at a moment when that planet is changing faster than ever. It is a singular creative partnership, uniting National Geographic's world-class natural history storytelling, the National Geographic Society's global community of Explorers and scientists and Rolex's Perpetual Planet Initiative in a commitment to the natural world - to capture Earth's wild places and the people protecting them for generations to come. Filmed over almost four years across nearly 30 countries, the series documents species and behaviors for the first time, including the elusive black rain frog, filmed for TV for the first time, and hyenas in the Congo hunting elephants at night. The series also features extraordinary footage of a rare wild African black panther and chimpanzees using unique tools to fish for algae. Spanning deserts, forests, jungles, mountains and islands, the series reveals how Africa's wildly varied ecosystems shape the animals that live in them, driving epic stories of adaptation, resilience and survival. Hulu: America's Funniest Home Videos (Season 37) (ABC) Hosted by Alfonso Ribeiro, America's Funniest Home Videos is the longest-running primetime entertainment show in the history of ABC. Each week, the AFV team evaluates thousands of user-submitted home videos to showcase America's real-life funny moments captured on video. AFV offers weekly cash prizes to the funniest or most unique videos submitted by families from across the nation. In its 36 seasons and more than 800 episodes to date, AFV has given away over $18 million in prize money and evaluated over 2 million video clips from home viewers. AFV has become an iconic part of American pop culture, as evidenced by its inclusion in the Smithsonian's permanent entertainment collection. Today, AFV is syndicated in over 103 territories around the world, spreading American humor and clumsiness across the globe! Hulu: FX's American Horror Story: 13 (Hulu Original) FX's American Horror Story, the global phenomenon that has garnered more than 100 Emmy nominations since its launch in 2011, returns for an unrivaled 13th installment that will do justice to everyone's most feared number. Bringing together an all-star cast, many of whom are reprising fan favorite roles, American Horror Story: 13 continues to build on the anthology's decades-long legacy that has been streamed more than 700 million hours across the globe and spawned a legion of dedicated fans. Created and produced by Ryan Murphy and Brad Falchuk, American Horror Story has redefined the genre with various installments featuring a creepy murder house, a coven of witches, a traveling freak show, a haunted hotel and the apocalypse itself. Which iconic horrors will return to haunt the hallowed halls of 13 and what new terrors await? Light your candles, draw your pentagrams and prepare for a supreme surprise. Disney+ and Hulu: Austin City Limits Music Festival 2026 Inspired by the iconic PBS series Austin City Limits, Austin City Limits Music Festival has grown into a two-weekend celebration featuring world-renowned and emerging artists across 8 stages in Austin's Zilker Park. ACL Fest showcases a diverse lineup spanning rock, pop, folk, indie, country, blues, electronic, and more. Disney+: The Banana Bowl The Banana Bowl will stream live on Disney+ and feature the top teams in the Banana Ball league facing off for the season championship. Known for blending athleticism with entertainment, the game will include one of the biggest performances the league has ever seen, bringing together all six teams, along with its signature on-field showmanship from first pitch to final out. Disney+: Big City Greens (Season 5) Big City Greens follows the offbeat adventures of 10-year-old Cricket Green, a mischievous and optimistic country boy who moves to the big city with his wildly out of place family - older sister Tilly, father Bill and Gramma Alice. Cricket's natural curiosity and enthusiasm lead him and his family on epic journeys and into the hearts of his new neighbors. The new season follows the family and their friends as they navigate some of their biggest adventures yet! Hulu: Celebrity Wheel of Fortune (Season 7) (ABC) Hosted by fan-favorite Ryan Seacrest and joined by beloved co-host Vanna White, Celebrity Wheel of Fortune welcomes celebrity contestants to spin the world's most famous Wheel and solve puzzles for a chance to win $1 million for the charity of their choice. After 43 seasons in syndication, Wheel of Fortune remains the No. 1 entertainment show on television. Both shows are produced by Sony Pictures Television and executive produced by Bellamie Blackstone. Disney+ and Hulu: CMA Presents I Will Always Love You: A Celebration of Dolly Parton (ABC) Following her passing on Aug. 25, the special will be a joyful, emotional celebration of the artist, songwriter, entertainer, humanitarian and entrepreneur whose music and generosity carried her from the mountains of east Tennessee into the hearts of generations around the world, told through performances, archival footage and personal stories that trace her extraordinary journey to becoming one of the most beloved entertainers and philanthropists in American history. Hulu: Clown Panic (Hulu Original) When children in a small South Carolina community report seeing clowns hiding in the woods in 2016, few believe them. But as sightings spread across the country, panic escalates into school lockdowns, police investigations and a nationwide media frenzy. Featuring chilling archive footage, viral internet videos and revealing interviews with witnesses, law enforcement, clowns and cultural commentators, Clown Panic examines the collision of fear, social media and modern America at a moment of deep national anxiety. Darkly funny, unsettling and unexpectedly emotional, the film uncovers how a bizarre urban legend spiraled into a global moral panic that has echoes that resonate today. Disney+ and Hulu: Coven Academy (Season 1) In the haunted heart of New Orleans, Coven Academy follows three teenage witches and their dangerously charming warlock peers at an elite magic boarding school where power is currency, secrets are lethal and attraction is a liability. Caught between ancient supernatural wars and forbidden love interests, the coven must decide how far they're willing to go to protect their city - and themselves. Disney+ and Hulu: Dancing with the Stars (Season 35) (ABC) Hosted by Alfonso Ribeiro and Julianne Hough, the hit series pairs celebrities with trained ballroom dancers to compete in themed choreographed dance routines that are judged by a panel of renowned ballroom experts, including Carrie Ann Inaba, Bruno Tonioli and Derek Hough. The show is produced in front of a live audience by BBC Studios Los Angeles Productions. Hulu: FX's The Drop: A Snowfall Saga (Hulu Original) FX's The Drop: A Snowfall Saga follows Snowfall characters Wanda Bell (Gail Bean) and Leon Simmons (Isaiah John) as they fight to reinvent themselves in '90s Los Angeles, where the fallout from the crack epidemic is fueling a new game: the rise of West Coast rap. Disney+ and Hulu: Handsome Handsome is a GLAAD Award-winning comedy podcast from Tig Notaro (Star Trek, The Morning Show, Zootopia 2), Fortune Feimster (FUBAR, The Mindy Project, Zootopia 2), and Mae Martin (Wayward, Feel Good, Zootopia 2). Each week, the hosts field a question from a guest and attempt to answer it together, covering an eclectic mix of topics. Spend time with the Jonas Brothers here and stay a little bit longer for deep conversations like never before. Hulu: FX's It's Always Sunny in Philadelphia (Season 18) (Hulu Original) In season 18, FX's It's Always Sunny in Philadelphia continues its return to its roots, with 10 jam-packed setups only the Gang could find themselves in. Charlie (Charlie Day), Mac (Rob Mac), Dennis (Glenn Howerton), Dee (Kaitlin Olson), and Frank (Danny DeVito) are wrapped up in salvaging inheritances from a dead woman, surviving tent encampments and the great inside-outside divide between the haves and have-nots, withstanding job loss at the hands of workplace automation, embracing a newfound appreciation for neurodivergence, questioning the fabric of society against conspiracy theories, and of course - the biggest elephant in the room - outlasting the public's pendulum swing against drinking. Not to mention battling nerds, LARPers, and a particularly petulant McPoyle clan at the Renaissance Faire or sportswashing their way back into the good graces of their community by sponsoring a Little League team. All the while trying to maintain order in their personal lives and at Paddy's, which have become increasingly lawless and erratic. Hulu: Grey's Anatomy (Season 23) (ABC) Recipient of the 2007 Golden Globe(R) Award for Best Drama Television Series and nominated for multiple Emmys(R), including Outstanding Drama Series, Grey's Anatomy is considered one of the great television shows of our time. The high-intensity medical drama, now in its 22nd season, follows a team of doctors at Grey Sloan Memorial who are faced with life-or-death decisions on a daily basis. They seek comfort from one another and, at times, more than just friendship. Together, they discover that neither medicine nor relationships can be defined in black and white. Hulu: The Mess Around with Hannah and Lamorne Go behind the scenes of Apartment 4D with the crew who called it home for seven incredible seasons. Each week, real-life friends Hannah Simone (Cece) and Lamorne Morris (Winston Bishop) rewatch their Emmy(R)-nominated series, New Girl, and reveal the never-before-told behind-the-scenes escapades. Speaking of besties - they're inviting all of the loft's favorite guest stars, writers, and directors to share their adventures on set. Hulu: The Mob (Hulu Original) Hosted by Emmy(R)-nominated actress Parker Posey, The Mob is a high-stakes reality competition series that sends a group of celebrities to a lavish Italian villa where they will shake down, hustle and whack their way to win up to $250,000 in cash prizes. Every episode, they will tackle mob movie-inspired jobs to survive. But every mob family needs a don, and whoever they choose will have absolute power - deciding who makes money, who stays, and who ultimately gets whacked. In a game where power demands absolute loyalty, can the don stay in control, or will the family rise up and overthrow them? Disney+: Pod Meets World After recapping all 7 seasons of Boy Meets World the sitcom they starred in as teenagers, and now with over 55 million audio downloads to their name, Danielle Fishel, Will Friedle and Rider Strong are taking their 30-year friendship to the next level. This newest chapter of the podcast will dig deeper into their undeniable chemistry through more shared '90s memories, random tangents, new side quests and exciting guests. They're back for a new era - so fans can join their three childhood best friends on Pod Meets World! Hulu: Prison Breaking With Sarah & Paul In the series, Sarah Wayne Callies (Dr. Sara Tancredi) and Paul Adelstein (Agent Paul Kellerman) rewatch and relive Prison Break episode by episode. The on screen adversaries and real life friends share never before heard stories from filming and welcome guests including actors, directors, and writers from the show's five seasons. They answer fan questions, run contests, and explore how television - and culture - has evolved since the series premiered in 2005. Hulu: Reasonable Doubt (Season 4) (Hulu Original) After a brutal attack leaves Jax's family and newly minted law firm shaken, nothing feels certain, especially their future. With Jax's most loyal client at the center of a spiraling media disaster, The Stewart Firm is thrust into a high-stakes battle where every move could mean survival ... or collapse of the firm. As grief lingers and pressure mounts, one question looms: Can they rebuild in time or will the cost of moving forward too quickly be everything they stand to lose? Hulu: R.J. Dorian, Donald Faison as Christopher Turk, Sarah Chalke as Elliot Reid and Ava Bunn as Sam Tosh. Hulu: Shark Tank (Season 18) (ABC) Shark Tank , the critically acclaimed and multi-Emmy(R) Award-winning business-themed unscripted series that celebrates entrepreneurship in America, returns to ABC and Hulu this fall for its 18th season with a powerhouse lineup of business tycoons and guest Sharks featured throughout the season. Hulu: Soulm8te Soulm8te follows a grieving engineer tasked with testing a ruthless tech giant's new artificially intelligent android. But when he attempts to program her to be a truly sentient soulmate, she develops needs of her own - unleashing a relentless spree of precision-engineered mayhem. Disney+ and Hulu: StraightioLab StraightioLab is an intellectual podcast where smart comedians George Civeris and Sam Taggart unpack the rich, multi-colored tapestry of straight culture. Each episode investigates a different "straight topic," from college fraternities and gender reveal parties to overhead lighting and themed restaurants. Over the last six years, George and Sam have welcomed countless superstar guests to the studio, toured the country, and been showered with accolades from once-prestigious magazines that have since made the switch to vertical video. Next stop? Winning the streaming wars once and for all. Disney+ and Hulu: Super Scam Me Award-winning journalist Mariana van Zeller is getting a new nose. And new hair. And a full makeover. Not for a magazine spread, but because she's about to go undercover for the strangest assignment of her career. She's trying to intentionally get romance scammed. In 2025 alone, romance scammers stole more than a billion dollars from American victims, and Mariana wants to know exactly how they do it. Armed with a new identity and a freshly-built dating profile, she becomes the bait, setting off on a journey at times absurd and yet deeply human, in which she starts dating a four-star general deployed to Syria, gets wooed by "George Clooney," and teams up with a hacker who helps her locate several scammers, including her own. Along the way, she exposes the tactics, the technology, and the psychology that have made these scams not just common, but nearly inescapable. Ego has funny, heartfelt conversations with her guests about the good, the bad and the not-so-pretty that have shaped their trajectories and made them who they are. In each new episode they unpack character motivations and storylines, share their unique perspectives, bring in special guests, reveal behind-the-scenes moments, and feature listeners in highly anticipated fan segments. That Was Us is produced by Rabbit Grin Productions. Disney+: VisionQuest Vision, rebooted and having escaped from those who sought to weaponize him, has been in hiding. Searching for new meaning, he consults the AI personas embedded in his programming, including F.R.I.D.A.Y., E.D.I.T.H., J.A.R.V.I.S., and the infamous Ultron. His discreet existence ends when a bounty placed on his head thrusts him on the run with Thomas Shepard, a mysterious boy who may be Vision's son, reincarnate. As Vision evades capture, he must confront his nature, resist Ultron's influence, and unravel the enigma that is his young companion if he's to survive. Hulu: Who Wants To Be A Millionaire?
