While the housing proposal has been dropped, Young said Tuesday the current library footprint was too small to accommodate the 21st-century features the community deserves.
» READ MORE: North Philly neighbors shout down Councilmember Young’s plan to replace their library
Young’s spokesperson, Yumeno Young, and Philadelphia Capital Program Office representatives said the remaining $8 million raised for the project remains committed to the library in its current location.
“Leadership is built on trust. And where is the trust? Because they’re not earning it,” said Emily Dumas, 38, who said she does not trust the $8 million would actually go to the current library building.
Nikol Ligon, 56, said she believed Young and the city ought to release the full funding for a wider renovation, and does not like that the Council member seems to have first and last say on a project that means so much to the community.
And Neferteri Raynor, 24, signed up this summer for a community advisory group Young’s office organized to gather feedback, but the group has held no meetings so far.
“We would love to have a level of certainty and transparency,” she said.
Election preview
Yumeno Young said an assessment may be conducted to determine what additional amenities and renovations could be constructed in the future, given the library’s current footprint, but it is unclear if or when that would happen.
The convoluted planning and decision-making confused State Sen. Sharif Street (D., Philadelphia), who spoke at the meeting in support of the residents.
“I don’t understand any of the process that was said today. … We need to come back with a better plan,” he said.
Young largely deferred questions to his spokesperson or the capital program office representatives, and said “we are working on this as a team” when residents implored him to speak more.
And community members said they were often left more confused by his answers. Siobhan Neitzel, the Brewerytown Sharswood Neighborhood Coalition colead of youth and education, said it felt as if Young was passing accountability onto others.
Some residents brought up the timing of the initial renovations, which are scheduled to be completed shortly before Young, considered the most vulnerable Council member, is on the primary ballot for reelection in May. The residents swore to use the library saga against Young.
While library staff have said they were told by capital program staff the renovation timing was related to Young’s reelection, Young denied there was any connection.
At points during the meeting, Young appeared to get frustrated. He said his goal is to find the best uses for taxpayer money.
“Your voices will be included in the process. … I’m not going to do anything just to do it,” Young said.

Title: A Northeast Philly woman who shot her boyfriend and left his body in a suitcase admitted killing him, prosecutors say
Article_Text:
A Philly woman who shot her boyfriend and left his body in a suitcase admitted to the killing, prosecutors say
Liza Ridley, 54, appeared in court Wednesday, where prosecutors played video of her abandoning a suitcase containing the body of Vincent Good in Kensington in May.
On a rainy May morning, pedestrians and cars passed Liza Ridley on Kensington’s Allegheny Avenue as she stood with a suitcase by her side.
Those passersby, prosecutors said, were unaware that the decomposing and dismembered remains of Ridley’s longtime boyfriend, Vincent Good, were arranged inside.
Those horrific details emerged during Ridley’s preliminary hearing on Wednesday in Common Pleas Court, where prosecutors said Ridley, 54, admitted to shooting Good in the head and leaving his body in their Northeast Philadelphia apartment this spring before moving his remains using a Lyft rideshare.
Assistant District Attorney Cydney Pope said Ridley shot Good, 53, seven times in the head and left his body on the couple’s mattress in their Mayfair apartment, sleeping next to the corpse as it decomposed in their room.
The body was likely there for two weeks or longer, prosecutors said. They also accused three people living in Ridley’s home of being complicit in the crime, saying it would have been impossible to ignore that something nefarious had happened to Good.
For example, Pope said, the smell of Good’s decomposition on bedsheets that had been thrown in the trash was so severe, homicide detectives could not bring them inside a police station for evidence processing.
And Pope presented Judge Gregory O. Yorgey-Girdy with additional evidence she said demonstrated Ridley’s culpability in the case.
That included surveillance footage captured at the intersection of F Street and Allegheny Avenue, where, prosecutors said, Ridley got out of a black Toyota and waited with Good’s remains while speaking on the phone.
She had traveled there using Lyft, accessing the rideshare app from an account registered to her daughter Liza Robinson, who lived with the couple, Pope said, citing cell phone data. Ridley eventually abandoned the suitcase in an alley a block away on East Hilton Street and left in another rideshare.
The suitcase was discovered the next day by a passerby who alerted authorities.
“I opened it up, I think it’s a body,” the man told 911 operators on a recorded call played during the hearing. “Oh, my God.”
Liza Ridley wore denim overalls over a white T-shirt as Pope presented those findings.
Prosecutors said Ridley, who was being paid by a contractor to be Good’s home health aide, told investigators that she and Good, who had struggled with alcoholism, had gotten into a fight in April that had turned physical before she shot him once.
Police recovered a six-shot revolver from her apartment, Pope said. Prosecutors say they will show that Ridley fired multiple times.
After hearing that evidence, Yorgey-Girdy held Ridley for trial on charges of murder and nine additional crimes, including abuse of a corpse and tampering with evidence.
Meanwhile, the remaining residents of Ridley’s apartment — Ridley’s sister, Bernadette Ridley, Robinson, and Robinson’s boyfriend, Gnaeus Daniels — appeared as codefendants.
Pope said Bernadette Ridley, who had recently moved in with Liza Ridley after returning home from being incarcerated, helped her sister carry Good’s remains down a flight of stairs and load the suitcase into the Lyft.
When homicide detectives interviewed Bernadette Ridley, they testified, she initially denied knowing about Good’s corpse, saying Liza Ridley had told her the foul smell coming from her bedroom was from a nearby sewer.
After being presented with evidence of her involvement, Bernadette Ridley admitted to assisting her sister, prosecutors said.
“‘I know it’s over for me,’” homicide detectives said she told them.
Yorgey-Girdy held Bernadette Ridley for trial on charges of obstructing the law, conspiracy, abuse of a corpse, and related crimes.
But the judge said prosecutors had not presented enough evidence to charge Robinson and Daniels with conspiracy and tampering with evidence, and he dismissed those charges.
Good’s mother, Deborah Good, said in an interview after the hearing that she and other family members were pleased that Liza and Bernadette Ridley’s cases were moving forward, even if the cases against Robinson and Daniels did not stand.
“She did a good job on the case,” Good said of Pope.

Title: Kelce brothers break down storylines from NFL Week 1 in 'New Heights'
Article_Text:
Jason Kelce praises the Eagles offense as he and Travis break down key NFL Week 1 story lines on ‘New Heights’
Travis might be biased, but his advice for quarterbacks was to "find the tight end." For the Eagles, that likely means Dallas Goedert, who had four catches for 77 yards and two touchdowns on Sunday.
On Wednesday, former Eagles center Jason Kelce said “You never want to overreact to Week 1.”
Still, Jason’s warning about reading too much into things too soon didn’t stop him and his brother, Travis, from dissecting all of the ins and outs of the NFL’s opening week on the latest episode of their podcast, New Heights.
‘Find the tight end’
He might be biased, but Travis had some advice for quarterbacks, including the Eagles’ Jalen Hurts.
“You want to be good at quarterback, just find the tight end,” Travis said when recapping the Eagles’ 24-22 win over the Washington Commanders.
While Jason acknowledged that most people were curious to see what the offense would look like under new offensive coordinator Sean Mannion, he said his biggest takeaway was how good Hurts looked.
» READ MORE: What we know (and don’t) about the Eagles entering Week 2 vs. the Titans
Both brothers credited Eagles tight end Dallas Goedert for helping with what Jason called “awesome plays,” resulting in four catches for 77 yards and two touchdowns.
“This offense I think will fit [Goedert] pretty well,” Jason said. “All this misdirection and stuff, they scheme things up, and it stresses those linebackers.”
He also acknowledged the struggles for the Eagles offensive line, including left guard Landon Dickerson, who was placed on injured reserve with a bone bruise on Monday.
“You could tell he wasn’t redirecting as well as he needs to or has,” Jason said. “And it’s a shame because when he is healthy, he is one of the best guards in the league. So he struggled a little bit in the game, and then I think Cam Jurgens had a couple holding calls. I don’t think he played as bad as I think what Twitter maybe seemed to say.”
Neither Kelce thinks there’s reason to worry just yet as the Eagles settle into this season and the new offense with a 1-0 record, which Travis said it “doesn’t get much better” than.
» READ MORE: Landon Dickerson revealed the cold reality of the NFL. Does anyone even care? | Mike Sielski
The return of the Chiefs dynasty?
During a dominant 31-10 Monday Night Football win over the Denver Broncos, Travis became second all-time in receiving yards for a tight end. He currently has 13,073 career yards and passed Dallas Cowboys legend Jason Witten (13,046) with a 59-yard catch in the third quarter.
But don’t get it twisted. Travis was adamant that it wasn’t a record, despite his brother’s protests that he “broke Jason Witten’s record.” Hall of Famer Tony Gonzalez remains the all-time leader with 15,127 career receiving yards.
Just being in conversations with players like Gonzalez, Witten, and other tight end stars from his childhood is a big deal for Travis.
“To be in the same talks as these guys at this point in my career, Jason [Witten], it’s an absolute honor to be in the same conversation as you,” Travis said. “I’ll have to just play another five years to catch Tony.”
Travis also gave credit to the rest of the Chiefs, including Patrick Mahomes, who returned from knee surgeryi and “did what he needed to do,” and running back Kenneth Walker III who, in his first game with the Chiefs, had 173 rushing yards on 23 carries, including a 60-yard touchdown. Walker, the Super Bowl MVP with the Seattle Seahawks last season, added a receiving touchdown in the fourth quarter.
“You can’t say enough about what Kenneth Walker is and what he’s going to be for this, this team and this organization and this city,” Travis said. “He’s one of those Kansas City guys, and you guys in Kansas City that don’t know him yet, to the core of who that guy is. He’s, he’s an A1 person.”
Down to a science?
The brothers discussed how other teams fared during Week 1. They took a look at how offenses seem to be trending upward with 10 teams scoring 30 or more points on Sunday, which is more than any Week 1 since the stat first started being recorded.
On the topic of firsts, they reviewed the first NFL Australia game, which the San Francisco 49ers won, 27-7, over the Los Angeles Rams.
The brothers focused on the teams’ travel. The Rams made the 15-hour flight one day before the game; the 49ers flew out a week in advance. Jason grew impassioned while not giving these studies much weight.
“To me, all these science, whatever they put in front of the team to sell you on the reason they’re doing it is you can find the science to say whatever ... you want to do,” Jason said. “You can pick and pull. They made a whole study out of saying chocolate’s healthy for you because it has, like, antioxidants in it.”

Title: The Academy of Natural Sciences building could be historically protected, but no one has ever nominated it
Article_Text:
Why isn’t the Academy of Natural Sciences building historically protected? No one ever nominated it.
The museum is the sole Parkway cultural institution not deemed historic by the city. Why? It was never nominated.
Even the Preservation Alliance for Greater Philadelphia was surprised that the Benjamin Franklin Parkway building that houses the Academy of Natural Sciences of Drexel University is not historically protected.
It learned after the academy announced its museum was closing that the building is “alone among the historic cultural institutions on the Parkway” as not designated historic by the city, said Paul Steinke, executive director of the Preservation Alliance.
The academy’s 150-year-old building houses the country’s first natural history museum. But it is not listed on the Philadelphia Register of Historic Places, a status that comes with protections against major alterations and demolition.
The museum is scheduled to close at the end of the month, and the academy plans to eventually relocate its collections and sell its building. The property’s zoning allows for low-rise, low-density residential buildings, such as townhouses or small apartment buildings. According to city records, the property’s assessed value is more than $28.7 million.
» READ MORE: The Academy of Natural Sciences is closing its museum after nearly two centuries
According to the Philadelphia Historical Commission, the academy considered pursuing historic designation for the building in the late 1980s but ultimately did not. On Wednesday, a spokesperson for the commission said it does not have a nomination from anyone in hand.
City Councilmember Jeffery Young Jr., whose 5th District includes the academy, said his office is looking into possible zoning changes to “protect and preserve that Parkway district,” including the academy’s building.
“We want to be able to utilize every tool we have available if necessary” to “preserve that public good in that area,” Young said.
Why hasn’t the building been designated historic yet?
“It wasn’t thought to be threatened, for one,” Steinke said. Designation happens only when someone takes the initiative to submit a nomination to the city, he noted, and that is commonly spurred by threats of redevelopment.
He pointed to another iconic Philadelphia spot that most people assumed was historically protected until a developer made plans to redevelop it: Jewelers Row, the oldest diamond district in the country.
In late 2019, Toll Bros. demolished several buildings on the 700 block of Sansom Street to build a 24-story housing tower that did not materialize. Developer Pearl Properties, which later took over the site, started making visible progress on its own housing tower this summer following years of delays.
For the academy’s building, Steinke said, the Preservation Alliance is looking into what it would take to do the necessary research, write and submit a nomination, and take it through the city’s historic designation process, which includes review by historical commission staff and public consideration by the commission and its committee on historic designation.
“We think it clearly qualifies for local designation,” Steinke said.
» READ MORE: The first complete dinosaur skeleton on view to the public made its debut at Philly’s Academy of Natural Sciences
The start of Philly’s museum mile
The academy moved to its current location on the Parkway in 1876, when the building opened for the Centennial. The building was designed by James Hamilton Windrim, an architect most famous for designing the Masonic Temple across from City Hall.
In the early 1900s, the academy building’s facade was redesigned in the Georgian style by the well-known Philadelphia firm Wilson Brothers & Co. Defining features of this architectural style include heavy use of red brick, symmetrical facades, centered entrances, and simple decorative elements, according to Steinke.
The academy said financial pressures and low attendance drove its decision to close the museum after nearly two centuries.
But Steinke said he hopes the outpouring of love and support people have been showing the museum since the closure was announced can help keep it where it is. When he visited on Sunday, he said, he “was heartened by the crowds of people, the families enjoying it.”
“It would be a real loss to lose that museum at the start of the museum mile,” Steinke said, referring to the section of the Parkway that hosts institutions such as the Rodin Museum, Calder Gardens, and the Philadelphia Museum of Art.
On Thursday, Councilmembers Young and Nina Ahmad plan to introduce a resolution that calls for Council hearings on the museum’s closure. They are also planning a rally to protest the closure at City Hall that morning.

Title: Thomas Bosworth, Philly personal injury attorney and TikTok influencer, arrested for assault
Article_Text:
Philly attorney and TikTok influencer ‘Tommy the Lawyer’ charged with assaulting his girlfriend
Thomas Bosworth has been expanding his legal practice, and social media presence, since his 2022 separation from Kline & Specter that sparked a long and ugly court battle.
A prominent Center City personal injury lawyer, known for his active TikTok account, choked his girlfriend and threw her to the ground during a dispute on a walking path in Lower Merion, according to police.
Thomas Bosworth, 37, has been charged with simple assault and harassment in connection with the Sept. 3 incident. He was released on $15,000 unsecured bail.
Bosworth, a resident of Gladwyne, did not respond to a request for comment. His attorney, Michael van der Veen, said in a statement that Bosworth “is presumed innocent, maintains his innocence and has full confidence in the courts.”
Bosworth, known to his 327,000 followers on TikTok as “Tommy The Lawyer,” gained prominence in 2022, when he won a $19.7 million verdict in a medical malpractice case as a 33-year-old attorney at Kline & Specter.
In the years since, he has opened his own law firm amid accusations from his former employer that he poached its clients and sanctions for his behavior from a federal judge.
Meanwhile, he has expanded his social media following through videos that give advice on everyday goods from his vantage point as a personal injury lawyer and the context for high-profile lawsuits he litigates.
On the day of the Lower Merion assault, four people told police they saw Bosworth attacking a woman on a section of the Cynwyd Heritage Trail behind Union Avenue in Bala Cynwyd, according to the affidavit of probable cause for his arrest. After choking the woman, the witnesses said, he threw her into bushes along the path, then walked away as she screamed.
The witnesses also said the woman slapped Bosworth and threw rocks at him while on the ground next to the trail, according to the affidavit.
Officers responding to the call found the woman with “redness on her cheeks and discoloration of the skin around her neck,” the document said. She told the officers she had fallen, and declined to speak with them further, as did Bosworth.
Witnesses later told police they overheard the couple arguing about Bosworth’s alleged infidelity, and the dispute escalated when the woman mentioned a text thread from his secretary he had deleted.
The assault took place in front of the couple’s newborn daughter, who was with them in a stroller, the affidavit said.
Bosworth’s arrest was not the first time in recent years that he has been the subject of scrutiny.
His separation from Kline & Specter in 2022 led to an ugly court dispute between the prestigious firm’s partners and their former young associate.
Tom Kline and Shanin Specter accused Bosworth of poaching clients, which he denied, and in return accused his former bosses of defamation. The parties reached a settlement in 2024 but have returned to court multiple times since, accusing each other of violating the agreement.
Kline and Specter are not the only ones who took issue with Bosworth’s conduct in the courtroom or online.
In 2023, Penn Medicine asked a Philadelphia judge to order Bosworth to stop posting on social media about a medical malpractice case he filed against the health system, saying he misrepresented facts and “poisoned” the potential jury pool. The judge sided with Bosworth.
That same year, a federal judge sanctioned Bosworth for “misconduct” during four expert depositions in a product liability case, saying the lawyer was “rude, demeaning, and obnoxious” to a female defense attorney.
And last week, the Pennsylvania Superior Court called Bosworth’s conduct in the courtroom “deplorable” even as it upheld the $19.7 million verdict he won while at Kline & Specter.
Bosworth had been accused of repeatedly ignoring the instructions of a Philadelphia Common Pleas Court judge during a medical malpractice trial in an attempt to inflame the jury.
On LinkedIn, less than two weeks after the alleged assault, Bosworth wrote about the decision to uphold the verdict without noting the admonishment.
“The courtroom is one of the only places left in our democracy where the everyday person can hold to task wrongdoers, no matter how rich powerful,” he said.
Bosworth is scheduled to appear for a preliminary hearing in the assault case Oct. 6.
Inquirer Lower Merion

Title: Political parties in Philadelphia can now spend raise and spend unlimited amounts in coordination with their candidates
Article_Text:
Philly’s political parties can now spend unlimited amounts in coordination with their candidates
In next year’s primary elections for mayor and Council, candidates endorsed by the Democratic City Committee could be able to access major financial advantages over their rivals.
Political parties in Philadelphia can now spend unlimited amounts of money in coordination with their chosen candidates, according to a new board of ethics policy approved Wednesday.
The policy, which was prompted by a recent U.S. Supreme Court decision, has the potential to dramatically increase the power of parties in Philly politics.
For instance, in next year’s city elections — when Mayor Cherelle L. Parker and all 17 City Council members will be up for reelection — the candidates endorsed by the Democratic City Committee could be able to access major financial advantages over their Democratic primary rivals, if the party chooses to coordinate with them.
Candidates are still bound by the city’s strict campaign finance rules limiting the size of donations to their campaigns — no more than $3,700 per year for individual donors, and $14,800 for organizations — and prohibiting them from coordinating with independent expenditure committees, or outside groups that spend money on candidates’ behalf.
But endorsed candidates will now be the only primary contenders allowed to coordinate with a group that has no restrictions on how much money it can collect: the party. The candidates, for instance, will be able to work with the party on messaging strategy, the timing of TV ads, and where to deploy door-knocking canvassers.
While the policy does not allow donors to require that parties spend their money on particular candidates, endorsed politicians with deep-pocketed backers can encourage donors to contribute to the party, with the understanding that the party will ultimately decide how the money is spent.
» READ MORE: Philly developers are planning a $1.5M campaign to protect City Council from progressive challengers
The impact of the new policy will depend on how aggressively candidates, parties, and donors seek to take advantage of it. But it has the potential to steer power in some elections back toward the city’s Democratic establishment after a period in which labor unions, special interest groups, and progressive super PACs have become increasingly influential.
“This Supreme Court ruling is going to have the effect of shifting power back to political parties and away from independent expenditures in a lot of ways,” said Philadelphia elections lawyer Adam Bonin.
In National Republican Senatorial Committee v. Federal Election Commission, the Supreme Court in June overturned limits on how much money parties could spend in coordination with candidates, citing parties’ free speech rights. The 6-3 decision, with the conservative justices in the majority, was widely seen as the latest in a series of cases that have demolished longstanding rules around money in politics.
But the NRSC case centered on a law related to general elections for federal office, and it was not initially clear whether the Philadelphia Board of Ethics would determine the ruling applied to local elections and to primaries.
The board, in a 4-0 vote with member Nelson Diaz absent, approved a policy that answered both of those questions affirmatively, meaning local political parties are now able to coordinate with their chosen candidates in primaries.
In deep-blue Philadelphia, where Democrats hold a 7-1 voter registration advantage over Republicans, the party’s primary contests usually determine the outcomes of elections.
In next year’s elections, progressives are hoping to make gains in Council, and Parker is aiming to secure a second four-year term. So far, Parker has attracted one announced Democratic primary challenger, former city official Shania Bennett. No Philadelphia mayor has lost reelection since the Home Rule Charter was adopted in 1951.
» READ MORE: No Philly mayor has lost reelection in modern history. So does Mayor Parker have anything to worry about?
The new policy holds that the party can only coordinate with its nominees in general and special elections. In primaries, the ethics board will allow the parties to set their own rules for determining their preferred candidates that they can coordinate with. The Democratic City Committee determines its endorsements by holding a vote among its ward leaders.
The policy, meant to clarify the city’s rules in advance of next year’s municipal elections, is temporary. The full details of the new rules will be fleshed out in regulations the board will tackle in the coming months.
Democratic City Committee Chairman Bob Brady said the party was “still reviewing the new guidelines.”
“Protecting constitutional rights remains a priority of the Democratic Party, especially the right to participate in our democratic process,” Brady said in a statement. “We will continue the work to ensure that the final implementation of these policies and laws will right the wrongs that have too long infringed on First Amendment rights.”
To be sure, there are significant roadblocks for candidates hoping to benefit from the new policy. In crowded primaries, for instance, the Democratic City Committee often declines to endorse when a majority of ward leaders fail to coalesce around one candidate. And the candidates and parties would have to find donors willing to give large sums knowing that they cannot control how the money will be spent.
Additionally, Bonin said, the new policy may still be more restrictive than what the Supreme Court decision appears to have envisioned because the board is seeking to maintain many of the city’s existing campaign finance rules.
“They are doing it in a way in which, initially, it seems they’re trying to change their rules as little as possible, while still recognizing they need to act,” he said.
The policy could also have an impact on elections for the two seats on Council that are set aside for minority-party or independent candidates. Republicans held those seats for about 70 years before Councilmembers Kendra Brooks and Nicolas O’Rourke of the progressive Working Families Party won them in the last two election cycles.
Before Wednesday, it appeared possible the ruling could create an uneven playing field, with the Republican City Committee being allowed to coordinate with its nominees while the Working Families Party was unable to do so because it is not a major political party under state law.
The language of the board’s approved policy, however, effectively gives the Working Families Party the same rights as the Democratic and Republican Parties because it fielded candidates in the most recent municipal election.
Republican City Committee chairman Vince Fenerty celebrated the ethics board’s decision.
“I’m very happy,” Fenerty said. “It will make our candidates be able to interact with other groups easily, and hopefully it will be a good day for the Republican Party of Philadelphia when we can have good funding to be victorious in some municipal elections.”
A Working Families Party spokesperson said this summer that the party opposed the Supreme Court’s attacks on campaign finance law, but did not rule out the possibility of the progressive group taking advantage of any new policy.

Title: William Johnson Jr., community-minded dentist and lifelong elite runner, has died at 95
Article_Text:
William Johnson Jr., community-minded dentist and lifelong elite runner, has died at 95
He saw patients for more than 40 years in Philadelphia and was a star distance runner at Norristown High School, the Penn Relays, and elsewhere.
William Johnson Jr., 95, of Philadelphia, a former Army dentist in France who later practiced for more than 40 years in Northwest Philadelphia, and a star distance runner at Norristown Area High School, the Penn Relays, and elsewhere, died Wednesday, Aug. 26, of congestive heart failure at his home near the Philadelphia Museum of Art.
Dr. Johnson grew up in Norristown, was part of his high school’s meet-winning mile and two-mile relay teams, and enlisted in the Army after graduating from New York University in the 1950s. His mother, Mary, wanted him to be a doctor. So, after she died when he was 6, he went on to earn a dental degree at Meharry Medical College in Nashville.
He spent five years as an Army dentist in France in the 1960s, reveled in the sophisticated social and cultural atmosphere in Paris at the time, and set up his own practice in the 1970s for what he saw were underserved communities around Chew Avenue and Slocum Street. He and his family lived above the first-floor office, and his son, Bill, and daughter, Jacqueline, both worked with him for a time.
“When we were young, he would tell us to stop running when he had patients,” his daughter said. His son processed X-rays and did other chores in the back room. “On Saturdays,” he said, “the office would be full of people of color. That’s how much he was needed.”
Dr. Johnson finally retired in 2014, at 83. Even then, his wife, Liz, said, “his loyal patients were reluctant to see him retire.”
Away from his patients, Dr. Johnson was a dedicated runner who rarely missed a daily workout. Wednesdays were half days at the office, so he saved his most grueling runs of the week for then.
» READ MORE: Why did best-selling author Carol Saline email The Inquirer’s obit writer?
“He wore a ski mask sometimes when it was cold,” his son said, “and when he was done it would be covered with ice.”
He won mile relay, two-mile relay, and other long distance races in high school in the 1940s, ran for the college team at NYU, and later finished first in masters division races at the Penn Relays. He was a longtime member of the Freedom Striders running club and most often ran in the lead pack in the Broad Street Run and other big road races.
He was also an amateur historian who loved to hash over stories about the old days in Philadelphia and Norristown. “He was analytical and liked to laugh,” his son said. “He was a model for me about the value of hard work and being humble.”
William Johnson Jr. was born Feb. 24, 1931, in Norristown. He lived with his father, William Sr., sister Jean, and brother Eddie after his mother died, and developed what his children called a “deep sense of family, independence, and faith.”
He played football as well as track in high school, joined the Alpha Phi Alpha fraternity at NYU, and worked in the New York garment district to make money. He enlisted in the Army after graduation to attend dental school.
He met Susie Jeffries in Tennessee while at Meharry, and they married, lived in Orléans, France, and moved to Philadelphia after he left the Army. They had two children. They divorced later.
In the 1990s, Dr. Johnson moved to the Art Museum area and married Liz Goldberg, also a dedicated runner. He and his wife traveled the world together, and she called him “an exuberant and colorful spirit” who “brought energy and joy to those around him.”
Dr. Johnson was interested in fashion, especially Ralph Lauren, and he and his daughter shopped together frequently. He liked music, French food, art shows, and gardening.
“Everything he touched seemed to blossom in his strong and capable hands,” his wife said.
He was curious about people and their lives, his children said. He followed current events, boxing, and the local sports teams closely.
He read the newspaper practically every day and recently learned to play the cello. He talked with his son and daughter every Sunday.
His daughter said: “He was a really smart, gentle, and kind person.”
» READ MORE: Survivors give advice about mourning their loved ones, as told to The Inquirer’s obit writer
His son said: “A lot of people have told me: ‘Your dad was the best.’”
In addition to his wife, children, and former wife, Dr. Johnson is survived by four grandchildren and other relatives. His sister and brother died earlier.
Private services were held earlier.
Donations in his name may be made to Meharry Medical College, 1005 Dr. D.B. Todd Jr. Blvd., Nashville, Tenn. 37208.

Title: Bucks County DA demands business records from alleged slumlords
Article_Text:
Bucks County DA demands business records from alleged slumlords
In April, the property on the 100 block of South Main Street in Dublin Borough was condemned because of alleged life-threatening conditions.
After hearing more horror stories about a dilapidated rental property that was condemned in April, Bucks County District Attorney Joe Khan said this week that his office has filed an amended civil complaint against the landlords and is demanding their business and financial records dating back to 2013.
In April, the property on the 100 block of South Main Street in Dublin Borough was declared unsafe and six tenants were effectively evicted, though they received county assistance to secure replacement housing.
Since then, a total of 13 former tenants — including a mother and her 11-year-old child — have complained about the conditions they endured, including years of not having a functional heating system for the building, Khan said.
The 35-page amended complaint names Richard Goetter, Ronald Goetter, and their fictitious business entity, R & R Enterprises, as defendants.
Richard Goetter could not be reached for comment on Wednesday. A person answering a phone number listed for Ronald Goetter in Arizona said he had died recently and declined to comment further.
Richard Goetter, who was described in the amended complaint as going to the property every Friday to collect rent payments, “has made no effort to make these affected tenants whole” since the district attorney’s office filed its lawsuit in April, the complaint said.
Additional tenants have come forward, “each sharing the same or similar descriptions of the disrepair, dangerous conditions, and lack of heat” going back to at least 2020, the complaint said.
“Defendants demanded rent and tenants unfairly paid full rent for a property that did not meet the most basic standards of habitability week after week, month after month, year after year,” the complaint said.
Khan said his office filed the civil complaint in Bucks County Court using the Pennsylvania Unfair Trade Practices and Consumer Protection Law to hold the landlords accountable.
The former tenants included a 63-year-old with an amputated leg who lived on the second floor with a roommate and required daily assistance.
The tenant had to provide their own space heater, and paid $230 a week for rent to Richard Goetter when he showed up on Fridays, the complaint said.
“Defendants’ business model profits by forcing vulnerable, low-income tenants to make an impossible choice between staying in an unsafe and unsanitary building today or risking imminent eviction and homelessness tomorrow,” the complaint said.
The alleged violations at the property date back to at least 2013, when a building inspection report said the property had no building-wide heat, the complaint said.
In 2024, Richard Goetter pleaded guilty after the Bucks County Health Department allegedly documented a rodent problem at the property, the complaint said. In 2016 and 2018, the agency received reports of alleged problems about a mice infestation and a toilet.
The building allegedly had black mold in the community bathroom, a large piece of plywood covering a hole in the floor of one of the bathrooms, rodent and cockroach infestations, and the overwhelming odor of human waste.
Khan said on Monday that his office is now pursuing the business and financial records of the defendants dating back to 2013.
Prosecutors are demanding “ownership documents, tax returns, insurance policies, rent payment records, and evidence of any taxpayer-funded emergency rent relief or nonprofit aid the business received since 2013,” the district attorney’s office said.
Prosecutors also are demanding “all written messages between the business partners regarding broken equipment, needed repairs, tenant evictions, and local code violations,” the district attorney’s office said.
“In the more than five months since we filed our action in court, R & R Enterprises has done nothing to make these tenants whole,” Khan said in a statement Monday.
“It’s now time to open up this business’ financial records to show where the money is so that we can help these victims recover and move on with their lives,” Khan said.

Title: Eagles' Cooper DeJean out of practice; Zack Baun earns NFC weekly honors
Article_Text:
Eagles defensive back Cooper DeJean held out of practice; Zack Baun earns NFC weekly honors
DeJean, who appeared to be wearing a sleeve on his left leg, was sidelined for Wednesday’s practice with calf and abdomen injuries.
Despite sitting out of Wednesday’s practice with calf and abdomen injuries, Cooper DeJean says he expects to play in Sunday’s game against the Tennessee Titans.
DeJean, 23, confirmed that he sustained an injury late in the second quarter of the Eagles’ season-opening victory over the Washington Commanders. After he tackled Commanders wide receiver Stefon Diggs on a reception, DeJean stood up and grabbed the left side of his abdomen. Additionally, DeJean appeared to be wearing a sleeve on his left leg at Wednesday’s practice.
“I hate it,” DeJean said of missing practice. “Wish I could have been out there today. Obviously, you’re missing a day, you’re not getting the looks. So you’ve got to do as much as you can on the side watching the reps and watching the film as well.”
He didn’t miss any snaps due to injury during the game, and he said Wednesday that he wasn’t affected much by it.
Still, he struggled at times in coverage. According to Pro Football Focus, DeJean conceded seven receptions on nine targets for 83 yards and a touchdown. Diggs did the most damage against DeJean, amassing four receptions on five targets for 55 yards and a touchdown in that matchup.
» READ MORE: What we know (and don’t) about the Eagles entering Week 2 vs. the Titans
After the game, DeJean said that he “wasn’t good enough” in his debut in his new role, which requires him to play safety in base defense and move to the slot in nickel.
“Sometimes my eyes get bad and that gets me in trouble,” DeJean said at the time. “Just got to be better with that. The good thing is it’s Week 1. We got a lot of games ahead of us and I got to continue to get better for our defense.”
On Tuesday, Vic Fangio agreed with DeJean’s assessment of his play, particularly regarding his eye discipline.
“I think it can happen at times, and at times it’s helped him, too,” the Eagles defensive coordinator said. “He’s just got to make sure he can stay tight enough to his assignment and not let his vision get too skewed to where he gets out of position.”
The Eagles will practice two more times this week before they travel to Nashville, Tenn., to take on the Titans. DeJean said he expects to practice at some point before the game.
Come Sunday, DeJean will be matched up against a familiar face in the slot — Wan’Dale Robinson, the former New York Giants slot receiver. Robinson, who is 5-foot-8, 185 pounds, reunited in Tennessee with Brian Daboll, the former Giants head coach who is now the Titans’ offensive coordinator.
Sunday against the New York Jets, Robinson caught two of three targets for 18 yards when lined up in the slot, according to Next Gen Stats.
He hasn’t had much success against DeJean. The Eagles defensive back wasn’t targeted on 16 slot matchups with Robinson last season, making him the only defender with a minimum of 10 slot matchups against Robinson to not see a target, according to Next Gen Stats. Still, DeJean expressed respect for the 25-year-old receiver.
“Shifty guy in the slot,” DeJean said. “Understands how to get open. Obviously, he’s played with the coordinator before, so understands the offense and the scheme. I feel like him and the quarterback already got a pretty good connection. So I’m looking forward to our matchup Sunday.”
If, for some reason, DeJean is not healthy enough to play against the Titans, or if he drops out midgame, Michael Carter II would be the next man up. Carter, 27, joined the Eagles at the trade deadline last year after beginning his career with the New York Jets as a fifth-round pick in the 2021 draft from Duke.
In Week 1, Carter played six defensive snaps — four at safety and two as the sixth defensive back in the dime package. He appeared in eight games with the Eagles at the end of last season, and 65 (25 starts) with the Jets over 4½ years.
Baun is NFC Defensive Player of the Week
The NFL named Zack Baun its NFC Defensive Player of the Week for his standout performance in Week 1 against the Commanders.
Baun, 29, racked up 12 tackles, two pass breakups, and a tackle for loss in the Eagles’ win. He was targeted six times in coverage and conceded three receptions for minus-2 yards, according to Next Gen Stats.
He is one of two defenders since the start of last season (with Cleveland Browns cornerback Denzel Ward) to allow negative receiving yards on at least five targets in a contest.
» READ MORE: Sielski: Landon Dickerson revealed the cold reality of the NFL. Does anyone even care?
Baun previously earned Defensive Player of the Week after a 2024 Week 10 showing against the Dallas Cowboys, in which he totaled eight tackles, two forced fumbles, and a fumble recovery.
He is the third Eagles linebacker to win the award more than once, joining Seth Joyner (three) and William Thomas (two). Since joining the Eagles two years ago, Baun has elevated his play from core special-teamer with the New Orleans Saints to All-Pro inside linebacker.
“He has this amazing work ethic,” coach Nick Sirianni said on Wednesday. “None of us know our ceiling. What I mean is, none of us know our actual potential, our ceiling, because so much can happen when you work your [butt] off. I may think to myself, ‘Well, my kids aren’t going to be NFL football players because I wasn’t,’ but that’s not fair to say because nobody knows what their potential is until they put the work in.
“That’s a great example of Zack: He is highly talented and he puts the work in.”
Other injury news
Defensive tackle Jalen Carter (wrist) also missed Wednesday’s practice, according to the team’s injury report. Edge rusher Jonathan Greenard, who missed the Week 1 win over the Commanders with a pectoral injury, was a limited participant.

Title: 8TH DISTRICT AD WATCH: A deeper dive into Bresnahan's data center bill, previous views
Article_Text:
Editor’s note: We are publishing a series of fact-checks of advertisements in the Pennsylvania 8th Congressional District race between incumbent Republican Congressman Rob Bresnahan of Dallas Twp. and Democratic challenger, Scranton Mayor Paige Cognetti. The election is key for both major parties’ hopes of holding a House majority the next two years.
The 30-second ad is paid for by Rob For PA, Bresnahan’s official political campaign, and was approved by the candidate.
Bresnahan, wearing a brown chore coat and with a typical Northeast Pennsylvania wooded area seen in the background, is the only voice heard throughout the ad.
“Northeastern Pennsylvania is our home,” he says as the ad begins. “But to big data, we’re just land and dollar signs.”
Bresnahan then mentions the fight residents of Archbald have been waging against several data center projects planned there and around Lackawanna County’s Mid Valley, and a headline from a July article in The Times-Tribune flashes on the screen as he speaks. The headline reads: “Archbald Residents Fighting Data Centers Get Win in Court.”
That, the incumbent said, is why he wrote a bill mandating developers seek and receive local approval before beginning construction on data centers. He added that the bill protects communities against legal fights from billion-dollar corporations. Bresnahan closes the ad with an insistence that local communities should get to decide where and whether data centers should be constructed within their borders.
Key claim
“No secret deals (with developers). No taxpayer handouts. Local control (over data center construction).”
Is it factual?
It is true that Bresnahan introduced legislation he believes will help small communities in the district combat the spread of data centers.
Titled the “Local Control Protection Act,” the bill:
- Removes the authority of federal courts to hear legal challenges against a local government’s decision to block or preclude a covered data center, as long as the decision was voted upon and made with documented findings.
- Bars federal agencies from issuing permits for data center construction or operation if the developer or owner is currently suing to challenge a local government’s zoning denial.
- Forces developers of approved data centers seeking federal incentives to file legally enforceable community benefit agreements and hire local labor.
Bresnahan introduced the bill in June, and it was referred to the Committee on Ways and Means and the Committee on the Judiciary for consideration. It has not moved from there in the three months since.
Bresnahan critics have noted the congressman’s previous more-friendly posture when it comes to data center development in the area. In 2025, he called data centers “catalysts for economic growth and technological innovation for our region.”
Bresnahan also holds stock in companies in position to profit from the industry’s spread. That includes between $19,005 and $110,000 worth of stock in Equinix, Digital Realty Trust, Iron Mountain and SBA Communications. The first three operate large-scale data centers, while SBA has a subsidiary that operates some smaller, regional data center facilities.
Bresnahan maintains he doesn’t personally trade his own stocks, a job he leaves to an independent third-party adviser.
“Favoring local control over data center development does not make someone anti-investment,” Bresnahan campaign spokesperson Samantha Bullock told CBS News. “It shows that they support the will of the people, and in fact it is important and responsible to consider the blue-collar jobs and economic development that might benefit a region like Northeastern Pennsylvania when addressing and legislating this issue.”

Title: 8TH DISTRICT AD WATCH: Cognetti administration's investment in police examined
Article_Text:
Editor’s note: We are publishing a series of fact-checks of advertisements in the Pennsylvania 8th Congressional District race between incumbent Republican Congressman Rob Bresnahan of Dallas Twp. and Democratic challenger, Scranton Mayor Paige Cognetti. The election is key for both major parties’ hopes of holding a House majority the next two years.
The 30-second ad is paid for by Paige For PA, Cognetti’s official campaign committee. The ad also was approved by Cognetti.
It begins with Bob , who identifies himself as a retired police detective, standing in front of a home, his sunglasses resting on top of a ball cap. Bob narrates the entire ad, and starts by discussing the changes he says he noticed in Scranton throughout his 27 years as a cop. Scranton, he said, was a “tough place on the brink of bankruptcy.” He alleges that corruption was rampant before Cognetti “took on the machine,” while black-and-white photos of disgraced former NEPA politicians, Scranton Mayor Bill Courtright and former Luzerne County Court of Common Pleas President Judge Mark Ciavarella, a central figure in the county’s Kids For Cash scandal, flash in the background.
Bob praises Cognetti’s work as Scranton’s mayor, insisting that she “stood up to Democrats in both Harrisburg and Washington” to secure more money for the city’s police force, saying Cognetti got the city more than $5 million in funding. He calls her “different” and “independent,” a leader who “does the right thing, no matter what the politicians want.”
Key claim
“(Cognetti) fixed the budget, turned down a pay raise and invested in our safety.”
Is it factual?
The narrator’s statements are true, but in some instances worthy of qualification.
Since Cognetti took office, more than $5 million in state and federal grants were indeed allocated to projects designed to benefit the city’s police department, according to city data. A large portion of that came from a $3.5 million federal grant secured in 2023 that paid for safety and survielance equipment that included new body and dashboard cameras, stun guns and virtual reality headsets for training.
The city also spent $1.5 million to bolster the city’s police vehicle fleet.
Securing state and federal grants for these projects, however, overwhelmingly comes down to collaborative efforts. While Cognetti’s administration works with Scranton’s City Council to pursue the funding, elected officials in Washington D.C. and Harrisburg must also pitch for it. The $3.5 million grant in 2023, for example, was secured federally by former 8th District U.S. Rep. Matt Cartwright.
In February, Bresnahan touted a $500,000 federal grant he secured for the city police department to upgrade equipment and modernize technology to increase officer safety and effectiveness.
As for Scranton’s finances, the claim that Cognetti “fixed” Scranton’s budget holds true, as well. The city exited Pennsylvania’s Act 47 municipal financial distress program after 30 years in January 2022, after her second year in office. Scranton also achieved its highest credit rating in decades during her tenure.
In January of 2025, City Council voted 3-2 to raise the mayor’s pay from $75,000 to $95,000, a 27% increase, starting in 2026. While running for reelection as mayor in the fall of 2025, Cognetti announced she would turn down that raise if elected.

Title: 'Facts, science, evidence': Commissioners OK data center health impact study
Article_Text:
SCRANTON — Capping months of sometimes contentious discussion over how to best approach the project, Lackawanna County commissioners awarded a contract Wednesday for a data center health impact study and could have the final report in hand by Christmas.
The pending assessment by Massachusetts-based EmPower Analytics Group will attempt to quantify the potential cumulative impacts of controversial data centers, power plants and related infrastructure proposed in the county on air quality and public health. The firm is behind a similar but more limited scope study of the proposed Wildcat Ridge Data Center Campus in Archbald.
The study in Lackawanna County, a hotbed for the data center industry, may be the first of its kind in Pennsylvania and possibly the nation, Commissioner Bill Gaughan said Wednesday.
Gaughan, an outspoken data center critic who raised the prospect of such a project in June, effusively thanked fellow Commissioners Thom Welby and Chris Chermak for supporting the initiative. Despite sparring last month over Welby’s and Chermak’s decision to solicit additional proposals for the study — Gaughan wanted to move forward with EmPower immediately — all three commissioners support the project’s goals.
It should provide an empirical, scientifically backed understanding of how emissions from and related to data center development might impact the area and the health of its people. Commissioners and members of a large and growing local data center opposition movement also see the study as potentially invaluable evidence in future legal battles over data center proposals galvanizing opponents from across the political spectrum.
Lackawanna County is currently home to more than a dozen proposed data center projects, with multiple proposals tied up in litigation, and several proposals to build power plants to accommodate the industry. Those controversial proposals complement others in neighboring Luzerne County and elsewhere in the broader region.
EmPower’s study will attempt to gauge the air quality and public health impact of all data centers, power plants and ancillary infrastructure proposed in Lackawanna County collectively and, where feasible, by facility. Assessing source-level emissions under typical and worst-case operating scenarios, the firm will create an inventory of proposed facilities, quantify how much pollution they would add, explore how that pollution would be dispersed and calculate its impact on health, with the cost of health outcomes “monetized using EPA’s economic valuation methods,” per its proposal.
“I believe what is happening across parts of this county represents one of the most aggressive attempts at exploitation we have seen in generations,” Gaughan said. “There are enormously powerful financial interests involved here. There are developers and corporations with armies of lawyers, consultants and lobbyists who can afford to sit in hearing rooms for months and try to essentially drag this thing out and make people wait and wait and wait.”
“The average resident obviously cannot compete with that, but government can and should,” he continued. “Government can give ordinary people something that money and public relations campaigns cannot manufacture: independent facts, science, evidence and the truth.”
During his remarks, Gaughan pointed to an American Lung Association report released in April that identified data centers as an increasing source of air pollution in the United States and warned that “communities located near large data center clusters often experience higher localized pollution burdens than regional averages.” He also referenced the EPA’s Monday announcement that it finalized the repeal of Biden-era regulations limiting greenhouse gas emissions by fossil fuel-fired power plants.
Data center opponents anxious about the impact proposed data center and power plant developments could have on their health and that of their children packed a commissioners meeting early last month and implored commissioners to move forward with the health study. Several data center opponents thanked commissioners Wednesday for taking action.
Welby emphasized that commissioners share the public’s concern about the potential health effects of data centers and power-generation facilities, noting his own “very strong feelings” about dubious safety claims that can later prove to be false. He used the example of Agent Orange exposure during the Vietnam War and mentioned the recent death of his nephew, Paul Welby, a Pennsylvania Army National Guard master sergeant who was exposed to toxic smoke from burn pits in Kuwait and passed away last month after a battle with esophageal cancer.
Predicting frightening findings from the data center health impact study, Welby said it will nonetheless provide “information that’s fair and honest and true.”
Chermak said he’s “hopeful that this (study) is going to be helpful in setting up guardrails for this industry in Lackawanna County.”
The county will pay EmPower a flat fee of $165,000 for the study. The firm’s proposal said it will provide a final report within 90 days of the project’s commencement.
Gaughan credited members of the local data center opposition movement for the county’s action on the impact study.
“Government did not lead you here; in many ways you led government here,” he said. “Today is not the end of this fight, but it is a really important day, because from this point forward when somebody tells the people of our county that there’s nothing to worry about we will be able to say ‘don’t tell us, show us.’ And this time we will have the science, in 90 days, to decide for ourselves.”

Title: Missoula Named 'Best College Sports Town' in USA TODAY Poll
Article_Text:
Missoula Named ‘Best College Sports Town’ in USA TODAY Poll
UM News Service
MISSOULA – Missoula, the home of the University of Montana Grizzlies, recently came out on top in the USA TODAY Sports Readers’ Choice 2026 for ‘Best College Sports Town.’
Griz Nation voted early and often to beat out communities that are home to some of the most well-known college athletics programs, including Tuscaloosa, Alabama – home to the University of Alabama Crimson Tide – and University Park, Pennsylvania – home to the Penn State Nittany Lions. Missoula was the only city in the Big Sky Conference to be named in the poll.
“Grizzly Athletics not only serves as the front door to the University, but to the Missoula community,” said UM President Jeremiah Shinn. “Being recognized as the ‘Best College Sports Town’ demonstrates the deep history and passion Griz Nation has for this place. With the school year underway, I can’t wait to experience it myself.”
Last year, a report from the Bureau of Business and Economic Research found that Griz Athletics contributes more than $94 million in total spending for Missoula-area businesses annually. Additionally, Grizzly Athletics supports 728 jobs in Missoula County.
“Weather doesn’t faze anyone here when it comes to the Griz experience at Washington-Grizzly Stadium,” wrote USA TODAY. “The team is excellent and always a threat to go deep in the playoffs. The atmosphere should attract ‘College GameDay’ one day.”
The impact of Griz Athletics is bigger than just football, as UM is home to 15 athletic programs and a growing roster of club sports.
Last year, the Montana Grizzlies women’s soccer team captured both the Big Sky Conference regular-season and tournament titles, becoming the first program in the conference to win three consecutive outright regular-season titles.
Griz Volleyball is back on the court this fall, fresh off one of the program’s best seasons since the 1990s, with 13 returning players – two of which were chosen for the Preseason All-Conference Team.
Basketball is also a major point of pride in Griz Nation. The Lady Griz have appeared in the NCAA Division I tournament 21 times to date and have advanced to the second round of the tournament seven times. The Montana Grizzlies basketball team was named regular-season and Big Sky tournament champions during the 2024-25 season.

Title: Ducks re-sign Cutter Gauthier to massive six-year deal
Article_Text:
After freeing up cap space last week by mutually terminating Chris Kreider’s deal, the Anaheim Ducks have now put that money to use. The Ducks announced that they’ve re-signed winger Cutter Gauthier to a six-year contract. Sportsnet’s Elliotte Friedman relays that the agreement will carry a $13.5M AAV. GM Pat Verbeek released the following statement on the signing:
"We are pleased to get Cutter signed to a long-term deal and have him in camp on time. He’s a major part of our young core, a pure goal-scoring talent that will continue progressing into an elite NHL player."
While the year-to-year details are not yet publicly available, Friedman adds that around $69.5M of the $81M of the deal is being paid in signing bonuses. That structure would not have been allowed after today as the new CBA comes into effect on Wednesday.
The 22-year-old was the fifth overall selection by Philadelphia back in the 2022 draft but made it clear soon after that he didn’t intend on signing with them. Soon after, the Flyers dealt Gauthier to Anaheim in exchange for defenseman Jamie Drysdale and a 2025 second-round selection. Gauthier then put pen to paper three months later, getting into the final game of the 2023-24 season, burning a year of his contract in the process.
Gauthier had a solid rookie season in 2024-25, picking up 20 goals and 24 assists in 82 games, finishing fifth in Calder Trophy voting. He then took a big step forward last season under new head coach Joel Quenneville, leading the Ducks in both goals (41) and points (69). He followed that up with a dozen points in as many playoff games, setting himself up for a big payday.
The value of that payday has certainly come in much higher than expected compared to just a few months ago. The five-year, $90M offer sheet that Philadelphia tendered to center Leo Carlsson earlier this summer (one that was matched) reset the top of the market and pushed Gauthier’s asking price even higher. Unlike Carlsson, Gauthier didn’t have the threat of an offer sheet available to him but he was still able to leverage his performance into a contract that puts him in a tie for the fifth-highest-paid player in the league.
Considering his career trajectory thus far, it’s fair to say that this contract is an overpayment in present-day value, and not by a little bit. However, both sides clearly feel that this type of performance is repeatable, giving him a chance to live up to the price tag as the deal goes on, while ensuring that a key scoring threat won’t be going anywhere anytime soon. The six-year term means that all five of Gauthier’s RFA years are covered plus one additional UFA-eligible season, while setting him up to hit the open market at the age of 28.
This time a year ago, things were looking up cap-wise for the Ducks. They had a promising young nucleus with plenty of salary cap space. But with Carlsson’s deal setting the stage for a big raise for Gauthier and the threat of an offer sheet pushing Pavel Mintyukov into a pricey second contract, their books don’t look anywhere near as clean now. Meanwhile, winger Beckett Sennecke, who will be extension-eligible next summer, is likely to see his price tag go up with Gauthier’s deal now serving as a potentially viable comparable down the road.
With the signing, Anaheim currently has just over $2M in cap room for the upcoming season, per PuckPedia. They can add to that amount by sending one of their goaltenders down, either Ville Husso or Laurent Brossoit, whoever loses the backup role to Lukas Dostal. That should give Verbeek ample flexibility to work with to start the season but if injuries strike early, they can shift Troy Terry to LTIR for some short-term relief on that front.
