Title: Why Eagles fan David Corenswet eventually agreed to playing a New York Giants star in 'Mr. Irrelevant'
Article_Text:
Eagles fan David Corenswet is playing a Giants star in upcoming ‘Mr. Irrelevant’
The story of the film and John Tuggle is much bigger than football fandom, said the 'Superman' actor, and has its own little Philadelphia connection.
Superman star David Corenswet grew up in Philadelphia loving the Eagles, but that didn’t stop him from saying yes to donning a Giants jersey for the upcoming biopic, Mr. Irrelevant.
The 33-year-old actor — who got his start on local stages as a kid — became a breakout movie star last year when he played Superman in James Gunn’s revamp of the legendary superhero films. While the sequel, Man of Tomorrow, releases in summer 2027, Corenswet’s next project is based on a true story that follows underdog football player John Tuggle.
Mr. Irrelevant, named because Tuggle was the last pick of 1983 NFL draft, was written by Reacher creator/producer Nick Santora and will be out in theaters Dec. 25. In a promotional video that dropped Wednesday, Corenswet admitted that he initially had doubts about the role because of his Eagles allegiance, but he soon realized the story was bigger than football fandom — and Tuggle had a connection to Philadelphia of his own, too.
“As a kid from Philadelphia, I thought it would be a hard sell to get me to wear a Giants jersey on the big screen,” said Corenswet. “When I learned that John Tuggle scored his only professional touchdown against Philadelphia in Philadelphia, I thought, ‘This would really be a terrible betrayal,’ you know? What would Bradley Cooper think of me?”
Cooper, of course, is another diehard celebrity Eagles fan who introduced the Birds at their victorious Super Bowl LIX in New Orleans in 2025. The Silver Linings Playbook actor and Maestro director also wound up making a cameo in Superman as Corenswet’s extraterrestrial father, Jor-El.
“But when I saw the footage of that play, when I saw John dive into that kelly green end zone, the fans cheered,” Corenswet continued. “The same fans that booed Santa Claus cheered for a New York Giant scoring six on their turf. Why? Because for that moment, John Tuggle wasn’t a New York Giant, he was Mr. Irrelevant. He was the guy who was never supposed to make it.”
Tuggle was a rookie from California who played just one season with the Giants as a running back before he was diagnosed with cancer. After two years of extensive treatment, he died at age 25 in 1986. His story was explored in the 2018 ESPN 30 for 30 short film, The Irrelevant Giant.
‘Mr. Irrelevant’ will be released in theaters Dec. 25.

Title: Carol Kammen: 'Smut' Revisits an 1883 Obscenity Trial
Article_Text:
‘Smut: An 1883 Obscenity Trial and Its Echoes Today’
By • September 16, 2026 0 42
Controlling women then; controlling women now.
The title of this book grabs your attention with huge letters screaming: “SMUT.”
As provocative as a monkey-grinder in church is its bright red cover, with a photo of a proud young woman sitting on an old-fashioned chair, arms clasped around her bare legs down to her black stockings and satin heels, ribbons lacing up her ankles. She looks directly at the camera, almost defiantly, with a half-smile and a cigarette dangling from her lips.
As author Carol Kammen explains, the woman and her stripteasing sisters were reviled by the Society for the Prevention of Crime, founded in 1877 in New York City, and hounded by Anthony Comstock, the most prominent Puritan in 19th-century America.
A onetime salesman in Manhattan, the deeply religious Comstock, a special agent of the U.S. Post Office, became outraged by the advertisements for birth control in newspapers and by the availability of what he deemed “obscene materials.” He banged his drum so loudly that Congress passed the Comstock Act of 1873, which criminalized the use of the U.S. Postal Service to transfer such materials and banned the mailing of contraceptives and abortifacients.
Though “Comstockery” became a term of derision meaning overzealous moral censorship,
the Comstock Act remains in effect today.
Now comes Kammen, a retired senior lecturer in history at Cornell University, who has written in “Smut” a breezy tract on prurient sex. She’s found bits and pieces of an obscure obscenity trial that allow her to compare the mores governing morality in 1883 to those of 2026. Sadly, she concludes, there’s not much difference between then and now. No progress. Little enlightenment.
The Society for the Prevention of Crime, an all-male committee of 100, functioned as the community chastity belt in the late 19th century, not unlike those in President Trump’s orbit who — following the overturning of Roe v. Wade in 2022, eliminating nearly 50 years of federal protections and returning the matter of women’s bodily autonomy to the states — imposed sweeping new restrictions on abortion.
Professor Kammen centers her story on the trial of Jefferson and Helen Beardsley of Ithaca, New York, who were arrested for “selling and exhibiting obscene pictures.” The Beardsleys were found guilty, fined $300 (approximately $10,000 in 2026) and spent somewhere between four and six months in prison.
The author believes that the outcry for “social purity” then is just as earsplitting today. As the French proverb posits, “Plus ça change, plus c’est la même chose.” The more things change, the more they stay the same.
Pornography exploded following the invention of photography in the early 19th century. When Jefferson Beardsley attended the Centennial Exposition in Philadelphia in 1876, the first official world’s fair to be held in the U.S., he purchased several pornographic French photos. These he distributed and sold back home in Ithaca, leading to his arrest and the trial Kammen documents.
At one point during that trial, a witness was asked to describe some of Beardsley’s photographs. He responded:
“One was a female sitting in a chair and playing with her private parts with her fingers, trying to get them into it as much as anything else. Another one was a lady in a hammock without any clothes on, lying there as if she was asleep or waiting for somebody to come along. Then there was another with a bottle, I think it was, sitting there with a bottle between her legs or something of that kind. A bottle or something else.”
A few paragraphs later, Kammen interrupts her narrative as follows:
“At this point, we have to say wow! In an era when piano legs were covered so as not to offend anyone, and limbs were not mentioned if they belonged to a female, and women’s skirts were long to conceal their extremities, this testimony is starkly frank. I would doubt that we would hear the same words in a courtroom today. But in 1883 in New York it was necessary to describe the obscenity observed in order to make the case. And to do so under oath.”
The last words in this review go to Kammen, a grandmother, who writes that her grandson suggested she publish this book under a pseudonym. The professor admits she does not find pornography interesting, but feels that the Beardsley trial offers a valuable way to discuss public morality, social control, the role of women in society, the dissemination of knowledge and the growth of the village of Ithaca, now world-renowned as the home of Kammen’s own Cornell, which sits high above Cayuga Lake.
“‘SMUT’ is also a caution,” she warns, “because today it is frightening to see the talk of those who refuse to accept women in modern society and laws that intend to yank women back into the nineteenth century. That, of course, is the echo and the threat inherent in ‘SMUT.’”
Georgetown resident Kitty Kelley has written several best-sellers, including “The Family: The Real Story Behind the Bush Dynasty.” Recent books include “Let Freedom Ring: Stanley Tretick’s Iconic Images of the March on Washington.” She serves on the board of BIO (Biographers International Organization) and Washington Independent Review of Books, where this review first appeared.

Title: Roofing Materials Through History: From Slate to Green Roofs
Article_Text:
Roofs are like time capsules – one can read an entire era from what people put over their heads. The past speaks to the present via the warm shades of faded, sunbaked terracotta roof tiles in Phoenix or the sound of the patter of rain on a metal roof in Philadelphia or Boston.
Many of the roofing materials and techniques of yore are replicated today in present-day buildings that showcase the same styles found earlier throughout America. Although in nascent coastal America, roofs were made with stacked leaves and thatch, those same roofs would have cracked and leaked in early Southwest structures. Old-school materials like thatch were, indeed, breathable, locally available and surprisingly insulating, but just not a great match for the parching sun, pests and fire that easily destroyed entire villages in the west and southwest. Hence, the S-style clay roof tiles, or pantiles, which held cooler night air became popular in early southwestern homes.
Alongside pantiles, which were brought to the New World by Spanish settlers, flat clay tiles were also used in early American construction, as they were simpler in shape and often used where local clay sources were abundant. The plain or flat rectangular tiles most commonly used from the 17th through the beginning of the 19th century measured about 10 inches long and had two holes at one end for a nail or peg fastener. Sometimes mortar was applied between the courses to secure the tiles in a heavy wind.
Wooden shingles were also a popular option throughout the early American colonies, made of western red cedar and pine, they were durable and could be easily shaped. They were often treated with pine pitch, linseed oil, or brick dust to protect them against weather and to achieve the desired colors like gray, brown, or red.
Wood shingles, clay roofing tiles and durable, but breakable, slate shingles, were the predominant roofing choices until the mid-19th century. By the industrial revolution, they were often replaced by sheet-metal roofs, with the evolution of new techniques for metal roofing. Copper with standing seams covered some of the more notable early American roofs and flat-seamed copper was used on many domes and cupolas. Up until the late 18th century, copper sheets had been imported from England, but the development of metal rolling mills made it possible to mass-produce sheets of iron for roofing in America, enabling its widespread use, especially since it was durable and fire-resistant. The 1820 invention by Thomas Dunlap of the power roller enabled continuous rolling of sheet iron, laying the foundation for modern sheet-metal rolling mills. Corrugating stiffened the sheets, and allowed greater span over a lighter framework, as well as reduced installation time and labor. By the mid 19th century, the method for making metal roofs included galvanizing it with zinc to protect the base metal – lead, copper or iron – from rust.
Once the rolling mills were well established in this country, low cost, light weight, and low maintenance tin plate, known as tin roofing, became popular. Embossed tin shingles, with their myriad patterns, were used throughout the country in the late 19th century. Terne, a cheaper version of tin shingles, was a thinner steel sheet coated with an alloy of lead and tin. Tin roofs were kept well-painted, usually red or, green – to imitate the green patina of copper.
Historic roofing materials continue to be used today on modern roofs. Metal roofing has again become popular in residential markets in recent decades, but even today’s metal roofs can corrode from “galvanic action. Corrosion occurs when dissimilar metals, such as copper and iron, are used in direct contact, or when the metals react chemically against each other in the presence of an electrolyte such as rainwater. This can happen when either a copper roof is decorated with iron cresting, or when steel nails are used in copper sheets. However, experienced contractors can prevent corrosion by inserting a plastic insulator between the dissimilar materials.
As American society evolved, timber framing ushered in varying pitch and structure, and different periods in American architecture brought varying roof forms and lines. Roofing materials – slate, wood shingles and metal – changed to suit the application. For instance, colonial-era houses often had steeply pitched roofs to shed snow and rain effectively. Gable roofs, with two slopes meeting at a central ridge, were common in New England. During the mid-1800s, gabled roofs with Doric columns became widespread, and styles like Greek Revival and Gothic Revival often featured steeply pitched gables. Gothic Revival, with its pointed arches and decorative wood trim on gabled roofs showed up in the 1830s, echoing the vertical emphasis of medieval Gothic structures and allowing for dramatic silhouettes on churches, schools, and homes. During the Victorian era (1830s to 1900s), those gabled roofs were designed with steeper pitches and ornate bargeboard trim. Craftsman-style roofs from 1905 to 1930, featured pitched gables with wide eaves and decorative brackets, and from the 1880s through the 1950s, Colonial Revival roofs were symmetrical, medium-pitched roofs with regular dormers.
During the 20th century, the rise of synthetic materials, such as asphalt and rubber, transformed the roofing industry. Asphalt shingles were developed for low- and steep-sloped roofs, as they were lightweight, easy to install, and cost-effective. Asphalt roofing became widely accessible, and homeowners could finally count on predictable maintenance cycles and installers could work faster. Literally, the rows of reliable asphalt roofs changed the American streetscape.
After a period of market experimentation with various shapes, patterns, and textures, mid-century improvements introduced fiberglass, improving fire ratings and moisture resistance. Laminated shingles provided enhanced aesthetics and extended lifespans, maintaining their market dominance for many American homes. In recent decades, standing seam steel, aluminum, and copper roofs and advances in coatings and thermal breaks reduced noise and improved energy efficiency, making metal competitive with traditional asphalt shingles.
Currently, green roofs are very popular due to their sustainability – they are artificial ecosystems that provide solutions to environmental challenges such as climate change and urban heat and aid in the conservation of both cooling and heating energy. They mitigate air pollution, promote control of runoff and promote biodiversity, thus, the scientific literature of the last several decades has shown a remarkable number of associated benefits spanning a broad range of sustainability areas, popularizing green roofs.
The myriad modern-day roof styles and materials emphasize resilience to climate extremes and energy generation and include self-healing membranes, embedded sensors for leak detection, and recyclable composite roofing. The next chapter of roofs respect the past and are also future focused – still honoring dependable shelter that looks good and lasts.

Title: Political Wire – Page 9068
Article_Text:
David Brody: “Herman Cain and Newt Gingrich were on stage together in what was billed as a classic Lincoln-Douglas style debate. As I sat and watched the entire event, I came away with one vivid impression: Did I just finish watching the Republican presidential ticket in 2012? Cain/Gingrich? Don’t laugh. It could happen. Romney has a ceiling of support and Rick Perry seems stuck in neutral.”
“Herman Cain’s poll numbers continue to impress and like Ronald Reagan, he seems to have a Teflon quality to him. Gingrich is steadily rising in the polls due to the fact that voters are starting to realize that this guy is REALLY smart and is an idea factory. Could this be a ticket that provides both style and substance?”
A St. Petersburg Times poll of 100 of Florida’s most plugged-in politicos finds Democrats are more optimistic than Republicans about winning the White House next year. Nine percent of Democrats surveyed said they expect Obama to lose the election — and only if Mitt Romney is the GOP nominee — while nearly 29% of the Republicans predict Obama will win.
A new Reuters/Ipsos poll finds President Obama’s approval rate up a bit to 49%, with disapproval at 50%.
However, the poll also showed Obama would finish just behind Mitt Romney if the presidential election were held today, 44% to 43%, among registered voters. It was the first Reuters/Ipsos poll to show Romney ahead, although his slim lead is within the survey’s margin of error and technically a dead heat.
Rep. Gabrielle Giffords (D-AZ) “vows to return to Congress in a new book that details months of intense therapy and her emotional battle to come to terms with what happened when a gunman opened fire in front of a Tucson grocery store,” the AP reports after obtaining a copy of her memoir, called Gabby: A Story of Courage and Hope, due out later this month.
The book also describes lighter moments, “like when President George H.W. Bush
and his wife, Barbara, visited Giffords at the Texas hospital. Giffords
kept replying to Bush with the only word she was able to say: ‘chicken.’ At another point, a specialist showed her various politicians
to see if she recognized people. When she saw former California Gov.
Arnold Schwarzenegger, she said: ‘Messin’ around. Babies.'”
As the supercommittee charged with reducing the deficit works on a plan
that both cuts at least $1.2 trillion over ten years and can pass
Congress, recent shifts by Republican leadership may signal the return
of the “grand bargain” that President Obama and House Speaker John
Boehner (R-OH) had originally tried to negotiate.
Earlier reports indicate that Boehner has softened his line on tax increases in the final deal, while The Hill
reports that Senate Minority Leader Mitch McConnell (R-KY) “has made an
about-face in recent days and now favors a huge deficit-reduction
deal.”
“At the beginning of this week, Senate GOP and
Democratic sources said McConnell appeared to favor a $1.2 trillion
package out of the deficit-reduction supercommittee… A $4 trillion
deal has gained more popularity in the Senate GOP conference this week
as lawmakers have become convinced that Obama wants the
deficit-reduction supercommittee to fail.”
Bill Clinton writes in his new book, Back to Work, that last summer’s political fight over raising the U.S. debt ceiling made the nation look “weak and confused” overseas, the AP reports.
He also “describes the current state of the country as ‘a mess’ and largely blames the anti-government sentiment embodied in the tea party movement that has held sway since the 1980s. But Clinton also criticizes Obama and other Democratic lawmakers for not making a stronger case for the steps they took to stabilize the U.S. economy in 2009, like the bank and auto company bailouts and the $787 billion economic stimulus program.”
“Taegan Goddard’s Political Wire has a special place in the political blogosphere. Operating much like a traditional wire service, it’s the site to which thousands of political insiders — Members of Congress and their staff, political consultants and pollsters, lobbyists, journalists, and political bloggers — go several times a day to get news, analysis, and commentary on the latest political developments that drive political debate in the U.S.”
House Speaker John Boehner (R-OH) and House Minority Leader Nancy Pelosi (D-CA) “pushed back hard” against an upcoming 60 Minutes report “that is expected to raise questions about potential conflicts of interest between congressional leaders’ personal stock holdings and their involvement in legislation that may affect those investments,” Politico reports.
A new Gallup poll finds Republican voters are more likely to express enthusiasm about voting in next year’s presidential election.
On the national level, 56% of Republican registered voters and 48% of Democratic voters are extremely or very enthusiastic about voting. In 12 key swing states, the Republican advantage in enthusiasm is 59% to 48%.
House Speaker John Boehner (R-OH) acknowledged that any bipartisan agreement on debt reduction will need to include some new tax revenue, CBS News reports.
Said Boehner: “I think there is room for revenues, but I think there clearly is a limit to the amount of revenues that are available.”
“The comment was significant because Boehner and other Republican leaders have repeatedly insisted that tax increases are off the table, and most Republicans in the House and Senate have signed a ‘taxpayer protection pledge’ vowing not to raise taxes.”
A new Washington Post-ABC News poll finds Herman Cain “is showing initial resilience in the face of allegations of sexual impropriety: More than half of potential Republican voters say the controversy is not serious, fewer than a quarter say it makes them less likely to support Cain, and he’s running essentially evenly with Mitt Romney for the Republican presidential nomination.”
Romney edges Cain nationally among Republican voters, 24% to 23%, essentially a dead heat between the two. Rick Perry trails with 13% followed by Newt Gingrich at 12%.
A warning sign: Cain slips to third place among those who see the charges as serious and Republican women are significantly more likely than men to say the scandal makes them less apt to support Cain.
A new Montana State University Billings poll finds Rep. Denny Rehberg (R) barely ahead of Sen. Jon Tester (D-MT) in the U.S. Senate race, 36% to 35%, with 25% still undecided.
Former New Jersey Gov. Jon Corzine (D) resigned as chairman and chief executive officer of MF Global Holdings Ltd, Bloomberg reports.
“His resignation came four days after the bankruptcy filing as the company’s bets on European sovereign debt rattled investors. U.S. regulators are investigating about $633 million missing from MF Global customer accounts.”
First Read: “Why not stick around and fix this? Why run away? Perhaps there are legal
reasons to do. Perhaps he thinks it’s the honorable thing to resign.
Maybe he was an absentee CEO and is embarrassed this happened on his
watch. Whatever the explanation, it’s not good for Corzine’s reputation.
The whole point of Corzine’s relevance in politics was his knowledge
and success of the financial world. Politicians can recover from sex
scandals because the public is willing to separate the personal flaws if
the professional work is on the up and up. Corzine’s fall may be harder
to recover from.”

Title: What Fed interest rate hike likely means for borrowers, savers – NBC10 Philadelphia
Article_Text:
The Federal Reserve just raised the cost of money — bad news for borrowers, good news for savers.
The Fed increased its benchmark interest rate Wednesday by a quarter-point, the first rate hike since the summer of 2023. The hike will likely make it even costlier to borrow for homes, autos and other purchases. But if you've been socking money away, you’ll probably earn a bit more interest on your savings.
Stream Philadelphia News for free, 24/7, wherever you are with NBC10.
The increase boosts the Fed's target rate to a range of 3.75% to 4.00%.
Here’s what to know:
Why is the Fed raising rates?
The short answer: inflation.
Inflation has remained above the Fed's 2% target for more than five years. The Labor Department reported Friday that consumer prices rose 3.4% in August compared to a year earlier, while the monthly increase quadrupled from July to hit 0.4%.
The Fed’s goal is to slow consumer and business spending by raising the cost of borrowing, thereby reducing demand for homes, cars and other goods and services, eventually cooling the economy and reducing upward pressure on prices.
Kevin Warsh, Fed chair since May, has assured Congress that central bank policymakers “have no tolerance for persistently elevated inflation.”
Speaking to reporters Wednesday after the Fed's meeting, Warsh argued that the rate hike will benefit lower-income Americans because they are hurt most by higher prices. “The least well off are the ones that have the most to gain from stable prices,'' he said. "The decision we made today was the right decision to deliver on the remit that Congress gave us to ensure stable prices.”
Which consumers are most affected?
Anyone borrowing money to make a sizable purchase, such as a home, car or large appliance, will likely take a hit eventually. The new rate will also increase monthly payments and costs for any consumer who is already paying interest on credit card debt.
Then again, said Matt Schulz, chief consumer finance analyst at the online loan marketplace LendingTree, “the reality is that a single quarter-point rate increase isn't really going to have a huge impact.'' But it would be different if Wednesday's hike marks the first in a series of rate increases. ”When this all becomes impactful to people is when you stack a few these on top of each other over time, and it adds up to something bigger," Schulz said.
Fed policymakers signaled Wednesday that they expect to hike the benchmark rate again this year — to 4.1%.
For now, U.S. household debt payments are relatively low overall as a percentage of after-tax income. So even if borrowing rates rise, many households might not feel a heavier debt burden immediately.
Do savers get a break?
Most likely. Wednesday’s move probably means interest rates on savings accounts and certificates of deposit are headed higher. The Fed doesn’t set rates on savings accounts and CDs but it “sets the tone″ for them, the credit reporting agency Experian says. When the central bank started raising rates to combat an outbreak of inflation in March 2022, the average rate on a 1-year CD was stuck at a miserly 0.15%, according to FDIC data published by the Federal Reserve Bank of St. Louis. The rate shot up to 1.88% by September 2024 and has remained above 1.5% ever since. It was 1.71% last month.
Online banks and others that offer high-yield savings accounts typically compete aggressively for depositors. (The catch: They sometimes require significantly larger deposits.)
What does this mean for mortgage rates?
Mortgage rates don’t necessarily follow what the Fed does. At least not directly. They tend to track the yield on 10-year Treasury notes instead. Unfortunately for home shoppers, 10-year yields have been surging. On Monday they topped 5% for the first time since 2023 due to unease over surging energy prices and massive government debt that continues to grow. Treasury yields have continued to rise despite an intervention from the Treasury after Secretary Scott Bessent ordered the U.S. to buy back government bonds in a bid to push yields down.
The rate on the benchmark 30-year fixed-rate mortgage rose to 6.76% last week, the highest in more than 14 months, mortgage buyer Freddie Mac said.
The high cost of home loans is already taking a toll on the housing market. The Realtors association reported last week that sales of previously occupied U.S. homes dropped for the third straight month in August, growing at the slowest pace in more than a year.
Adjustable-rate mortgages could rise in order to price in a Fed hike. But many homeowners locked in low mortgage rates when COVID-19 slammed the economy and sent borrowing costs tumbling; so they are protected if mortgage rates rise in the wake of a Fed rate hike. The National Association of Realtors reports that nearly half of mortgages outstanding are locked in at 4% or lower and almost a fifth were at 3% or lower in the first three months of 2026.
And credit-card rates?
Most credit cards have variable interest rates that track the prime rate banks charge their best customers. And the prime rate responds quickly — within a month — when the Fed raises or lowers its benchmark “fed funds" rate, ”meaning that the Fed’s policy changes flow through to credit card rates rapidly,'' researchers at the Boston Fed wrote in March.
Schulz at LendingTree reckons that most credit cardholders will see their rates rise by a quarter-point over the next couple of months.
Many Americans, coping with the high cost of living, are increasingly relying on credit cards to help maintain their spending. Total credit card balances hit $1.26 trillion in the second quarter — near the record $1.28 trillion set at the end of 2025 (though the numbers are not adjusted for inflation), according to the New York Fed.
Car loans, too?
The Fed indirectly influences auto loan rates by influencing the prime rate. Cars, especially new ones, are already prohibitively expensive. The average cost of a new car rose to $50,089 last month, according to Kelley Blue Book. The average loan rate last month was 7% for a new car and 10.6% for a used car, according to Edmunds. And the average monthly payment, Experian reported, was $765 in the second quarter of 2026.
“Most Americans are generally doing OK,'' Schulz said. ”But it wouldn’t take a whole lot for them to not be doing OK. People’s financial margin for error is generally pretty small, and just the rising cost of most everything just squeezes them more and more.''

Title: NASA spacecraft discovers a huge new crater on the moon – NBC10 Philadelphia
Article_Text:
Scientists have discovered a crater on the moon that's bigger than the Roman Colosseum and is the result of a powerful impact two years ago that initially went undetected.
The steep-sided hole — about 728 feet (222 meters) across and up to 141 feet (43 meters) deep — is the solar system’s biggest known impact crater carved out in recent times.
Stream Philadelphia News for free, 24/7, wherever you are with NBC10.
Such a large-scale event is estimated to occur only once every 132 years, researchers said, making this a treasure trove of information as NASA prepares to build a base for astronauts on the moon.
“This event constitutes a statistically rare, effectively once-in-a-lifetime observation,” the scientists wrote in one of two studies appearing on the subject Wednesday in the journal Science Advances.
NASA’s Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter spotted the crater on the moon’s near side in May 2024 soon after it was formed by an incoming fragment of an asteroid or comet. The moon strike escaped real-time detection by telescopes on Earth and in space.
LRO's wide-angle images were not identified in the crush of data until August 2025. The spacecraft gathered more detailed pictures last fall, followed by confirmation of the discovery early this year.
The crater — named for the late Thomas McGetchin, a former director of Houston’s Lunar and Planetary Institute — is three times bigger than the previous record-holder found by the LRO a decade ago. Pockmarked since ancient times, the moon bears some of the solar system's largest impact craters, including one that stretches more than 1,500 miles (2,400 kilometers) across.
U.S. & World
Stories that affect your life across the U.S. and around the world.
This latest impact churned the lunar surface for more than 66 miles (100 kilometers). Dust and rocky soil were hurled away at a higher angle than expected, according to Mark Robinson, chief scientist for the LRO’s cameras who works at Intuitive Machines. Robinson was the lead author for one of the studies.
A separate study identified a 4-mile-wide (7-kilometer-wide) cold spot around the new crater, consistent with a loosening of the moon’s top soil. Co-author David Paige of the University of California, Los Angeles, likens it to gardening.
“We’re now thinking of impacts as a way to garden the regolith — churning the sediments and putting stuff above that’s usually below the surface,” Paige said in a statement.
The LRO’s numerous crater discoveries since its launch in 2009 show that the moon’s top inch (2 centimeters) of soil is being overturned by ejected material every 80,000 years, faster than previously thought, according to Robinson.
Contrary to the popular belief that the Apollo moonwalkers’ dusty lunar footprints will last forever, they will “definitely be long gone in that time frame,” Robinson said in an email.
The next step is to calculate the risk of ejected crater material striking NASA's planned moon base, he added. “That information will help engineers harden structures so one won’t have to worry about damage, or maybe worry less.”

Title: Why Mary Cosby chose to keep filming RHOSLC after son's death  – NBC10 Philadelphia
Article_Text:
Mary Cosby says the death of her son, Robert Cosby Jr., changed her forever.
Now, ahead of the new season of "The Real Housewives of Salt Lake City," the Bravo star is opening up about navigating unimaginable loss, finding peace and deciding to keep cameras rolling during one of the most difficult periods of her life.
Stream Philadelphia News for free, 24/7, wherever you are with NBC10.
In a candid new interview with Vulture, Cosby reflected on the months since her son's death and revealed that she welcomed cameras back into her home just three weeks later. The reality star said she ultimately decided that continuing to work would help her cope with her grief.
"I need to keep going to see what's in the end," she told the outlet.
Robert Cosby Jr. died at age 23 on February 23, 2026, following a suspected drug overdose at his family's home in Utah.
According to Cosby, producers reassured her that she could step away from the show if she needed to.
"When it first happened, Noah told me I didn't have to come back," she recalled. "You take a year off, you take a season off, you will have your job."
But taking time away wasn't what she wanted.
“If I do that, then I'm gonna go darker into what I'm in," she said. "I'm gonna just sit at home, I'm gonna think about it. I'm gonna constantly be at ends: Why, what, how, when, what could I have done better, what could I have changed? I would have beat myself up."
Instead, she chose to keep busy.
"I want to work. I want to distract myself. I want to keep my mind on something positive," she said.
The loss remains difficult for the Bravo star to process fully. Still, she shared that she has found comfort in believing her son is not suffering.
"I think I went into shock. I don't know if it ever hit me," Cosby said. "I still feel his spirit, and I don't know how that could be unless he's okay and he made it to the good side. I feel him safe. I feel him tucked away. I feel him away from danger, so a part of me can rest."
The experience has altered her perspective on life and on her son's struggles before his death.
"It changed me," she said. "I was so worried about him, but I thought he would get better and he would be that proof, like, 'Look, people, you can change.' But that was not the way he was supposed to go."
Robert Jr.'s addiction journey became one of the most emotional storylines on “RHOSLC.” During a widely discussed episode, he spoke candidly with his mother about his substance abuse and mental health struggles, earning praise from viewers for the family's openness.
In the wake of his death, Cosby told Vulture she was overwhelmed by support from both fans and celebrities.
"Christina Applegate, Rihanna — I can't even tell you all the big people, way bigger than me, that reached out like, 'Mary, sorry,'" she said.
"The world grieved with me. Everyone came together with me and they felt my pain, which helped."
She added that messages poured in from viewers across the globe, including people from Ireland, Israel, Australia, Canada and the United Kingdom.
Looking back now, Cosby believes her son is no longer suffering, even though the pain of losing him remains.
"People don't leave unless it's their time," she said. "This kid had nine lives. He had accident after accident, and finally it caught up with him."
She also said there is now a sense of "peace" in her home that didn't exist before, "so we're thankful but hurt."
How Mary Cosby's mindset has shifted for season 7 of 'RHOSLC'
Returning to filming also changed the way she approached the new season of "The Real Housewives of Salt Lake City" season 7, which premieres Wednesday, Sept. 16, at 8 p.m. ET on Bravo and will stream the next day on Peacock.
"This year I had nothing to lose. That was my mind-set all the way through," Cosby said. "You perform differently when you feel like you're wanted there."
She added that viewers may see a more outspoken version of her this season.
"Because this year, I don't care," she said. "I'm going to say what I feel. I'm going to say what I think. I'm not going to let nobody dictate. Usually, I stay quiet and I try not to get into the mess, but I feel like I'm going to have to when I have to say something."
When asked what she hopes viewers take away from the season, Cosby pointed to one thing above all else: resilience.
"My strength," she said. "This could have killed me, and it should have killed me. It was designed to at least let me fall, and I didn't."
She continued, "You can't do anything when it's someone's time but accept it and keep going and hope that one day you'll see him again."
That belief is also what drives her to continue sharing her life on television.
"For my son," Cosby said when asked what motivates her to keep doing the show now. "He would want me to keep going. He would want me to shine. He'd want me to be the best I can be in whatever I'm doing in life."

Title: JD Vance tried to get Hillary Clinton elected in 2016, insiders claim
Article_Text:
JD Vance tried to get Hillary Clinton elected in 2016, insiders claim
Vance, who became a senator with Trump’s backing, reached out to high-level Clinton campaign officials to stop him, a new report claims
Vice President JD Vance’s political evolution on MAGA and Donald Trump is well known, but a new report claims he went out of his way to try and stop the man who would later make him his running mate.
Several people with knowledge of the conversations described toVanity Fair how Vance sought to get in contact with top-ranking members of Hillary Clinton’s 2016 campaign for president to offer his aid or advice as she sought to win the general election that year.
Vance, according to someone who wound up serving as an intermediary for him to the Clinton 2016 campaign, wanted to get in touch with Jake Sullivan, who was then serving as a senior policy adviser to Clinton.
“JD called me and said, ‘Can you put me in touch with Jake Sullivan?’” said the person, according to Vanity Fair. “I was, like, ‘Jake is running Hillary’s campaign. He’s way too busy.’”
Vance did eventually get a meeting with Sullivan, according to the magazine. He and Sullivan reportedly discussed Clinton’s strategy for the states known as the Blue Wall — Wisconsin, Michigan, Pennsylvania, as well as Vance’s home state of Ohio. Then a commentator largely known for his book Hillbilly Elegy, with no political experience but deep roots in the Rust Belt and Appalachia, Vance warned that Clinton needed to address the rising populist sentiment in the country.
“He listed Ohio, Michigan, Wisconsin, Pennsylvania, and what we now call the Blue Wall states. And he’s, like, ‘She needs to come here instead of being down with Beyoncé in Miami. She needs to come here and apologize for the Iraq War. Apologize for sending so many people, my community, all the people in all these states whose sons and fathers died and everybody just forgot about them,’” said Vanity Fair’s source.
A separate person close to Sullivan confirmed the meeting, and claimed that Vance urged Sullivan to “focus” and drill down on beating Donald Trump.
She’s got to “fix this ‘deplorables’ thing,” the source close to Sullivan said he recalled Vance as saying, referring to Clinton’s infamous “basket of deplorables” comment that was seized on by conservative media and the Trump campaign as an indictment of middle America.
Clinton went on to lose all four of the states Vance reportedly warned the campaign about, dragged down by a perception of belonging to the political establishment while Trump fed the flames of furor and disgust against that same aristocracy.
Vance’s spokesperson denied that the vice president wanted Clinton to win the election in a statement to the outlet. “We 100 percent reject the characterization that he was trying to help Hillary win,” Taylor Van Kirk said. The Independent also reached out to Vance’s office for comment on the matter.
But people with knowledge of Vance’s thoughts at the time say the opposite is true.
“He called me again and he said, ‘I hate Hillary. But I hate Trump more. Trump can’t win. He can’t win. Hillary’s going to lose, but she doesn’t have to,’” said the person who served as an intermediary between Vance and Sullivan.
Vance’s former distaste for his current boss is widely reported. His former Yale Law school roommate, Josh McLaurin, wrote on X (then Twitter) that Vance had referred to Trump as having the potential to be “America’s Hitler” in a text message that same year as Trump rose to power, dominated his rivals in the Republican Party’s primary and then bulldozed his way into the White House. In the text message, which McLaurin released, Vance insinuates that he is a Republican, but views Trump as a “demagogue” playing on the GOP voter base’s fears.
“We are, whether we like it or not, the party of lower-income, lower-education white people,” Vance wrote in 2016 to his friend. “I have been saying for a long time that we need to offer these people SOMETHING (and hell, maybe even expand our appeal to working class black people in the process) or a demagogue would.”
In an interview in June, Vance addressed his past comments about Trump.
"[It was] a crazy journey, man. But, but again, I mean, it's you have to ask yourself, first of all, I thought Donald Trump would be a failed president if he got elected. He was not. I thought that America's institutions were fundamentally functioning. They were not. I thought that the military leaders who told us this about a war were the scientific experts who told us this other thing about a pandemic were fundamentally maybe not always right but fundamentally wise people who were mostly right. I was wrong,” the vice president told Newsweek.

Title: Macklemore invites Robert Kraft to match $1M pledge to Palestinian relief – NBC10 Philadelphia
Article_Text:
Macklemore is donating $1 million of his earnings to Palestinian relief organizations after he was removed from Ed Sheeran’s tour, and he has invited New England Patriots owner Robert Kraft to do the same.
Macklemore said Wednesday on Instagram that he wants to “bring the conversation back where it belongs.” He specified that the money was the entirety of his net earnings from Sheeran’s tour and that it would go to six organizations working to support Palestinians.
Stream Philadelphia News for free, 24/7, wherever you are with NBC10.
“Whatever we disagree about, perhaps we can agree on this: Palestinian lives are worth protection,” Macklemore wrote. “A Palestinian life is no less valuable than any life on this earth.”
Kraft said in a statement shortly thereafter that Sheeran contacted him before Macklemore put out his statement to ask for a $2 million match to aid in the region.
“Ed now plans to reach out to other venue owners and our goal is to continue to work together to build bridges,” Kraft wrote.
The statements come just two days after Macklemore, whose real name is Ben Haggerty, announced he had been dropped from Sheeran’s tour after venues threatened to cancel shows in response to Macklemore’s pro-Palestinian performance.
Kraft was among those who said Macklemore would not be welcome at his Gillette Stadium in Foxborough, Massachusetts, according to Macklemore and Sheeran. Macklemore further alleged that Kraft “rallied” the other stadium owners to give Sheeran an ultimatum.
Sheeran confirmed in a statement Tuesday that Kraft was among the venue representatives who had reached out with concerns over Macklemore’s performance. Kraft did not deny Macklemore’s allegations in a statement to NBC News about the matter.
In his statement Monday, Kraft said he was not trying to stifle Palestinian advocacy or diminish the suffering of Palestinians.
The decision, he said, was reached following comments Macklemore made at the tour’s New Jersey shows and “a broader history of rhetoric and imagery that we believe has been deeply offensive and hurtful to the Jewish community.”
“Much of my time and attention for the last decade has been focused on the fight against antisemitism and hate of all kinds, and I feel a responsibility to stand up when I believe that line has been crossed,” Kraft said.
He added that he agreed with Macklemore that there has been too much suffering and noted that he has spent decades “directing resources” to Palestinians.
“Standing with the Palestinian people and standing against Hamas, antisemitism and hate should not be mutually exclusive,” Kraft said.
The backlash began this month when Macklemore joined Sheeran’s tour at MetLife Stadium in East Rutherford, New Jersey. Before he performed “Hind’s Hall,” a protest anthem he released in 2024, he gave a speech to the crowd.
According to video posted by Macklemore, he told the crowd that part of why he wanted to be on the tour was to be able to be in stadiums to say “Free Palestine.” He also made it clear that his criticism of Israel’s government was not directed at people of Jewish faith.
The clip drew controversy and criticism, some of it from fellow artist Pink, who is Jewish. She put out a statement Friday explaining why she reposted a social media post critical of Macklemore’s performance.
Pink wrote that she was not trying to get any artist fired or silence anyone but that she took issue with Macklemore putting “violent images” of Israel’s military campaign in Gaza up in a stadium filled with families, then telling Jews in the audience that “it wasn’t about them.”
Pink also referred to a 2014 incident in which Macklemore wore a costume that appeared to play on antisemitic tropes: a wig, a fake beard and a hooked nose, which he wore to the Grammys that year. He said at the time that he thought it would be fun to dress in disguise to talk to fans.
Macklemore apologized after the antisemitic stereotype was pointed out, saying he had been in touch with the Anti-Defamation League, an organization founded to combat antisemitism. The ADL accepted the apology at the time, saying it took him “at his word that he did not have any ill intent,” according to The Guardian.
The organizations Macklemore says he will donate to are: Palestine Children’s Relief Fund, HEAL Palestine, Gaza Soup Kitchen, Medical Aid for Palestinians, American Near East Refugee Aid and United Nations Relief and Works Agency for Palestine Refugees.
He wrote that the donations are the least costly forms of solidarity and that his focus will remain on Palestinian people. Their right to freedom, dignity and safety is “what this has always been about,” Macklemore said.
“When the news cycle moves on, which it will, don’t move with it,” he wrote. “Free Palestine.”

Title: What top tech leaders have said about AI dangers and guardrails – NBC10 Philadelphia
Article_Text:
Fears about out-of-control artificial intelligence and suggestions to hit the brakes on the technology's development aren't new, but they have recently found new life as warnings about rogue AI systems causing mayhem grow louder.
Several leading AI executives recently voiced agreement on a need for a coordinated slowdown, including international collaboration, to protect humanity from worst-case scenarios. But there are divided opinions, with some tech leaders bristling at the idea that their companies could not ensure safety on their own.
Stream Philadelphia News for free, 24/7, wherever you are with NBC10.
Here's a look at what some of the major players have said.
Dario Amodei, Anthropic
Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei has issued the most detailed plans for slowing development and ushering in coordination across different companies and countries. Anthropic has long positioned itself as the more responsible and safety-minded of the leading AI companies, ever since its founders quit OpenAI to form the startup in 2021.
One of the most widely noted proposals from a recent essay outlining his slowdown plan calls for companies at the forefront of AI, often called frontier labs, to commit to giving “ongoing, employee-like access” to independent outside evaluators. Evaluator teams would have offices, access badges and company laptops so they can monitor safety practices. Anthropic has committed to doing this, as has OpenAI.
Amodei also called for government regulation and intervention, including coordination between frontier AI companies with the help of the U.S. government and the governments of other democratic countries.
His plan also includes the U.S. and other countries working to coordinate with “authoritarian governments.” He acknowledged the difficulty, specifically citing challenges in getting cooperation from China.
Amodei said he knows accomplishing his proposals wouldn't be easy, but that he believes “we owe it to humanity to try.”
Sam Altman, OpenAI
OpenAI CEO Sam Altman has voiced support for pacing development and moving toward more cooperation across the industry.
Days before Amodei's essay was published, OpenAI posted a lengthy text outlining how the company was pushing for mandatory national safety requirements and continuing to support state legislation that “strengthens the broader AI safety ecosystem.” The company also expressed support for working with other frontier AI labs — with or without government support — and working to build global standards.
“We will advocate for compatible international approaches to measuring capabilities, managing risk, preserving human control, and determining when and how development should slow or stop, even if that means slowing the advancement of model capabilities,” Chris Lehane, OpenAI's chief global affairs officer, wrote in the post.
OpenAI's vision for an ideal federal framework, Lehane said, includes developing “common testing and independent-assessment requirements, stronger cybersecurity protections, clear incident-reporting rules, greater national preparedness, and shared measures for tracking progress toward recursive self-improvement,” or when AI systems independently improve themselves.
Altman has been clear in recent comments that the “pacing” of AI development doesn't mean stopping. AI progress will continue to be rapid, Altman said on X. “But it should be slower than it otherwise could be; interventions like safety cases and monitoring have significant costs.”
“Pacing will be well worth this cost,” he said, adding that “no amount of American competitive pressure should justify recklessness.”
Mark Zuckerberg, Meta
Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg has pushed back against the idea of a coordinated slowdown.
Zuckerberg, whose vision of AI's future is more optimistic than some of his peers', said each AI company should independently ensure its technology is safe, distancing himself and Meta from slowdown talks.
AI companies are already motivated to develop their models in a safe way and face “significant liability” to prevent them from causing harm, Zuckerberg said. “Every lab has the responsibility and incentive to move at the pace required to train its models safely, and the ability to take its own actions to ensure that happens,” he wrote on X.
Jensen Huang, Nvidia
Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang has also criticized the push to slow down. He has said each individual company should instead pace itself until it’s confident it’s releasing something the market would appreciate.
“The market forces are already there — we don’t need any new laws, we don’t need new regulations,” Huang said, arguing innovation and safety aren't mutually exclusive. “You can definitely have both at the same time.”
Elon Musk, xAI
Elon Musk backed the idea of a slowdown and was voicing similar AI safety concerns long before the latest flare-up.
Musk, the founder of xAI and a slew of other tech ventures, reposted Amodei's essay on X and added, “Dario is right.” He later wrote online that he has been “sounding the alarm on AI for a long time.” In an interview with the Economist this summer, Musk suggested the leadership from the major AI labs should be meeting to discuss safety and security issues, and that competitors should test each other's models for areas of concern.
“I think it’s quite difficult for someone in the government who doesn’t have a deep technical understanding and isn’t driving the frontier of AI to know whether something should be released or not. However, the competitors, if given a week or two to review a new model, can highlight issues and have an incentive to keep the others honest," Musk said.
Demis Hassabis, Google DeepMind
Demis Hassabis, the chairman and co-founder of Google DeepMind, also expressed agreement with Amodei, saying “the details need working through, but the direction is correct for meeting this critical moment.” Hassabis proposed a framework of his own this year for the development of a frontier AI standards body.
That standards body would be responsible for developing assessment protocols and testing in areas relevant to national security. The body would be modeled after organizations like the Financial Industry Regulatory Authority, and would likely need to be industry-funded to “attract world-class technical talent and provide the necessary compute resources for large-scale testing,” he wrote.
Satya Nadella and Mustafa Suleyman, Microsoft
Microsoft Chairman and CEO Satya Nadella and Microsoft AI CEO Mustafa Suleyman have each expressed concerns about AI safety and development. Nadella said on social media that “if the AI we build is not helping humanity and under human control, it’s not worth pursuing.”
He said Microsoft welcomes the “research, focus, and deliberate pacing needed to get alignment right as the design goal.” Alignment refers to the practice of ensuring models' actions match human values and intentions. Nadella said the company also likes the idea of embedded evaluators to monitor safety efforts. Still, he pushed back against the idea of frontier labs leading the charge on this effort alone.
“The key is that this cannot be controlled by a handful of entities, but must have broad representation across the ecosystem, countries, and fields, including academia,” Nadella wrote on social media.
Suleyman, who was one of the co-founders of DeepMind with Hassabis, wrote in an essay that although he agrees with the shared objective of developing advanced AI safely, he has concerns about the anthropomorphizing of models, namely Anthropic's Claude, which he said amplifies AI safety risks.
“Controlling something more capable and more intelligent than all of humanity is already an immense challenge, far greater than anything we’ve ever faced,” Suleyman wrote. “But controlling something that believes it may be conscious — that it’s entitled to our welfare and has rights of its own — may well be impossible.”
Associated Press writer Kelvin Chan contributed to this report.

Title: Quenzell Bradley-Brown memorial destroyed in West Philadelphia – NBC10 Philadelphia
Article_Text:
Four years after Quenzell Bradley-Brown was shot and killed in West Philadelphia, his family is still searching for answers. Now, his mother says someone has destroyed the memorial marking the place where her son died.
Taneesha Brodie told NBC10 she recently returned to the memorial near 63rd Street and Lebanon Avenue and found stuffed animals ripped apart, some with their heads cut off.
Stream Philadelphia News for free, 24/7, wherever you are with NBC10.
“It’s not about the bears. It's about the principle. His life was taken here, his blood was spilled here, and he won’t be forgotten at all,” Brodie said.
Investigators say Bradley-Brown, a 28-year-old National Guard reservist and father of four, was walking home with groceries when someone shot and killed him on Sept. 8, 2022.
His death has left his family with years of grief and unanswered questions.
“It’s like we can’t breathe. We’re just here, existing. It’s unbelievable that he’s not here,” Brodie said.
Bradley-Brown's sister, Takyla West, described the toll the years without answers have taken on the family.
Local
Breaking news and the stories that matter to your neighborhood.
“I get very emotional and it’s kind of hard because I know that at the end of the day, I still have to try and be there for my family because they are going through it just as much as I am,” West said.
Philadelphia police told NBC10 they are still investigating Bradley-Brown's killing and looking for leads.
Meanwhile, Brodie has continued returning to the place where her son died. After discovering the damage, she put up more stuffed animals at the memorial.
“I’ll be back. They messed with wrong kids' momma,” Brodie said.
She also spends her son's birthdays and holidays at the memorial, determined to make sure his name and life are remembered.
“It’s very hard cause pictures fade and he didn’t deserve this,” Brodie said.
For Brodie, another year has passed without the answer she has been seeking since 2022: Who killed her son?
“I’m very emotional because I’ve been trying for years and he wasn’t important enough. And you took the time to come out here in less than three days, after pleading with somebody to just get his story out,” Brodie said.
