Title: Mayor Parker creates task force for data center guardrails – NBC10 Philadelphia
Article_Text:
Amid concerns from communities across the country and calls for a moratorium in Philadelphia, Mayor Cherelle Parker signed an executive order to create a task force to establish guardrails for any potential data centers in the city.
Parker initially announced on Monday, Sept. 14, that she had mobilized the task force across the city’s Planning and Development, Sustainability, Public Health, the Water Department, Licenses and Inspections and Clean and Green departments over the summer.
Stream Philadelphia News for free, 24/7, wherever you are with NBC10.
“This week, I will sign an Executive Order to formalize the Task Force,” Parker wrote on Monday. “By putting rigorous guardrails in place, we will ensure that any incoming tech infrastructure directly serves our vision of a safer, cleaner, and greener Philadelphia."
On Wednesday, Sept. 16, Parker officially signed the order, NBC10 confirmed.
According to Parker, the task force’s mission is to “establish enforceable standards for data centers that protect our infrastructure, water supply, and local neighborhoods.”
Data centers are facilities used to house computer systems and serve as infrastructure for storing and processing information. They also support the global financial system, cloud services, machine learning and artificial intelligence (AI).
Rising electricity costs and a strain on electric grids fueled by the growth of the AI industry have led to significant backlash to proposed data centers from communities across the country, including towns and neighborhoods in New Jersey and Pennsylvania. Other critics of data centers have expressed concerns about their environmental impact as well as AI’s potential threat to millions of jobs.
On Aug. 18, 2026, Pennsylvania Gov. Josh Shapiro signed an executive order which he said would place the strictest guardrails in the nation on data centers and developers. The order includes requirements for large data center projects to disclose projected water and energy use and pay for costs associated with connecting to the electric grid.
In July, Philadelphia’s planning commission held an informational meeting in which they identified two potential locations – one on 3143 West Passyunk Avenue and the other on 2600 Grant Avenue – where a large data center could be built. Officials have said there are no plans to build a data center in Philadelphia at this time, however.
In response to the meeting, concerned residents and groups have called for Philadelphia to issue a moratorium on data centers. Protesters held a “No Data Centers in Philly” rally outside City Hall early Monday afternoon, hours before Parker’s announcement on the task force. They urged City Council to pause potential data center development in Philadelphia and establish guardrails.
“Two potential data center sites have already been identified in Philly, but right now our city has no rules on how communities should be protected,” organizers wrote. “That’s a recipe for disaster. City Council can and must pass a moratorium and pause data center construction so leaders and Philadelphians can write strong guidelines to protect our health, affordability, and quality of life. We can’t let an industry that raises our PECO bills, pollutes air and water and powers surveillance expand without guardrails; that’s what will happen if Council doesn’t act.”
Vincent Thompson, communications director for Philadelphia City Council President Kenyatta Johnson, issued a statement in response to the protest protest.
"Philadelphia City Council members and Mayor Cherelle Parker's administration continue discussions on the future of data centers in the city,” Thompson wrote on Monday. “At this time, no legislation or resolution has been introduced in City Council."
Parker then made her announcement on the data center task force a few hours later.
During an interview with NBC10's Lauren Mayk for her Battleground Politics podcast, Pennsylvania House Speaker Joanna McClinton said that the state "wouldn't be in a space for a moratorium" on data centers. She also mentioned potential legislation that would continue to place guardrails on data center development in Pennsylvania, however.
NBC10 investigative reporter David Charns toured one of the largest data centers in the country to examine the questions driving the nationwide debate over how they’re impacting the environment and communities. You can read and watch his full report here.

Title: Philly officials give update on city's municipal trash contract – NBC10 Philadelphia
Article_Text:
Philadelphia officials laid out plans Wednesday for where to send Philadelphia's waste, with a new contract on the table that would burn less trash than before.
During a news conference, Managing Director Carlton Williams shared new details of a plan that will now head to City Council amid growing debate over the city's waste disposal strategy.
Stream Philadelphia News for free, 24/7, wherever you are with NBC10.
Councilmember Mark Squilla said he will introduce the "Zero Waste Circular Economy Act" on Thursday, which outlines a long-term plan to move away from landfills and incineration.
"The plan sets goals for achieving a 60 percent overall waste diversion rate," Squilla said.
The news briefing came just over a month after NBC10's Lauren Mayk reported on the controversy surrounding the city's negotiations over a new contract with waste management company Reworld amid debate over where the city's trash will end up.
One of the main questions surrounding the city's solid waste contract is how much waste would be sent to the company's incinerator in Chester, Pennsylvania, and whether City Council will approve the agreement. The city collects more than 600,000 tons of trash each year, and deciding where that waste ends up has become the subject of growing debate.
Currently, about 40% of Philadelphia's trash is sent to an incinerator. In late July, Sanitation Commissioner Crystal Jacobs Shipman said that percentage could change under a new agreement but declined to provide specifics while negotiations continued.
Local
Breaking news and the stories that matter to your neighborhood.
"It very well could be less than 40%," Shipman said.
On Wednesday, officials said the Zero Waste Circular Economy Act will bring a "modernized strategy" to how the city disposes of trash, but said it will take years to implement.
Councilmember Jamie Gauthier has expressed opposition to a new contract with Reworld and introduced legislation that would prohibit Philadelphia from sending its trash to incinerators.
"There is a cleaner and safer alternative that we can choose today," Gauthier said.
She argued that sending more waste to landfills is a better option than incineration and said City Council should reject the agreement when it comes up for a vote.
Following Wednesday's news conference, Gauthier said the new plan is "not enough."
Now, it's up to City Council to decide whether to approve the proposed plan. If the plan is not approved, the process will start over.

Title: Indiana man travels to Montgomery County to be with teen: Docs – NBC10 Philadelphia
Article_Text:
A 20-year-old man from Indiana is facing charges after he traveled to Montgomery County to engage in sex acts with a teen he met on Roblox, an online gaming platform, prosecutors said.
According to prosecutors, Ian Anderson was living in Indiana when he first began chatting with his then-13-year-old victim. At some point, Anderson traveled to Montgomery County and rented an apartment in the area to be close to his victim and be with her in person, prosecutors said.
Stream Philadelphia News for free, 24/7, wherever you are with NBC10.
Chats obtained by authorities show that Anderson knew his victim was underage and told her he loved her and planned to take her away from her family when she was a legal adult, prosecutors said.
The chats also showed that the teen protested Anderson's move to Montgomery County, prosecutors said.
In one incident, Anderson snuck into the teen's home while her parents were sleeping, prosecutors said.
According to court documents, Anderson faces 24 felonies, including statutory sexual assault, child sexual abuse material and disseminating photo/film of child sex acts or child sexual material.
Resources for victims of sexual assault are available through the National Sexual Violence Resources Center and the National Sexual Assault Telephone Hotline at 800-656-4673.
Local
Breaking news and the stories that matter to your neighborhood.
As of Wednesday afternoon, Anderson remained in custody unable to post his $1,000,000 bail, according to court documents.
Anderson requested a reduction in his bail at a court hearing on Wednesday, but the judge denied the request.
Anderson's lawyer declined to comment for this article and Roblox has not provided comment as of this article's publishing.
Protecting children from online predators
Leslie Slingsby, CEO of Mission Kids Child Advocacy Center, said that crimes against children are rising, particularly online.
"So, actually, the NICMIC, the National Center for Exploited and Missing Children, saw a 158% increase on child solicitation and enticement cases in 2025 versus 2024," she said.
In the in-person world, child victims know their abusers as members of their community 90% of the time, Slingsby said. But online, victims are less likely to know their abusers, she said.
To protect children, parents need to do more than set parental control settings on phones and devices, Slingsby said. In order to ensure children are safe, parents should check apps and text messages and talk with their child more than once about the dangers of being online.
"Even though sometimes kids think that they are in a mature relationship, this is something in person or online that we need to educate children about," Slingsby said. "Kind of the power dynamics and the age dynamics regarding relationships, and what healthy and unhealthy relationships look like."

Title: An Israeli documentary on the war in Gaza sets off a firestorm – NBC10 Philadelphia
Article_Text:
An Israeli documentary about the civilian death toll in the war in Gaza has sparked fierce backlash at home after being awarded the special jury prize last week at the Venice Film Festival, drawing anger from top officials and even calls to strip the filmmakers of Israeli citizenship.
Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu has accused those behind the film “NAZA” of incitement and antisemitism, while the head of the Israeli military has vowed to track down the soldiers who cooperated with the project.
Stream Philadelphia News for free, 24/7, wherever you are with NBC10.
Shot on the rooftops of Tel Aviv at night in extreme secrecy over three years, “NAZA” features testimony from 24 Israeli military insiders, including intelligence officers and soldiers, who give insight into the war in Gaza and what they say is the systemic killing of Palestinian civilians.
They allege that Israel uses artificial intelligence to identify and bomb potential targets of the militant Hamas group in Gaza — often knowing that many civilians will likely be killed in an attack. The Israeli military has acknowledged using AI to help identify targets but says that a human being makes the final decision before a strike is carried out.
The documentary set off a firestorm in Israel
The reception in Venice set off a firestorm among Israel’s leading politicians and military officials, many of whom have described “NAZA” as anti-Israel and lacking context. They all acknowledged they have not seen the film.
Netanyahu, his Cabinet members and also the prime minister's opponents in next month’s key elections have all lambasted the film, describing it as antisemitic and a part of a broader campaign to defame Israel.
“We are fighting global antisemitic incitement,” Netanyahu said on Monday. “When it comes from within us, it’s simply unbearable.”
Israel's Culture Minister Miki Zohar called on Monday for the documentary’s Israeli co-directors, Yuval Abraham and Rachel Szor, to be stripped of their citizenship. Lt. Gen. Eyal Zamir, the Israeli military’s chief of general staff, asked military prosecutors to investigate potential leaks in the film.
“This is a dangerous attempt to deny us the legitimacy to defend ourselves against the worst of our enemies,” Zamir said.
Co-produced by The Guardian and Jonathan Glazer, who was behind the 2023 Oscar-winning “The Zone of Interest,” the film is the second documentary from Abraham and Szor. It follows their 2025 Oscar-winning “No Other Land,” which chronicled Palestinians in part of the occupied West Bank as they face home demolitions by Israeli troops and attacks by Israeli settlers.
“NAZA” — an acronym used by Israel's military that means collateral damage — “reveals in detail the systems behind Israel’s calculated mass killing of Palestinian civilians in Gaza,” according to a synopsis from The Guardian.
The film is not yet available to audiences, though the filmmakers have said they intend to seek distribution in Israel, Europe and the United States.
“The testimonies it contains are true and we believe they deserve to be heard. The interviews were given by confidential journalistic sources," The Guardian said in a statement.
Criticism of the film highlights the divide over the war
In an interview with journalist Raviv Drucker on Israel’s Channel 13, Abraham said the attacks on him and Szor showed why many of the film’s participants wanted to remain anonymous. Abraham defended the film’s process for verifying the accounts and events described.
Abraham also questioned why Israeli journalists had done little to investigate civilian deaths and the military’s rules of engagement during the war.
“Many soldiers told me they had been waiting for a chance to talk about this,” he said.
Many of the film’s central claims had been previously reported, but Israel’s response echoes how officials have reacted in the past to prominent criticism of the country’s conduct — attacking critics, questioning their motives and challenging the credibility of the allegations.
The response also reflects the chasm between how the war in Gaza is seen in Israel and how it's seen internationally. Israelis have largely seen the war as an act of self-defense after Hamas-led militants attacked Israel on Oct. 7, 2023, killing some 1,200 people and taking 251 hostage — the deadliest day in Israel’s history.
But internationally, it has drawn widespread condemnation and accusations of war crimes. Nearly three years of war have destroyed most of Gaza and killed at least 73,789 Palestinians, according to the Gaza Health Ministry, which does not distinguish between civilians and combatants.
Doron Spielman, a spokesperson for Netanyahu's office, said Israel denied the film's allegations and questioned Abraham and Szor's motivations.
“What they wanted was awards from overseas from Israel haters. And they wanted standing applause,” he said, referencing the 25-minute applause that viewers in Venice gave the film.

Title: Dream Chasers Summit inspires the next generation
Article_Text:
Meek Mill returned to North Broad Street as thousands of Temple students and Philadelphia high school seniors gathered for a day of candid conversations on success, leadership, ownership and overcoming adversity.
Photo by Betsy Manning
The Liacouras Center was buzzing with energy last week as more than a thousand Temple students and Philadelphia high school seniors gathered for the Dream Chasers Summit. More than a decade after the summit first came to Temple, its return to North Broad Street gave a new generation of students the chance to learn from those who had turned their ambitions into success and consider what it will take to pursue their own.
Held Sept. 10, the summit united Temple University and Philadelphia native and multiplatinum hip-hop artist Meek Mill around a shared goal: connecting students with leaders whose experiences reflected many of the realities and aspirations shaping young people today. Through wide-ranging conversations, speakers shared the lessons and defining moments that influenced their personal and professional journeys.
“What stood out to me most was the energy in the building and how engaged the students were throughout the day,” said Arthur Johnson, vice president and Debbie and Stanley Lefkowitz ’65 Director of Athletics. “You had Temple students and high school seniors from the School District of Philadelphia hearing directly from people who have achieved success in sports, music, business and entertainment, and who were vulnerable and candid about the challenges and setbacks they faced along the way. To hear about the work required to achieve and maintain success, and to see students listening, asking questions and really connecting with those stories was powerful.”
Rather than traditional lectures, the summit unfolded through a series of conversations designed to connect students with leaders who could speak firsthand about navigating adversity and building successful careers.
The day’s programming centered on five themes: Respect the Game: From the Locker Room to the Boardroom; All Eyes on You: Athlete Power, Purpose and Leadership; How Far We Came: Building Businesses That Build Community; Dreams Worth More Than Money: Turning Culture Into Ownership; and Dreams & Nightmares: Adversity, Second Chances and the Power to Rebuild.
The summit opened with remarks from David W. Brown, Temple’s executive director of community impact and civic engagement; Jessica Jackson, CEO of REFORM Alliance; and Tony B. Watlington Sr., superintendent of the School District of Philadelphia.
For Brown, the value of the summit extended beyond what students heard from the stage.
“One of the things that makes this experience so important is that students can see that you can start anywhere and get to anywhere,” Brown said. “Whether they ultimately come to Temple or not, they have an opportunity to experience the kind of learning and connection that an institution like Temple fosters. When you bring together like-minded young people who are here to learn, share knowledge and build relationships, the possibilities for where they go from here are limitless.”
Among those sharing their experiences with students throughout the day were Wallo, author, motivational speaker and co-founder of the Million Dollaz Worth of Game podcast; Larry Miller, FOX ’82, chair of the Jordan Brand Advisory Board; Shawn Gee, president and co-owner of Live Nation Urban; and Chamillionaire, rapper, entrepreneur and venture capitalist.
Temple voices also helped guide the day’s conversations. Claire Smith, founding executive director of the Claire Smith Center for Sports Media and assistant professor of practice in Temple’s Klein College of Media and Communication, moderated a discussion on athlete leadership.
Jonathan Howe, assistant professor and director of the AIRE Lab in Temple’s School of Sport, Tourism and Hospitality Management, led a conversation on building businesses that strengthen communities, while Lauren Bullock, associate professor of instruction and director of sports media at Klein, moderated a discussion with Chamillionaire about turning cultural influence into ownership.
Throughout the summit, speakers challenged students to think intentionally about the resources already at their fingertips. Meek, reflecting on how technology and social media helped him market his music, tell his story and build his brand, encouraged students to view their phones as tools for creating opportunities.
“You can meet people, you can go anywhere, you can connect,” Meek told students. “You can build brands, you can shoot a movie, you can record an album, you can start a clothing line. You can do anything with this, but it’s about how you see it.”
The summit culminated with Dreams & Nightmares: Adversity, Second Chances and the Power to Rebuild, a conversation that brought Meek together with Miller and moderator Wallo to reflect on the experiences that shaped their lives and careers.
For Meek, the conversation became an opportunity to reflect on his deep connection to Philadelphia. From growing up in North Philadelphia to becoming an internationally recognized artist and entrepreneur, he spoke about how his experiences in the city influenced both his resilience and his approach to success.
“Philadelphia, to me, made me on every level—from my aggression, the way I attack success,” Meek said. “I’ve been all over the world, but Philly’s always going to be home.”

Title: Storylines to follow as Giants head to LA
Article_Text:
Giants
                
17 Sep 2026, 01:03 GMT+10
            
Matt Citak
The New York Giants got their 2026 campaign off to an encouraging start.
Under the lights of primetime, John Harbaugh's squad began the season with a 28-20 divisional victory over the Dallas Cowboys. It was a well-balanced performance from the Giants as all three phases stepped up when they were needed.
But Week 1 is in the rearview mirror. The attention now turns to this week's opponent.
The Los Angeles Rams took part in the NFL's first ever regular-season game in Australia last week, but wound up falling to the San Francisco 49ers, 27-7.
Here are five storylines to follow in this week's matchup on Monday Night Football.
Turning the focus towards LA
The Giants set the tone early in their Week 1 victory over the Cowboys. The defense forced a quick three-and-out on the Cowboys' opening drive, which was followed by the offense putting together a 10-play, 83-yard drive that took over six minutes off the clock and resulted in the first touchdown of the season. It was the first of four drives by the Giants that reached double-digit plays, as all three possessions in the second half were 12 or more plays.
As encouraging as the performance on Sunday night was, it was far from perfect. The Giants fumbled the ball four times against the Cowboys, only one of which resulted in a turnover, and totaled 114 yards on 10 penalties. The penalty yardage was the most of any team in Week 1. Going up against a Rams team that made it all the way to the NFC Championship last season, Harbaugh acknowledged that they will need to clean some things up heading into Week 2.
"Everything you do before is a foundation for what you're going to do next," Harbaugh told the media Monday. "So, we're building on our foundations every single day, what's under us and what we have banked, so to speak. Try to maintain an understanding of that but we also understand that how you play this week is not going to be good enough to win next week.
"How we played this last night will not win the game next Monday night. It won't be good enough. So, we've got to improve. We've got to keep improving and we've got to put everything we've got into this week to improve the most that we possibly can if we're going to have the best opportunity to win this game. So, we've got a lot to do."
Donald, Rams defense next test for Dart
Jaxson Dart had a promising start to his second NFL season. The 23-year-old quarterback completed 23 of 29 passes (79.3 percent) for 230 yards, three touchdowns and no interceptions. This earned him a passer rating of 134.2, by far the highest mark of his 13 NFL starts. Dart also continued to be a threat on the ground, adding 59 yards on eight carries (7.4 avg.) prior to his final three attempts in victory formation. Not only was this perhaps the best overall performance of his young professional career, but he also became the first quarterback in NFL history with three or more passing touchdowns, 50 or more rushing yards and a passer rating of 130.0 or higher in the season opener.
Dart and the rest of the offense face a tough test this week as they fly across the country for a primetime matchup against the Rams. The Los Angeles defense struggled in Week 1, allowing the 49ers to total 379 yards and three touchdowns, all of which came from the arm of Brock Purdy. The veteran QB finished with 205 yards and a 73.5 completion percentage in the season opener in Australia, earning a passer rating of 105.6, with an additional 29 yards on five carries (5.8 avg.).
The Rams defense will look a little different on Monday than it did in Week 1. For starters, reigning Defensive Player of the Year Myles Garrett will not be out there after being placed on injured reserve due to a knee injury. However, the unit might be getting some reinforcements. Three-time Defensive Player of the Year and eight-time first-team All-Pro Aaron Donald, who officially came out of retirement last month, is gearing up for his return to the field and might be out there for the Week 2 matchup.
"Expect him to play like Aaron Donald, which is a game-wrecking type player inside," Harbaugh said. "Penetrating, active movement player who can wreck the game, really any particular play in a lot of different ways, run and pass. So, we're expecting him to play. We're planning for him to be out there."
"For the longest time that I can remember, he's one of the most dominant players that I've watched," Dart added. "So, getting the chance to go out there and compete against him, it's going to be really cool just to be on the same field as him. He's a great player, and I've heard that he's kept himself in really good shape. So, it's going to be a great competition."
Rams are 'a very well-coached football team'
The Rams scored only seven points during their trip to Australia, due in part to converting on only two of nine third downs. But make no mistake, this is still one of the most talented offenses in the NFL, led by reigning league MVP Matthew Stafford. The veteran quarterback led the league with 4,707 yards and 46 touchdowns through the air last season as he finished the season with a career-high 109.2 passer rating. Coming off a game in which he was held to just 155 passing yards and no touchdowns, Stafford presents the Giants defense with a daunting challenge.
"This is a very well-coached football team," Harbaugh said of the Rams. "Great football coach, Sean McVay. They play fundamental football. They're very disciplined. That's really their calling card. The schemes are excellent, but more so it's the fundamental nature of the way they play that makes them who they are as a football team. And that's our challenge. And then Matthew Stafford epitomizes that at the position. He's accurate. He's on time. He gets the ball where it's supposed to go. He doesn't make too many mistakes. So, that's a big challenge for us."
Los Angeles made a big splash last offseason when they brought in wide receiver Davante Adams. The veteran made his presence felt early and often last year. Almost every time the Rams got into the red zone, Stafford would look towards his big, reliable target, which led to Adams catching a league-high 14 touchdown passes.
While Adams led the Rams in receiving touchdowns last season, there is no doubt that the focal point of passing game is fellow wideout Puka Nacua. In his third NFL season last year, Nacua led the NFL with 129 receptions, which he took for 1,715 yards and 10 touchdowns. Even during a down game for the offense last week, Nacua still finished the game with five receptions for 74 yards. Not only does the young receiver make an impact as a pass-catcher, but he is also one of the best blocking wide receivers in the NFL, something that caught the eye of John Harbaugh.
"You have to respect him as a football player," the head coach said of Nacua. "I mean, he does, he is, his picture is next to "football player" in the dictionary, for sure, because he does it all. He'd probably run down a kickoff and tackle if they'd let him. He's that kind of a guy. And he makes contested catches. He blocks the lead play. He's in there on play actions. But not just him, all the guys do that, all their guys do all the jobs, the way they're built."
Nabers 'looked good' & other injury updates
The big storyline heading into Week 1 was the health of wide receiver Malik Nabers. The star wideout practiced in full all week but was listed as questionable on the final injury report. Nabers went through his pregame warmup on Sunday and declared himself ready to go, which led to him catching six passes for 69 yards on a team-high nine targets. More important than his stats was the fact that Nabers, who was on the field for 52 percent of the team's offensive snaps (36 snaps), came out of the game healthy.
"I think good," Harbaugh said on how Nabers looked. "I haven't really asked him directly, but the trainers said he looked good. He was out here today. He looked good. So, it looked like it was an A, I would say, but you should ask him. Seemed good, though."
Running back Tyrone Tracy Jr. was absent from Wednesday's practice due to an illness. The head coach said Tracy was sent home Tuesday in part to keep the rest of the locker room healthy.
"He had the flu," the head coach told reporters Wednesday. "Bad flu deal, so hopefully be back tomorrow. Expect him to be back tomorrow if it clears up a little bit. So, he came in yesterday morning not in good shape. They sent him home. You worry about this. You don't want to get everybody sick. So, that's part of it."
Schedule change
With the game on Monday, the Giants' practice schedule looks a little different this week. Wednesday's practice was more of a walk-through, or an "ACT practice" as Harbaugh calls it. Thursday's session will then be what a normal Wednesday practice is like, Friday will be like a normal Thursday, and so on and so forth.
The biggest change on the schedule is the team's travel day. The Giants typically fly out the day before an away game, but with a cross-country trip on the horizon, the team will fly out on Saturday, a day early. Harbaugh did this during his time in Baltimore and even back to his days as special teams coordinator in Philadelphia, and now he brings this philosophy to the Giants.
"You get a chance to kind of get your clock set just a little bit," the head coach said about flying to the west coast a day early. "We go ahead and get our clock set. We go out late, so the guys are up a little later on the travel night two days before. So, we try to get them ready to be at their peak at night. That's kind of the idea. Same thing we did at home, but now it's on the road, so that's really the process."

Title: Temple Jazz Orchestra brings its music on tour across Europe
Article_Text:
Capping off a standout year, Temple Jazz Orchestra performed at jazz festivals in Italy, France and Spain.
Photo by Jesse Deems
The Temple Jazz Orchestra has deep roots in Philadelphia, but this summer, they got the chance to take their act on the road. The award-winning jazz band, composed of undergraduate and graduate students from Boyer College of Music and Dance, performed for members of the Temple community at Temple Rome before traveling to France to perform at Jazz in Marciac and then Spain for the Santander Music Festival and Xabia Jazz Festival. 
“What other collegiate jazz band gets invited to headline at premier European jazz festivals?” said Robert Stroker, vice provost for the arts and Joslyn G. Ewart Dean of Boyer College of Music and Dance and the School of Theater, Film and Media Arts. “The reputation of our students and faculty continues to open doors to new experiences. We’re all incredibly proud of them, and excited to see what new opportunities lay ahead.” 
With long travel days, little sleep and performances almost every day, band Director and Director of Jazz Studies Terell Stafford recognizes the trip was hardly a vacation.  
“This was such a grueling trip for everyone, sometimes playing until late into the night and then waking up for a 4:30 a.m. departure for the next city,” said Stafford. “For the students, it was a reality check that life on tour can be exhausting, but that is balanced with being so appreciated for doing what you love. The band played phenomenally and the audiences were tremendously receptive.” 
The experience taught students how to care for themselves while meeting the demands of professional touring. 
“Trips like this are really important for learning how to keep yourself in good condition as a musician,” said Jesse Deems, BYR ’26, trumpet player and first-year student in the master in jazz studies program. “It’s the exhilaration you get while performing that reminds you why it’s all worth it.”  
The trip came during a banner year for the Temple Jazz Orchestra. In January, the band took first place at the 2026 National Collegiate Jazz Championship at Lincoln Center, where it competed against nine of the country’s top collegiate jazz ensembles. The band and its members also earned numerous individual and ensemble honors.
In March, the band traveled to Japan for performances in Kyoto and Tokyo, recording a second installment of its Live from Japan series, following Live from Japan, volume 1, recorded during the band’s 2025 Japan tour. 
In April, Philadelphia City Council presented a privileged resolution honoring the Jazz Orchestra and Stafford for the national championship. Councilmember at-large Nina Ahmad described the achievement as “a source of pride for Philadelphia” in her introduction of the resolution. 
Despite the rigorous itinerary, students still had some time to enjoy cultural exchange and personal reflection. For Kiara Rouse, saxophone player and Class of 2029 jazz performance saxophone major, the trip expanded her perspective on what’s possible in the art of jazz. She noticed that musicians she encountered in Europe seemed less constrained by traditional expectations of the genre and more willing to explore new forms of expression. 
“It made me realize that there's so much more music out there and that there are so many other places with so many other kinds of music, and that it's still worth it to experience that, too,” said Rouse. 
The experience of traveling together also strengthened the students’ collective bond that generates the shared trust necessary to perform at a high caliber.  
“These are truly elite musicians. I feel blessed to play with them every day,” said Deems. “There’s so much humility, and I think that very heavily contributes to the success of the band.”

Title: SNAP changes in October: Benefits to increase with state costs – NBC10 Philadelphia
Article_Text:
The Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program (SNAP), commonly known as the food stamp program, will have new changes starting Oct. 1, 2026.
Although the maximum benefits families can receive to purchase food will increase, states will be responsible for covering 75% of the program's administrative costs, up from the current 50%. The additional expense could put greater pressure on state budgets.
Stream Philadelphia News for free, 24/7, wherever you are with NBC10.
What does this mean? Here's what you need to know:
Will SNAP benefits increase in October?
The program includes increases to the maximum benefits available to U.S. households participating in SNAP.
Keep in mind that this does not mean every family will receive an increase in their monthly benefits. SNAP calculates each household's benefit amount based on factors including net income, household size and eligible deductions.
These are the maximum monthly benefits starting Oct. 1, 2026, according to the U.S. Department of Agriculture (USDA):
States will take on higher SNAP costs
Starting Oct. 1, states will be responsible for covering 75% of SNAP's administrative costs, up from the current 50%.
According to experts, the change could lead to cuts to the program because of the additional financial burden at the state level.
The change was established by the One Big Beautiful Bill Act signed by President Donald Trump in July 2025. The law reduced the federal government's share of SNAP administrative costs from 50% to 25%, shifting a greater portion of those expenses to the states.
For more information about the SNAP food assistance program, click here.
What has changed under the Trump administration?
The Trump administration's tax law included the largest cuts to SNAP in the program's history.
An estimated 5 million fewer Americans, including families with children, have stopped receiving monthly food stamp benefits.
The law established that people receiving food stamps must work, volunteer or participate in training programs for at least 80 hours a month, or 20 hours a week.
Under the new requirements, able-bodied adults without dependents between the ages of 16 and 59 who are able to work and do not have qualifying dependents, and who do not meet the requirement, can receive SNAP benefits for only three months within a 36-month period, unless they qualify for an exemption.

Title: Cumulus Neuroscience Presents Data at the ISCTM 2026 Autumn Conference
Article_Text:
Interim data show high adherence and usability for remote, multimodal brain monitoring in borderline personality disorder and therapy-resistant depression, and a two-minute digital cognitive task performing comparably to clinical benchmarks for Alzheimer's trial pre-enrichment.
BELFAST, Northern Ireland, Sept. 16, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- First Published: 16 September, 2026
Cumulus Neuroscience presented three posters at the International Society for CNS Clinical Trials and Methodology (ISCTM) Autumn Conference in Philadelphia, Pennsylvania. Two of the studies were conducted in collaboration with a top 20 pharma company and academic partners; the third is an encore presentation of work first shown at the Alzheimer's Association International Conference (AAIC) 2026 in London on 15 July.
Traditional clinical trials for disorders of the central nervous system (CNS) are long, costly and can be burdensome for participants. The NeuLogiq Platform was purpose-built by Cumulus in collaboration with 10 top biopharma companies to generate objective, clinical-quality data through frequent, repeated digital measurements collected in the clinic or in the home. Together, the three posters presented at ISCTM address a common question: whether patients across very different CNS indications will engage with high-frequency digital measurement, and whether the resulting data are good enough to change how trials are designed.
The first poster titled, "Usability and adherence to remote, longitudinal assessment of EEG, cognition, mood and sleep in Borderline Personality Disorder," reported interim data from a study conducted with a top 20 pharma company and a UK-based academic partner. Clinical trials in borderline personality disorder (BPD) frequently fail to demonstrate efficacy, in part because participants improve across all treatment arms and because symptom variability is poorly captured by infrequent clinic visits. The seven-week observational study recruited 51 participants (31 patients with BPD, 20 healthy controls) and deployed multiple digital measures including NeuLogiq Platform EEG and cognitive assessment, wrist-worn actigraphy and twice-daily mood ratings. Requested engagement with the NeuLogiq Platform alternated between high- and low-intensity phases to test relative acceptability, while requested engagement with the actigraphy and mood measures remained constant throughout.
Interim analysis of 47 participants found mean adherence to NeuLogiq cognitive and EEG sessions above 85% in the BPD cohort across every phase of the study, alongside median mood-assessment adherence of approximately 90%. System Usability Scale scores averaged 82.2 at onboarding and 80.2 at debrief, indicating excellent usability with no additional difficulty for patients relative to controls. Adherence data for the wrist-worn actigraphy measures were still being analysed at the time of submission. The authors concluded that the combined digital approach is broadly acceptable and usable in this population, and that adherence at this level meets a baseline prerequisite for clinical trials designed around lower clinical contact and higher measurement frequency.
The second poster titled, "Assessing neuroplasticity and cognition with a portable platform throughout esketamine treatment for therapy-resistant depression," reported interim data from an ongoing study conducted with a top 20 pharma company and an EU-based academic medical centre. The single-centre, parallel-group study will enroll 54 patients with therapy-resistant major depressive disorder, randomised with respect to observation timeframe rather than to treatment: one group is observed during esketamine initiation and the other during the clinically indicated waiting period beforehand, with all patients continuing standard antidepressant treatment. Across a 22-day window, four structured in-clinic visits - including visually evoked potential (VEP) modulation, auditory steady-state response and resting-state EEG - are combined with twice-daily at-home cognitive and mood assessments on a dedicated tablet.
In an interim analysis of 15 data-complete participants, 98.7% of in-clinic sessions and 90.5% of scheduled at-home behavioural sessions were completed and yielded analysable data, after accounting for technical issues and non-compliance. Mean System Usability Scale score was 88.5 and patient-reported burden for at-home assessments was minimal. The authors concluded that repeated cognitive and neurophysiological assessment using a portable platform is highly feasible and well tolerated in therapy-resistant depression, and that the observation-window randomisation allows the effects of esketamine on neuroplasticity and cognition to be captured within a naturalistic clinical context. Final results are anticipated in Q3 2027.
The third poster titled, "A two-minute digital cognitive task as a pre-enrichment screening method for Alzheimer's disease trials," was an encore presentation of data first reported at AAIC 2026 in London. The work evaluated a symbol-coding task (Symbol Swap), a two-minute tablet-based NeuLogiq Platform task, across three independent studies - CNS-101, Fastball i4i and BioHermes-2 - in collaboration with the University of Bath and the University of Bristol. The pooled analysis covered approximately 1,280 participants assessed at more than 25 sites in three countries and three languages, using both autonomous at-home and assisted in-clinic administration.
Across the three studies, Symbol Swap discriminated between control, MCI and Alzheimer's dementia groups comparably to established clinical screeners that require 20 to 45 minutes of clinician time, in just two minutes and with substantially less participant and site burden. On the pre-enrichment question itself it outperformed those benchmarks, showing stronger associations with biomarker-defined Alzheimer's pathology (blood plasma p-tau217) than the clinical comparators, including in cognitively unimpaired individuals where the benchmark performed close to chance - suggesting it could flag those most likely to be amyloid- or tau-positive and improve the efficiency of downstream plasma, PET or CSF screening. Digitally administered and automatically scored, Symbol Swap scales readily across large, multi-site trials in both in-clinic and at-home workflows, making it an attractive first-line enrichment filter with the potential to cut screen-failure rates and accelerate recruitment into Alzheimer's trials.
"What these three posters share is evidence that patients will engage with frequent digital measurement - and engage well," said Brian Murphy, PhD, Cumulus Co-Founder and CSO. "In borderline personality disorder and in therapy-resistant depression, two populations where trial designs have long been constrained by what can realistically be asked of participants, we saw adherence and usability scores that would support studies built around lower clinical contact and much higher measurement frequency. Alongside that, our Alzheimer's work shows how much signal a well-designed two-minute task can carry. Taken together, these data point toward CNS trials that are shorter, smaller and less burdensome, without giving up sensitivity."
Cumulus supports precision in CNS clinical trials for its industry partners by enabling in-clinic and remote monitoring of patients across multiple domains of brain function. To learn more, visit www.cumulusneuro.com.
About Borderline Personality Disorder (BPD)
BPD is a mental health condition characterised by instability in mood, self-image and relationships, alongside marked impulsivity. Symptoms typically emerge in adolescence or early adulthood and fluctuate considerably over short timescales, which makes the condition difficult to assess with infrequent clinic-based measurement. There are currently no approved pharmacological treatments for BPD.
About Therapy-Resistant Depression
Major depressive disorder (MDD) affects an estimated 5% of adults worldwide. A substantial proportion of patients do not respond adequately to two or more courses of antidepressant treatment, a presentation described as treatment- or therapy-resistant depression. Esketamine is one of a small number of options approved for this population, and is thought to act in part by enhancing synaptic plasticity.
About Alzheimer's Disease (AD)
Alzheimer's is a progressive disease that affects brain function, memory and other cognitive abilities. It is the most common cause of dementia, affecting millions of people worldwide. Symptoms usually develop slowly and worsen over time, including memory loss, confusion, difficulty with language and communication, mood swings, and changes in behaviour and personality. While there is no known cure, there are currently over one hundred Alzheimer's disease clinical trials underway.
About Cumulus Neuroscience
With a mission to generate the data and insights required to accelerate diagnosis and management of central nervous system (CNS) disorders for millions of patients and caregivers around the world, Cumulus Neuroscience is advancing NeuLogiq, an AI-based, multi-domain digital biomarker platform to enable better, faster decision making in neurology and neuropsychiatry clinical trials and patient care. Designed for and with 10 of the world's leading pharma companies, the platform enables decentralized trials and is already making a difference in the development of therapies for Alzheimer's Disease, depression and schizophrenia.

Title: Vinton County children endangerment case increases interest in bill to ban child marriage in Ohio
Article_Text:
(Ohio Capital Journal) — An ongoing children endangerment case in Vinton County where 16 children where found in “terrible” conditions has sparked more interest in an Ohio bill that would ban child marriage.
Law enforcement authorities allegedly found 16 children in a Hamden house when conducting a search warrant for a parallel investigation on June 30. The Vinton County Sheriff said livestock were kept in better conditions than the children.
Elizabeth Siders, the now 33-year-old mother of all 16 children who range in age from 18 months to 18 years, married Gary Siders Jr., when she was 15 years old in West Virginia. Siders Jr., is now 36, and was 18 at the time they wed.
“At that age you’re very impressionable,” said Ohio state Sen. Bill Blessing, R-Colerain Twp.
The Siders’ eldest child was born two months after they got married.
“The Vinton County thing just proves beyond a shadow of a doubt that marriage under the age of 18 is bad, is wrong, and leads to dire consequences,” said Ohio state Sen. Bill DeMora, D-Columbus.
“We need to put an end to this and there’s no legitimate reason why anybody should get married under the age of 18. … It’s just ludicrous.”
DeMora and Blessing introduced Ohio Senate Bill 341 earlier this year, which would require Ohioans to be at least 18 to get married.
Under Ohio’s current law, 17-year-olds are able to marry someone up to four years older than them, as long as a juvenile court signs off on it.
“Eighteen is a magic number,” Blessing said. “You’re truly an adult at that point. You can vote. You can buy cigarettes. You can do a whole host of other things that adults can do.”
The bill passed out of the Ohio Senate Judiciary Committee in June, but did not go to a full Senate vote before lawmakers went home for summer break. It has received only supporter testimony.
Gary Siders Sr., 73, Catherine Siders, 67, Gary Siders Jr., 36, and Elizabeth Siders, 33, are each facing 16 counts of felony endangering children in Vinton County Common Pleas Court. They have all pleaded not guilty.
West Virginia lawmakers passed a bill in 2023 that set the minimum age to get married at 16.
“Child marriage not only brings no benefit, but it also destroys girls’ lives, and it often leads to devastating outcomes,” said Fraidy Reiss, Unchained At Last founder and executive director.
“This unfortunate story that has gotten these headlines is just one more reminder — child marriage is dangerous.”
More than 5,000 Ohio children have been married as minors since 2000 and nearly 300,000 minors nationally were married between 2000 and 2018, according to Unchained At Last, an organization dedicated to ending underage marriage.
Seventeen states have a law banning child marriage, according to Unchained At Last.
Michigan and Pennsylvania have banned child marriage, making it all the more important for Ohio to follow suit, Reiss said.
“When one state bans child marriage, what we see is parents taking their kids to the neighboring state to marry them off there instead,” she said.
California, Mississippi, and New Mexico have no age minimum to get married, according to Unchained At Last.
“If we can (pass the Ohio bill), that sends a strong message to California or some of these other states that have no minimum to get your act together and do this,” Blessing said.
Ohio lawmakers will come back after the November election. Any bill that does not pass before the end of the year must be reintroduced in the new General Assembly to be considered.
Blessing is confident the bill will pass during lame duck, likely as part of an omnibus bill, meaning two or more bills combined into one.
“I’m upbeat about it,” he said.
“There might be members who would in a vacuum vote no, but to some degree, doing it in an omnibus bill gives them cover to vote for something like this, even if they don’t like Senate Bill 341.”
DeMora said he will offer up S.B. 341 as an amendment for bills that are voted on during lame duck session.
“It’s too important not to vote on this thing,” he said.
Reiss said she is hopeful, but not confident Ohio lawmakers will pass the bill.
“Banning child marriage — a human rights abuse that destroys girls’ lives and creates a nightmarish legal trap for them — banning this human rights abuse costs nothing,” she said.
“It has a zero-dollar price tag. Why have legislators not yet passed this?”

Title: PA Elected Leaders on Artificial Intelligence Doom Warnings
Article_Text:
A dire warning from an artificial intelligence researcher last week stoked global panic about the industry. Since then, several elected leaders in Pennsylvania have commented on the issue.
Jacob Coxon, a researcher at Anthropic (an AI company with Google and Amazon as investors) quit his job on Sep. 8 and in an X post said “The people building AI earnestly believe that it could kill us all by the end of the decade.”
The rest of his post said the global race to develop the technology pushes companies to keep researching despite the risks.
Several leaders of AI companies (Dario Amodei of Anthropic first, then Sam Altman of OpenAI and Elon Musk with SpaceXAI) have since agreed that a slow down is needed and government guardrails could help. Amodei specifically called on the U.S. and other governments to work with authoritarian governments and verify a global slowdown.
In a series of posts on Truth Social, President Donald Trump initially said a strong presidential administration is the only guardrail AI needs, then called the warnings “a hoax”— saying progress should continue in the face of ongoing competitiveness with China and other nations for infrastructure.
The national saga has inspired several Pennsylvania leaders to add comment.
Democratic Gov. Josh Shapiro posted on socials that warnings from AI leaders were a “bright flashing red light” and cautioned that private industry alone should not decide the fate of artificial intelligence.
State Sen. Art Haywood, a Democrat from Philadelphia, announced plans for legislation around artificial intelligence development on Tuesday. Haywood wants laws that “would require AI companies to report how they identify, mitigate, and govern substantial risks.”
On the Republican side, Attorney General Dave Sunday published a statement on the national fears, saying guardrails are needed to “reap the benefits technology can provide, while protecting ourselves from the potential harm that has been warned of so starkly over the past week.”
GOP gubernatorial candidate Stacy Garrity has not commented directly on the recent cautions; when asked today about “fears of what the industry could do”, Garrity answered with her position of pausing development on data centers.
Other senate Republicans at the presser commented that the risks are real and should be managed, but that race with China is not going away.
“They understand that they’re losing the race to us, and they understand how important it is,” said Sen. Chris Gebherd, a Republican in south east Pennsylvania. “That does not mean that we should be reckless, and we should be, you know, going full speed ahead without any concerns about what the… where the end is going to be.”

Title: National Child Safety Week Urges Proper Car Seat Installation
Article_Text:
PennDOT and its safety partners are reminding parents and caregivers the importance of child passenger safety. The National Child Safety Week campaign runs from September 20 until September 26 and follows the theme this week is “In It to Win It - Safety Starts with the Right Seat.
“The first step to protecting children when riding in a vehicle is making sure they are properly buckled in each time to maximize the potential safety benefits in the event of a crash,” said Mike Tautin, a Community Traffic Safety Project Coordinator with the Highway Safety Network. “Car seats, booster seats, and seat belts are proven tools to save lives, but they must be used correctly to be effective.”
It was reported on the Pennsylvania Traffic Injury Prevention Project (PA TIPP) that between 2021 to 2025 81%% of children under age four that were in a vehicle collision and were in the correct car seat sustained no injuries.
The following Pennsylvania laws are in place for proper car seats:
- Birth to Age 2 – Must be secured in a rear-facing car seat.
- Age 2 to 4 – Must be properly restrained in an approved child safety seat anywhere in the vehicle and should be in a rear-facing seat until the child outgrows the maximum weight and height limits designated by the car seat manufacturer.
- Ages 4 to 7 – Must be restrained in an appropriate booster seat and use a harness belt.
- Ages 8 and 18 – Must be in a seat belt regardless of where they are seated in the vehicle.
Following installation of car seats drivers should register online here with the manufacture for updates on recalls and safety notices.
PennDOT does provide over 75 fitting stations where trained technicians can assess child safety seat for proper installation.
Several free events will be held throughout Pennsylvania and can be found online here.

Title: Multi-Agency Resource Center to Aid Erie Storm Recovery
Article_Text:
The Shapiro Administration will be supporting a Multi-Agency Resource Center (MARC) following the request of Erie officials.
This center will assist those in the community who have suffered significant losses due to the severe storms and heavy rain that swept the Erie area two weeks ago.
The MARC is open to residents and business owners in the Erie County area who were affected.
“Strong wind from the severe storms caused significant damage to many homes, businesses and public property across Erie,” said Pennsylvania Emergency Management Agency (PEMA) Director Randy Padfield. “Having necessary resources and services available in one location for the community makes it a little easier for everyone to navigate the recovery process.”
Pennsylvania state agencies scheduled to participate or provide information include:
- PA Department of Agriculture
- PA Department of Human Services
- PA Emergency Management Agency
- PA Insurance Department
- PA Office of the Attorney General
Some resources include information on checking insurance coverage for damages, benefits, and disabilities support, community support services, and other recovery information and resources.
“From the beginning of this devastating storm, our focus has been on our Erie community and making sure our residents have the support and resources they need," said Mayor Daria S. Devlin. "We are so grateful to PEMA and our state partners as we continue this work. We know there is still a lot to do, but we will continue to show up for our residents, work together, and do everything we can to help our community recover.”
“The damage from these storms has affected families, businesses and communities across Erie County, and this resource center brings the people and services they need together under one roof,” said Erie County Executive Christina M. Vogel. “We will continue working with our state and local partners to make sure our residents have the support they need to recover and rebuild.”
The Erie County online portal can be found online here.

Title: Federal judge names court-provided attorney for Daryl Heller in securities fraud case
Article_Text:
A federal judge on Wednesday said she will appoint a former federal prosecutor to step in as the new attorney for Lancaster County businessman Daryl Heller in his $402 million securities fraud case.
During a telephone conference Wednesday, U.S. District Judge Catherine Henry said Jason Bologna, a Philadelphia-based attorney at Buchanan Ingersoll & Rooney PC and former assistant U.S. attorney, agreed to be the court-appointed attorney for Heller, describing Bologna as “ready, willing and able.”
Bologna will replace Christopher Adams and Danielle Gordon of McCarter & English, the firm that has represented Heller since March 2025. Adams, who works out of the firm’s New Jersey office, filed a motion late last month asking permission to withdraw as Heller’s counsel because of exhausted legal defense funds and a breakdown in communication with Heller.
Heller, 56, pleaded guilty Aug. 10 to one count of securities fraud stemming from a massive ATM investment scheme that defrauded roughly 2,700 investors. The single count carries a maximum penalty of 20 years in federal prison.
At a hearing in Philadelphia last week, Adams said Heller could no longer afford private counsel because the bulk of Heller’s assets remain tied up in an ongoing personal bankruptcy proceeding. At the hearing, Adams said Heller had used $300,000 from an unencumbered retirement account to cover legal fees.
Henry had initially sought ways to keep McCarter & English on the case at the court-appointed rate of $177 an hour — a sharp reduction from Adams’ customary billing rate of $900 an hour.
During Wednesday’s brief telephone conference, Henry said Adams had offered a possible replacement attorney, but she opted to appoint Bologna because he is local and available.
Henry said Heller’s financial situation now qualifies him for a court-appointed attorney. However, Henry added that if she determines during a sentencing hearing that Heller has the funds, he will have to reimburse the cost of his court-appointed defense.
Change comes at critical time
Henry said she would give Bologna time to familiarize himself with the case before making any changes to the court schedule, which includes a crucial loss calculation hearing – currently scheduled for Dec. 1 – that will determine how much financial damage is directly attributable to Heller's fraud.
Under federal sentencing guidelines, the judge’s determination of the loss amount will directly drive the recommended prison sentence, with a higher amount possibly pushing it to the 20-year maximum.
Heller remains free on $500,000 bail, although Henry previously warned that establishing even a fraction of the alleged $402 million loss could trigger immediate detention under federal sentencing guidelines.
Bologna, who will help Heller navigate that hearing, spent more than 14 years as an assistant U.S. attorney in the Eastern District of Pennsylvania where his prosecutions of white-collar crimes included mail and wire fraud cases.
Bologna left the U.S. Attorney’s Office in 2022 to enter private practice, where his clients have included Christopher Phifer, a former CEO of several Pennsylvania medical practices who was acquitted by a jury on corporate embezzlement charges.
Bologna also represented former Temple University basketball guard Hysier Miller during a gambling probe that resulted in Miller being permanently banned last year from college sports for betting on games he played in. In comments to the media at the conclusion of the case, Bologna noted that the NCAA didn’t find evidence that Miller shaved points.
Via email Wednesday afternoon, Bologna said that he couldn’t comment on his upcoming appointment as Heller’s attorney until he confirms he doesn’t have any conflicts of interest and knows he can actually take the case.
Adams did not respond to a request for comment.

Title: Second water pipe connecting to Susquehanna River could cost $122M, Lancaster public works chief says
Article_Text:
Editor's note: The correct amount of capital improvement plan budget needing to be refinanced as a result of the second pipeline has been updated in the paragraph titled Budget query.
When: Lancaster City Council special meeting, Sept. 14. Council member Amos Stoltzfus was absent.
What happened: A potential second large-diameter water pipe, leading from the Susquehanna River to the city’s Conestoga River water treatment plant, could cost up to $122 million, Department of Public Works Director Stephen Campbell told council.
Background: In the early 2020s, the Environmental Protection Agency issued strict new, unfunded quality standards for drinking water contaminated by forever chemicals, called PFAS, Campbell said. Initial estimates were that PFAS affects 12% to 15% of water sources nationally, he said, but now it is estimated to affect 63% of the water supply in Pennsylvania alone. The new standards shortened requirements for cleaning up PFAS to five years from 10 years, he said, thus forcing Lancaster to consider installing a second pipe within the five years of the capital improvement budget.
First pipe: The city is working on the last two phases of replacing the large-diameter steel pipe, installed in the 1950s, that carries treated water from the plant to the reservoir and to the city’s water customers, Campbell said. Cost to complete the remaining phases is about $67 million, he said, with about $31.5 million of that to be paid in 2027 of the capital improvement budget.
Second pipe: A second large-diameter pipe would bring source water from the Susquehanna River to the Conestoga water treatment plant, Campbell said. The Susquehanna has far less PFAS concentration compared to the Conestoga because it is a much larger river, he said.
Quotable: “The solution to pollution is dilution,” Campbell told LNP | LancasterOnline.
By the numbers: The project would cost $1 million per year in 2027 and 2028 for engineering design, Campbell said. Initial estimates are costs of $40 million each year for 2029, 2030 and 2031, for the $122 million total, he said, but these are just “placeholders.”
Budget query: During the hearing, one community member had questions for Campbell and Amanda Bakay, the city’s acting administrative director. Tim Stuhldreher, former editor of One United Lancaster and former journalist with LNP | LancasterOnline, said the proposed budget indicates at least $282 million of the $549.91 million capital improvement plan would require new financing.
Quotable: “The immediate question, for any city resident, I think, would be ‘how does this affect my taxes and utility rates?’” Stuhldreher said.
Response: City administration will return to council within the next few months with a more detailed report on costs of the upgrades needed for the water system to meet the EPA’s standards.
Next meeting: Council will meet at 6:30 p.m. Sept. 22. A second reading of the capital improvement plan budget is scheduled during a special meeting at 6 p.m. Sept. 30.

Title: Texas and feds announce noncitizen voting charges against seven people – Houston Public Media
Article_Text:
This coverage is made possible through Votebeat, a nonpartisan news organization covering local election administration and voting access. Sign up for Votebeat Texas’ free newsletters here.
State and federal officials on Tuesday announced charges against seven people accused of voting in federal elections while not eligible citizens.
The Texas Secretary of State’s Office separately said it had referred 117 cases of potential noncitizen voting to the Texas Attorney General’s Office for investigation. It also confirmed that 578 other registered voters flagged last year as potential noncitizens by a federal database are, in fact, U.S. citizens.
The criminal charges announced Tuesday, all in Tarrant County, are the result of a collaboration between the Texas Attorney General’s Office, the U.S. Attorney’s Office for the Northern District of Texas, the FBI, and Homeland Security Investigations, a division of the U.S. Department of Homeland Security, according to a press release from Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton, a Republican. Six of the accused were indicted last week, the U.S. Attorney’s Office for the Northern District of Texas said, and the seventh person was charged in a criminal complaint.
Those charged include Mexican citizen Carlos Salas Barrios, who was arrested for voting in the 2024 election, though his ballot was ultimately rejected, according to a statement from the U.S. Department of Justice. Also charged was Nigerian national Joshua Nmelichukwu Akpom, who was arrested for making false statements in relation to naturalization, according to the release. Akpom voted illegally in the 2018 general election, but was not charged in relation to that due to the statute of limitations, according to the U.S. Department of Justice statement.
Nigerian national Helen Mayen Adams, Indian citizen Khalwinder Singh Bhengura, Mexican citizen Moises Anwar Arellano-Alba, Democratic Republic of the Congo national Celestin Katubadi, and Mexican citizen Rocio Thrasher were all charged with illegally voting in the 2024 election and false statements of citizenship to register to vote. Katubadi cast a provisional ballot that was ultimately rejected, the U.S. Department of Justice statement said.
Paxton’s office didn’t immediately respond to a request for comment, and no additional details were immediately available.
Votebeat on Tuesday could not immediately find reliable contact information for the people charged.
There are more than 18 million registered voters in Texas, and more than 11 million cast ballots in the November 2024 general election. Seven people make up a tiny fraction of that number.
Nonetheless, the charges come as President Donald Trump’s administration has sought to crack down on what it has asserted is an increase of noncitizens registered to vote in the country. His administration has reportedly surged resources into investigations connected to potential cases of voter fraud and noncitizen voting.
Earlier this month, the Justice Department charged five people in Pennsylvania, Wisconsin, and New Jersey with voting-related crimes.
State confirms citizenship for more than 500 flagged voters
In a separate news release Tuesday, the Texas Secretary of State’s Office said it had referred 117 potential cases of noncitizen voting to the Office of the Attorney General for investigation. The cases are not tied to a specific election. The referrals are part of “a larger update on Texas’ ongoing efforts to review voter citizenship ahead of the Nov. 3 election,” the news release said.
Texas officials last October sent counties a list of 2,724 potential noncitizens generated by checking the state’s voter roll of more than 18 million registered voters against a federal program used to verify citizenship, known as SAVE.
Soon after the state transmitted the names, counties began to investigate the flagged registrants, and quickly confirmed that at least some were citizens. In addition, county officials found that hundreds of the flagged voters had registered through the state Department of Public Safety, which requires proof of citizenship, such as a passport, and keeps copies of such documents on file.
The Texas Secretary of State’s Office told Votebeat and the Texas Tribune that it did not initially check the registrants flagged as potential noncitizens against DPS records before sending the list to county election officials to investigate. That decision prompted a March lawsuit from voting rights groups and some Texas voters who said the state should have done so. The lawsuit is still pending in federal court.
In May, state officials confirmed they would check the DPS records. In July, Christina Adkins, the state elections director, told county officials the state had been able to confirm some of the flagged voters were citizens, and said county officials should immediately reinstate any incorrectly flagged voters who had been removed from the voter roll.
The Tuesday news release said officials were able to confirm citizenship for 578 voters, and of those, 506 were flagged because their passport information was not added to the federal SAVE program until after Texas had initially checked its list.
County voter registrars in Texas received a directive to reinstate the incorrectly flagged voters Tuesday, Kristin Miles, president of the Texas Association of County Election Officials, said in a statement. Miles said the registrars “are grateful that due diligence performed at the state level has brought resolution for impacted voters.”
Natalia Contreras covers election administration and voting access for Votebeat in partnership with the Texas Tribune. Natalia is based in Corpus Christi. Contact her at ncontreras@votebeat.org.

Title: Hand soap recall affects products sold in 15 states and at Ingles
Article_Text:
Hand soap recalled for potential contamination of antibiotic-resistant bacteria
(Gray News) - Six hand soaps distributed to 15 states have been recalled because they may be contaminated with bacteria.
The hand soaps were distributed by Intercon Chemical Co. to 19 wholesale companies and one retail company across 15 states, including California, Georgia, Illinois, Iowa, Maryland, Mississippi, Nebraska, New York, North Carolina, North Dakota, Pennsylvania, South Carolina, Texas, Washington and Wisconsin, according to the U.S. Food and Drug Administration.
EN ESPAÑOL | Retiran del mercado jabón de manos por posible contaminación con bacterias
Four of the hand soaps are potentially contaminated with unspecified bacteria. Two of the soaps are sold under the Laura Lynn brand, which is sold at Ingles grocery stores.
The recalled hand soaps include:
- 301 cases of 8-ounce Laura Lynn Honey Apple Crisp Liquid Hand Soap with UPC 086854074305; lot codes C3576 and 26-01804; best by dates of Nov. 5, 2026, and March 2028.
- 294 cases of 7.5-ounce Laura Lynn Foaming Pear Scent Hand Soap with Moisturizers with UPC 08685407408, lot code 26-01001 and best by date March 13, 2028.
- 1,040 cases of 28.7-ounce Summit 150 Foaming Hand Soap with lot codes BF97303, BF97304 and BF97305; UPC 810080570030 and best by dates of Feb. 3, 2028, Feb. 4, 2028 and Feb. 5, 2028.
- 224 cases of 33.8-ounce Vestis Foaming Hand Soap, Fresh Pear Scent with UPC 810080570405, lot code 26-03091 and best by date May 2028.
The other recalled soaps are potentially contaminated with several types of Pseudomonas and Serratia bacteria, which are known to be resistant to antibiotics and can cause complications including blood infections, pneumonia, urinary tract infections, eye infections, brain infections, bone infections and heart infections.
The hand soaps include:
- 693 cases of 28.7-ounce Intercon Foaming Pear Hand Soap with Aloe with UPC 789745002981; lot codes AF97312, 26-01001 and 26-01803 and best by dates of Jan. 12, 2028, March 13, 2028, and March 2028.
- 143 cases of 34-ounce Clearly Better by Intercon Foaming Pear Hand Soap with Aloe with UPC 789745002615, lot codes 26-01001 and 26-01803; with best by dates of March 13, 2028 and March 2028.
The soaps may be found in businesses and public places, in addition to Ingles grocery stores.
Anyone who has purchased or used the recalled hand soaps should stop using them right away and contact their doctor if they have developed symptoms of illness.

Title: Ed Sheeran's Tour Support Acts Drop Out After Macklemore Exit
Article_Text:
Ed Sheeran Tour Support Acts Drop Put After Macklemore Exit
Ed Sheeran’s Tour Support Acts Drop Out After Macklemore Exit
Ed Sheeran's current U.S. tour appears to be all but upended as his support acts drop out after Macklemore's exit.

Ed Sheeran has found himself in an impossible position after all his supporting acts for his Loop Tour have dropped out. Several acts have said that after Macklemore was asked to leave over his pro-Palestine comments, they followed suit in solidarity.
As reported by The Independent, Ed Sheeran was on the U.S. leg of his worldwide Loop Tour with Macklemore among the many supporting acts for the event. Macklemore was the first to leave the tour and stated that the promoter requested that the Seattle rapper exit the tour due to his support of Palestinians, often seen as an affront to Israel.
Sheeran attempted to soften the blow of Macklemore’s stance and his unceremonious exit by saying he was not “complicit” and that the call was made by the promoter. Shortly after, other acts on the tour, including Sheeran’s band, issued social media statements that they could no longer go forward with the tour despite the massive economic loss it would bring upon them.
Finneas, the brother of Billie Eilish, took to social media to explain his position on not joining Sheeran in South America later this year.
“Artists must not be silenced when they speak up for the oppressed,” Finneas wrote. “I have decided to withdraw from my upcoming tour dates with Ed Sheeran. I stand with Palestine and its people.”
Beoga, an Irish band, posted a statment on Instagram explaining why they will leave the tour and, in a bold move, decried the promoter’s support of Israel and Zionist policies.

Title: Gold, silver prices fall as Warsh signals more tightening ahead - Kitco PM Report
Article_Text:
(Kitco NewsWire) - Spot gold and silver prices are lower in late-afternoon U.S. trading Wednesday, after the Federal Reserve raised interest rates for the first time since 2023 and signaled that more tightening may be needed to contain inflation. At the time of writing, spot gold was trading near $4,261.80 an ounce, down 0.72%, while spot silver was trading at $62.82, down 1.16% on the session.
North American equity markets closed lower after Fed Chair Kevin Warsh’s press conference pushed yields and the dollar higher. The S&P 500 fell 33.92 points, or 0.4%, to 7,551.81, the Dow Jones Industrial Average dropped 631.21 points, or 1.2%, to 51,461.90, the Nasdaq Composite slipped 3.15 points, or less than 0.1%, to 25,978.42, and the Russell 2000 fell 11.47 points, or 0.4%, to 2,858.81. European markets finished higher before the Fed decision, with the STOXX Europe 600 up 0.46% to 637.09. London’s FTSE 100 rose 0.28% to 10,688.47, Germany’s DAX gained 0.61% to 25,558.88, France’s CAC 40 added 0.62% to 8,140.59, and Italy’s FTSE MIB climbed 0.80% to 51,969.12.
The latest positioning shifted back against precious metals after the Fed raised the target range for the federal funds rate by 25 basis points to 3.75% to 4.00% and the updated projections showed 16 of 18 officials saw at least one more hike by year-end. Warsh said inflation remains too high, and the market read the decision as more than a one-and-done response to oil-driven price pressure. The two-year Treasury yield rose to about 4.734%, the 10-year yield moved back to 5.00%, and the dollar index climbed to 100.25. Thursday’s jobless claims, Philadelphia Fed manufacturing index and housing starts now become the next checks on whether the economy is strong enough to absorb tighter policy. For gold, the message is rate-negative: the expected hike was priced, but the dot plot and Warsh’s tone kept the real-yield channel in control.
Precious metals surrendered the pre-Fed relief bounce. Gold fell back toward the $4,257.42 support area and remains below the $4,313.67 resistance level from the latest technical grid. Silver dropped below its $63.3172 pivot and is testing toward $62.1558 support after failing to hold above the $64.3018 resistance area. The late-session move shows that dollar and yield sensitivity still outweighs safe-haven demand when the Fed is actively tightening. Bulls now need a quick break in yields, or the path of least resistance remains toward lower support.
