Title: Opening acts drop out of Ed Sheeran's tour one month ahead of Charlotte date
Article_Text:
Ed Sheeran's tour of North and South America has been roiled by the decision this week to drop Macklemore as an opener because of the rapper's onstage pro-Palestinian comments. Since then, all of Sheeran's other supporting acts have dropped out, including a group that performs with Sheeran during part of the show.
Sheeran, who is scheduled to perform in Philadelphia on Saturday, said the decision to cut Macklemore from the Loop Tour was the promoter's, not his own. The “Thrift Shop” rapper exclaimed “Free Palestine” during the Sept. 5 date in New Jersey.
Other WRAL Top Stories
“To all of my Jewish brothers and sisters, criticism of Israel, criticism of apartheid, being against genocide, it in no way is criticism of you,” he said during the New Jersey concert. “This message is for peace, love, for all human beings to be treated with dignity, respect, and equality.”
Macklemore has said his removal was the result of an effort led by Robert Kraft, the billionaire owner of the New England Patriots. His Kraft Group also owns Gillette Stadium, where the NFL team plays and where Sheeran is scheduled to perform later this month. Kraft's involvement was implicitly cited in some of the statements from the supporting acts who left Sheeran's tour Tuesday, decrying the influence of money.
Here's where things stand with Sheeran's tour.
Finneas, Lukas Graham, Aaron Rowe and Beoga all quit
The Danish band Lukas Graham and Irish singer Aaron Rowe were scheduled to replace Macklemore as the opening acts on Sheeran's remaining U.S. tour dates. Finneas, the American singer and close collaborator with sister Billie Eilish, was down to open for Sheeran on four of his South American dates. Beoga, an Irish folk band, had been performing with Sheeran for part of his set since his tour began in January in New Zealand.
“Artists must not be silenced when they speak up for the oppressed,” Finneas wrote.
The announcements from each supporting act came roughly within an hour of each other Tuesday. Earlier that day, Sheeran posted his own statement blaming the promoter for Macklemore's removal and maintaining that he refused to be drawn into a public discussion about the war in Gaza.
Rowe and Beoga cited their country’s history to explain their decision. “We are Irish people who understand colonialism. As founding members of the Irish Artists for Palestine movement, we are committed activists for justice and will continue to be,” Beoga posted.
Rowe called Sheeran a friend. “But as Irish people we know all too well about genocide, forced famine and violent occupation,” he wrote, adding that he couldn’t “stand by and allow billionaires to use their position of power to silence the rightful voices of those who speak up.”
Lukas Graham also appeared to take a veiled shot at Kraft, writing: "Money doesn’t give you the right to own the conversation. Nobody’s bank balance should decide who gets to speak or which suffering we’re allowed to acknowledge."
Kraft's representatives did not respond to an emailed request for comment Tuesday, but in a statement Monday, he wrote that the decision to cancel Macklemore was a result of the rapper's recent comments “and a broader history of antisemitic rhetoric and imagery.”
“This decision is not about diminishing the suffering of innocent Palestinians or denying anyone the right to advocate on their behalf. Their pain and loss are real,” Kraft said.
Charlotte tour date
WRAL reached out to Tepper Sports & Entertainment, which owns and operates Bank of America Stadium, about the status of Sheeran's Oct. 17 North Carolina tour stop.
We asked:
- Did Robert Kraft reach out to Tepper Sports & Entertainment about a 'stadium boycott' related to the show's opener, Macklemore?
- Did Tepper Sports & Entertainment participate in a 'stadium boycott' to have Macklemore removed from the tour?
- How is Bank of America Stadium handling the changes to the Loop Tour that's now just over one month away?
Tepper Sports & Entertainment has not responded.
Sheeran hasn't commented since the supporting acts dropped out
After Macklemore issued a lengthy statement Monday about being removed from the tour, Sheeran took to Instagram to lay out his side.
“Macklemore coming off tour was the promoter’s decision, it was not mine,” he wrote Tuesday. “I would never let down the fans who had made plans, nor would I abandon the touring crew and the other support acts and musicians who rely on me for work and to make a living.”
Neither Sheeran nor Macklemore has posted since those supporting acts left the tour, and Sheeran's representative didn't respond to an emailed request for comment. The promoter, Messina Touring Group, also hasn't responded to requests for comment.
In his statement Tuesday, Sheeran said he was “not complicit” and that he had his own views on the war in Gaza.
“There is a reason I do not use my professional platform for politics — my audience includes young people, often children, of all backgrounds. Those who come to my show do not expect a political forum,” he wrote.
While Sheeran has not been as politically vocal as many fellow artists, he has expressed support for some causes in the past. He performed at the Concert for Ukraine in 2022, which raised money for Ukrainians affected by the Russian invasion, and collaborated with a Ukrainian band on a charity single. He has also campaigned against racism in the U.K. and criticized his country's government for cutting arts funding.

Title: Colombian community in Reading gathers to support earthquake victims
Article_Text:
Colombian community in Reading gathers to support earthquake victims and connect with loved ones
Members of Union Colombiana in Reading, Pennsylvania, are finding ways to connect their homeland after a devastating earthquake in southwestern Colombia.
Members of Union Colombiana in Reading, Pennsylvania, gathered to pray, reflect, and organize aid for victims of a 7.4-magnitude earthquake that struck southwestern Colombia, killing hundreds and leaving the region in ruins.
Heartache and helplessness from afar
Juan Carlos Ramirez expressed his deep connection to his homeland, saying, "Mi familia colombiana, mi patria colombiana," which translates to "My Colombian family, my Colombian homeland."
For Alba Fernandez, the gathering evoked powerful emotions. "I left the country when I was 14 and I didn't go back for a long time," she said. "When I went back, I realized that my heart belonged there."
Andrea Yoder shared her sadness over the destruction caused by the earthquake. "Ver la 
destrucción por el terremoto me hace sentir muy triste," she said, which translates to "Seeing the destruction from the earthquake makes me very sad."  
She also described feeling helpless. "Me hace sentir un poco impotente de no poder ayudar a las personas como quisiera," she said, which translates to "It makes me feel a little helpless that I can't help people the way I would like to."
Finding solace through prayer and community
Despite being far from home, Yoder said she has found solace in prayer. "Nuestros corazones necesitan hablar, necesitan desahogarse y, más aún, desahogarse con Dios," she said, which translates to "Our hearts need to speak. They need to release what we're feeling, and especially to do that with God."
The women have organized donation drives and held a vigil for the lives lost, creating a space for reflection and connection. "We're able to gather here, we're able to really just get people to, you know, just slow down, reflect, you know, just provide some solace to our, our, our friends and families back home," Fernandez said.
Union Colombiana invited Ramirez to lead prayers during the vigil. "God talks about how one day everything will perish, but three things will remain, and that's faith, hope, and love," Ramirez said.
Ramirez expressed his longing to be in Colombia to help. "Quisiera estar ahí para mover bloques. Pero no puedo estar ahí," he said, which translates to "I wish I could be there. I wish I could help pick up debris, but I can't be there."
He reminded the group of their shared love for their homeland. "Es el amor que tenemos como colombianos para salir al frente y hacer algo para nuestra patria, para nuestra comunidad," he said, which translates to "It’s the love we have as Colombians that allows us to step forward and do something for our homeland, for our community."
Fernandez emphasized the importance of the gathering.
"Having a space like this where we can come together and just reflect, you know, and just have a time to pray and hope that our people back home are on the path to recovery," she said.
Through prayer, music, and community, the group found a way to channel their emotions into action, bridging the distance between Pennsylvania and Colombia.

Title: Ventura Music Festival Presents Pacific Jazz Orchestra: A Tribute to Quincy Jones Featuring Vocalists Nayanna Holley & Adam 'Aejaye' Jackson
Article_Text:
Program, Led by Multi-GRAMMY®-Nominated Artistic Director Chris Walden, Spotlights the Late Producer/Composer's Masterful Early Work
Sunday, October 18, 2026, 3:00 PM, at Camarillo's Rancho Campana Performing Arts Center
VENTURA, Calif., Sept. 16, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- Ventura Music Festival presents Pacific Jazz Orchestra: A Tribute to Quincy Jones, an exploration of Jones' masterful early work from the 1950s and 60s, featuring guest vocalists Nayanna Holley and Adam "Aejaye" Jackson, Sunday, October 18, 2026, 3:00 PM, at the Rancho Campana Performing Arts Center in Camarillo.
Pacific Jazz Orchestra Artistic Director Chris Walden, a seven-time GRAMMY®-nominee and lead arranger for the Oscars, leads the group's driving 19-piece Big Band Ensemble through his original arrangements of Jones' genre-spanning work onstage and onscreen, transporting the audience to the icon's musical roots.
Highlighting Jones' prolific output, the program features selections from his big band recordings, among them The Quintessence (1962), which exemplify his innovative approach to jazz orchestration. Also featured are some of Jones' masterful arrangements for legendary singers such as Frank Sinatra and Sarah Vaughan, including his collaboration on Vaughan and Violins (1959), in which Jones' orchestration beautifully complements her vocal prowess.
From Jones' contributions to film and television scoring, the Pacific Jazz Orchestra Big Band Ensemble performs themes from The Pawnbroker (1964) and In the Heat of the Night (1967), which illustrate his tremendous versatility and uncanny ability to convey complex emotions through music as well as his significant impact on the soundscape of American cinema.
Jones was a household name for decades, but long before Michael Jackson and "We Are the World," the musician/arranger/producer worked his way up, first from humble beginnings as a jazz trumpeter and then scoring films when he moved to Los Angeles. His lifelong impact is considerable, including a long list of those whom he mentored, among them Walden himself.
Holley, a vocalist and vocal contractor, has been a member of the house band for NBC's The Voice for more than ten seasons and performed for several seasons in the house band of American Idol. Her film credits include The Color Purple, The Eternals, Encanto, Coming 2 America, and Mulan. As a background singer, Holley has toured with P!nk, Kelly Clarkson, St. Vincent, Robbie Williams, Selena Gomez, and Sheryl Crow, among others. As a vocal contractor, Holley assembles and hires singers for film and TV programs such as the Academy Awards, The Voice, American Idol, The Talk, and The Late Late Show with James Corden.
Jackson is a seasoned vocalist and songwriter who brings a soulful blend of R&B, soul, and jazz to the stage. The Detroit-born vocalist, actor, and dancer began singing in church at age three. He has toured and recorded with Toni Braxton, John Tess, Billy Griffin, David Foster, Charo, Vesta Williams, Linda Hopkins, Harvey Mason. Josh Groban, Stevie Wonder, Melissa Manchester, Kenneth "BabyFace" Edmunds, Macklemore, Carole Bayer Sager, Patti Austin Marilyn McCoo and Billy Davis Jr, to name a few. His other passion is mentoring at-risk youth through such organizations as The Coalition for At Risk and Restoring Youth and In A World With Books.
Pacific Jazz Orchestra has garnered critical acclaim for thrilling performances that "entertain, inspire, and enrich" (Variety). Major funders for Pacific Jazz Orchestra include GRoW @ Annenberg Foundation; the Alesia Alpert Family Foundation; the Natalie Cole Foundation; the Ella Fitzgerald Foundation; and Anonymous.
Rancho Campana Performing Arts Center is located at 4235 Mar Vista Drive, Camarillo, CA, 93010. For tickets ($15-$109) and information, visit https://www.venturamusicfestival.org or call (805) 648-3146.
For information about Pacific Jazz Orchestra, visit www.pacificjazz.org.
About Pacific Jazz Orchestra
PACIFIC JAZZ ORCHESTRA embraces and reflects the diverse and enthralling soundscape of Los Angeles, where the 40-piece ensemble was born, bred, and resides. The ultimate cross-over sensation, the nimble hybrid jazz big band and string orchestra comprised of powerhouse LA studio musicians deftly navigates musical styles ranging from jazz, Latin, soul, and R&B, to pop, musical theater, symphonic, and cinematic soundtracks.
Founded in 2022 by seven-time GRAMMY®-nominated composer/arranger/conductor Chris Walden, Pacific Jazz Orchestra has garnered critical acclaim for thrilling performances that "entertain, inspire, and enrich" (Variety). As artistic director and conductor, Walden creates a melting pot of original music and unique arrangements for every show, each with a specific theme, distinctive jazz flair, and lush orchestrations.
The ensemble is also noted for its ambitious collaborations with a wide range of guest artists, among them acclaimed singer/songwriter Rufus Wainwright, singer/actress Katharine McPhee, GRAMMY®-winning vocal group TAKE 6, and Tony Award-winner Aaron Tveit. Other projects have featured eminent violinist Caroline Campbell, celebrated saxophonist Ben Wendel, GRAMMY®-winning artist Ledisi, R&B/soul singer Adam "AeJaye" Jackson, vocal stylist Sheléa, and veteran blues and funk singer Billy Valentine.
Pacific Jazz Orchestra presents an annual concert series at various Southern California venues and has toured to Japan with its 18-piece big band configuration. It is LA's first resident jazz orchestra since 2006, when the Henry Mancini Institute closed its doors after an acclaimed ten-year run. A 501-(c)(3) non-profit organization, Pacific Jazz Orchestra is sponsored in part by the Herb Alpert Foundation. Its Advisory Board Members include David Foster, Quincy Jones (in memoriam), Monica Mancini, Alan Bergman (in memoriam), Rickey Minor, Harvey Mason Jr., and Ledisi.
About Chris Walden
Seven-time GRAMMY®-nominated composer/arranger CHRIS WALDEN is the artistic director and conductor of Pacific Jazz Orchestra. Hailed as a "distinguished conductor" (Audio Media International) and "gifted and well-connected arranger-composer" (Santa Barbara Independent) who pens "exquisite string arrangements" (The Arts Desk), Walden "has built an illustrious career working behind the scenes with some of music's biggest names" (grammy.com).
He has scored more than 40 feature and TV films and written more than 1,500 orchestral and big band arrangements for such artists as John Legend, Michael Bublé, Aretha Franklin, Paul McCartney, SEAL, Stevie Wonder, Rihanna, Barbra Streisand, and Josh Groban. He has also collaborated as an arranger and bandleader with jazz artists Diana Krall, Herb Alpert, Michael Brecker, Arturo Sandoval, and the Count Basie Orchestra and served as the lead arranger for the Academy Awards, Kennedy Center Honors, American Idol, and even the Super Bowl, arranging Jennifer Hudson's National Anthem performance. In addition to working closely with producers David Foster, Tommy LiPuma, and Phil Ramone, Walden's credits include conducting the Los Angeles Philharmonic, Hollywood Bowl Orchestra, Holland's Metropole Orkest, Boston Pops, Philadelphia Orchestra, Pittsburgh Symphony, and WDR Big Band Cologne, among others.
The German-born musician, who performs on trumpet and flugelhorn as well, composed music for German films and TV before emigrating to Los Angeles at the age of 29. Walden, who lives in Los Angeles, has served as trustee on the national board of the Recording Academy and past president of the American Society of Music Arrangers and Composers (ASMAC).
About Ventura Music Festival
The Pacific Jazz Orchestra concert is one of five events in the Ventura Music Festival's 2026 Fall Series, running October 11 through 18. The series opens October 11 with Tea and Trumpets, VMF's beloved signature afternoon tea and brass quintet experience, returning by popular demand. On Thursday, October 15, Artistic Director Nuvi Mehta leads Birth of Impressionism, a Classical Edge Concert blending live performance, history, and discovery at Ventura College Performing Arts Center. Friday, October 16 brings TAKE3 -- Where Rock Meets Bach -- to Ventura Music Hall, with a conservatory-trained, rock-star-electrifying violin, cello, and piano trio. On Saturday, October 17, the two most decorated fiddle players in IBMA history -- Michael Cleveland and Jason Carter -- perform at Mission Park in Ventura. The season closes December 15 with the celebrated twelve-voice ensemble Chanticleer in a special holiday concert at Ventura Center for Spiritual Living. Tickets for all VMF-presented Fall Series events are available at venturamusicfestival.org or by calling (805) 648-3146.

Title: Lumen Field Ranks #2 Loudest NFL Stadium, Study Finds
Article_Text:
Lumen Field Ranks Among the NFL’s Loudest Venues
Every NFL fanbase claims their stadium is the loudest in the league. Commercial Acoustics measured it, scoring all 30 stadiums on a 100-point scale that weighed architectural design, sustained crowd noise, peak volume during big moments, and how the stadium's layout channels sound back toward the field.
Kansas City topped the list at 97 points, and the Chiefs have the hardware to back it up — Arrowhead Stadium holds the Guinness World Record for loudest crowd roar at any sporting event, measured at 142.2 decibels back in 2014. For reference, that's louder than a jet flying 100 feet overhead.
Where Seattle Fits Into the Picture
Lumen Field landed second overall at 95 points, trailing only Arrowhead. New Orleans' Superdome came in third at 93, followed by Minnesota's U.S. Bank Stadium and Buffalo's Highmark Stadium rounding out the top five.
Here's the number Seahawks fans should actually be bragging about, though: when researchers adjusted for stadium size and measured noise per 1,000 seats, Lumen Field came out on top of the entire league. Seattle's design — steep upper decks, a partial roof that traps sound and reflects it straight back down onto the field — punches above its capacity in a way even Arrowhead's massive crowd can't quite match pound for pound.
Why the Design Matters More Than the Crowd Size
Philadelphia, Green Bay, Denver, Pittsburgh, and Detroit filled out the rest of the top ten, each earning their spot through some combination of passionate fans and stadium architecture built to hold that energy in.
For anyone in North Central Washington who's driven over the Cascades for a Seahawks game, this data confirms what the ringing in your ears already told you. Lumen Field isn't just loud because Seattle fans show up—it's loud because the building was engineered to make sure every bit of that noise hits the playing field. Seeing a game live at Lumen Field is like attending a rock concert. You should bring earplugs, or stuff wrapped paper napkins into your ear canal to save your hearing. Been to a game? You'll know all about the volume. The shrill shriek - aimed at disrupting the opposing team's offense.

Title: You Nearly Missed: Bilal expanding the boundaries of soul at the Pearl
Article_Text:
You Nearly Missed: Bilal expanding the boundaries of soul at the Pearl
Get the best of Vancouver in your inbox, every Tuesday and Thursday. Sign up for our free newsletter.
The company an artist has been known to keep often speaks volumes.
Hard-core fans know Bilal as one of the most uncompromising and enduring voices in experimental soul. The Philadelphia–spawned singer first carved out a name for himself in the ’90s as a member of the Soulquarians, a New York collective whose rotating cast included Erykah Badu and future members of the Roots. Since then he’s collaborated with some of the biggest names in hip-hop, appearing on tracks with everyone from Kendrick Lamar and Dr. Dre (“Fallen” and “These Walls in case you’re keeping score) to Beyoncé and Badu (“Jump in the Air & Stay There” and “Everything I Do”). Add to this list Mac Miller, Scarface, Common, J Dilla, De La Soul, the Roots, and Ghostface Killah, and Bilal has some serious names in his Rolodex.
Still, at heart, he’s a solo artist. And in that guise, like all visionaries, he takes the approach that boundaries are there to not only be pushed, but lovingly exploded.
When Bilal first burst onto the scene with 2001’s 1st Born Second, he was slotted in the neo-soul section of your favourite record store. Subsequent albums showcased him as an artist with zero interest in being pigeonholed. A Love Surreal from 2013 swung from glitched-out R&B to sundappled MOR. He subsequently unleashed his inner jazz demon with 2015’s In Another Life.
With Grammy-nominated comeback album Adjust Brightness from 2024, Bilal proved himself one of those rare musical anomalies: a songwriter with no shortage of new ideas despite having been in the game for decades.
The album was in many ways rooted in the singer’s growth as a person. Not content with just making music, he took up painting with a passion. Travel—perhaps the most important thing one can do to expand their worldview—led him to life-changing experiences such as seances in Morocco, where he also chose to live for a while.
Add the mind-bending mess that was COVID to the equation, and with Adjust Brightness you got not so much a record as a sprawling work of ambitious art. From the woozy round-midnight deconstructed jazz of “Adjust Brightness” to the thin-white-duke trip-pop of “Evr Chngin Nrml” to genre-mashing marvel that is “Quantum Universe”, Bilal showcases himself as someone who, in his late 40s, is just getting going.
The man, who heads to Vancouver this week with breakout R&B queen Yaya Bey, runs with some heavy hitters. There’s a reason for that: Bilal is considered, not only by his fans but also his peers, a true giant in the game.

Title: Data center proposed for Swatara Twp. behind WITF
Article_Text:
Corscale, a data center developer and operator based in Texas, purchased the property in Swatara Twp. with plans to build a data center.
Haley O'Brien / WITF
A 157-acre property in Swatara Township could soon become the site of a $10.5 billion data center campus that has drawn strong opposition from residents who worry about the project’s impact on their quality of life.
Corscale, a Texas-based data center developer, presented plans for its US Highlands East Project at the township’s planning commission meeting Sept. 8.
The proposed development would be located along Highland Street, bordering I-283 behind the WITF Public Media Center and the Red Lion Hotel. It would also sit near nearly a dozen homes.
The project would include two one-story buildings, about 372,000 sq. ft. each, as well as a PPL switch station and a private substation.
About a dozen residents who spoke at the meeting earlier this month raised concerns about the project’s power use, water consumption and stormwater management.
“That’s a lot for us,” said commissioner Tom Connolly. “Some of them certainly had concerns.”
Corscale representatives answered questions and shared land development plans at the Sept. 8 meeting.
Erik Draaisma is executive vice president at Corscale, the Texas-based developer with three data centers in Virginia and others in development.
“This project is fully funded, it’s not speculative,” he said. “And we do have a very far developed tenant in tow.”
The tenant will not be revealed until that is made final.
Power was noted as a concern from residents at the start of the meeting.
“I’m worried about power generation,” said Megan O’Neil. “I would like to have that addressed and the backup source. The backup source being maybe wind or solar and not generators.”
The Pennsylvania Public Utility Commission released an independent analysis this week that found that the grid cannot keep up with the rapidly growing electricity demand sparked by data centers.
Draaisma said the location was chosen partially because of its proximity to power lines.
“It’s no secret data centers need a lot of power,” he said.
Draaisma said PPL confirmed the availability of grid power for the project.
“The power is coming from the grid,” he said. “And we are paying for all of that.”
The public asked about stormwater management. Bill Rearden from Bohler Engineering said that tests confirmed that the plan in place would meet the township’s requirements.
Draaisma said this project will require minimal water use, consuming about 7,000 gallons a day in a closed loop system.
“A midsize office building is probably the equivalent of that,” he said.
Draaisma said the tenant will not generate their own power onsite as a primary source. The property will include about 12 generators for backup.
Connolly said he was pleased the developer directly answered residents’ questions.
One resident, Justin Bradnick, applauded the project and encouraged the commissioners to think about ways to spend the tax revenue to benefit residents in the township.
“Provide paid firefighters, after school care, summer programs. All this can be done,” Bradnick said. “Everything is going up and the township needs the monetary resources to provide what we want for its citizens.”
Resident Damond Wagner requested more specifics about what will actually be inside the buildings.
“I think there needs to be a bit of transparency between the developer and the community,” he said.
Corscale plans to host an information session in October to provide more details.

Title: School District of Lancaster board told of improving financial position
Article_Text:
School District of Lancaster has significantly improved its financial standing, repaying loans it took out earlier this year to cover expenses, Chief Financial Officer Marcia Stokes said during Tuesday night’s board meeting.
The district has paid off a $10 million loan from First National Bank that it took out in July and some $19 million borrowed from its capital reserve account between April and July.
“I can say with confidence you have no balance on your (short-term loan), and you have no money owed between the general fund and the capital reserve fund,” Stokes told board members. “That is because we have started to receive our real property tax revenues and started to receive our state subsidies.”
The district’s general account stood at $14.1 million July 31. That account jumped to $24 million by Sept. 1, Stokes said — the exact amount recommended by the Pennsylvania Department of Education. State guidelines say a school district should keep about 8% of its spending plan in that fund, which means the district should have about $24 million, based on projected $300 million in expenses for 2026-2027.
The capital reserve account, mainly used for maintenance and building projects, held $16.2 million July 31. That balance increased to about $29.8 million by Sept. 1.
“The capital reserve fund has been made whole,” Stokes said. “It’s back to just shy of the $30 million cash balance that should be in the capital reserve accounts.”
The district needed to borrow money to pay teacher salaries and expenses over the summer, a time school districts traditionally see little revenue coming in, Stokes said.
“July was a difficult month from a cash flow perspective because it's not a big month that we receive a lot of state aid, and it's the very beginning of the time where we start our tax collection,” Stokes said.
For example, the district collected $28.9 million in property taxes in August, up from $10 million received in July. In addition, money from the state budget hit $18 million in August, compared to $3.4 million in July.
Administrators, who closed on the short-term loan July 6, repaid $5 million Aug. 4, $2.5 million Aug. 13 and $2.5 million Aug. 20.
Larger challenge remains
While the short-term improvement in the district’s financial condition mostly resolves the larger fiscal challenges it faces, district officials still must deal with the fallout after announcing in January they had failed to account for about $15 million in expenses during the 2024-2025 budget year, including about $8.1 million for salaries and benefits for 83 employees.
Administrators also are dealing with a structural deficit that sees district expenses increasing 4.1% each year while revenue grows by about 3.3% each year, prompting officials to borrow money from its capital reserve account.
Cost-cutting, budget adjustments, furloughs and other changes over the past six months now predict the district will end 2026-27 about $750,000 in the hole. Board members reduced the projected deficit from $27.8 million by voting to pay down debt, eliminating 92 staff positions and trimming some $14.5 million from this year’s spending plan.
State audit not unusual
Stokes also echoed comments by other district officials this week that a state Department of Education compliance audit that began Aug. 17 is not out of the ordinary. She assured board members that the education department will review all 500 public school districts within the next several years.
Those audits stopped in 2022 due to a funding shortage at the Pennsylvania Bureau of Performance Audits, Stokes said. The education department restarted compliance reviews in the 2024-25 school year.
“I do want to make sure that everybody understands that it’s routine, and it’s far beyond just finances,” said Stokes, who added that she didn’t know how long the audit would take. The audit covers district operations from July 1, 2024, through August 1, 2026.
A state official said the education department has increased the number of district compliance audits it conducts, Superintendent Keith Miles said.
“The deputy secretary came to our all-superintendent meeting (and) told us that these were ramping back up, and I know for certain at least one additional district in our Lancaster Lebanon group, OK, is undergoing the same process,” said Miles, referring to the Lancaster-Lebanon Intermediate Unit 13 service area.
Administrators also have started preparing for the district’s 2025-26 fiscal year audit. Representatives from CliftonLarsonAllen, the private firm hired to review the district’s books, are expected to visit the district Oct. 19 and have already received financial documents, Stokes said.

Title: Store director claims Target fired him for reporting race discrimination
Article_Text:
He says Target investigated him - not the manager he reported
A former Target store director alleges the retailer fired him for reporting race discrimination.
A longtime Target employee with consistently strong reviews and no prior discipline claims the company terminated him after he raised a team member's complaint about race-based scheduling at another store - and investigated him instead of the manager he reported. The federal complaint was filed September 14, 2026 in the Eastern District of Pennsylvania.
The store director joined Target in approximately June 2018 as a senior team leader in human resources, according to the filing. He was promoted repeatedly - to executive team leader in 2019, then store director in February 2022. He ran multiple Philadelphia locations before taking charge of Target's Springfield, Pennsylvania store in May 2024.
His reviews were consistently strong, the complaint states. Target rated him as having "Delivered Exceptional Outcomes" and praised him for building talent, developing leaders, and turning "one of the most operationally challenged stores" into "a sales success story." In 2024, a Target senior vice president recognized his team for a shortage improvement of more than $1.5 million. The filing notes Target never issued him any written discipline before terminating him.
The complaint alleges the store director had raised race discrimination concerns on multiple occasions before the events that led to his firing. Before December 2024, he used Target's Integrity Hotline to report what he believed was discriminatory conduct at another Target store - including schedule manipulation that cut white employees' hours and hiring directives that favored Black applicants, the filing states. He raised the issue again with his district senior director in December 2024 and was told to keep using official channels, according to the complaint.
On April 7, 2025, a team member from the other store called and told the store director that the same manager was still cutting the hours of white employees and favoring Black employees in hiring, the filing alleges. The store director told the team member to report the complaint to the Integrity Hotline. Within hours, he escalated the complaint to his district senior director and a human resources business partner, according to the complaint.
What happened next, the complaint claims, was the opposite of what the store director expected. Target did not investigate the manager he reported. Instead, the filing alleges, his district senior director referred him to the Integrity Hotline for communicating with a team member "off the clock" - even though that communication was the team member's call reporting race discrimination.
On May 2, 2025, according to the complaint, the district senior director arrived at the Springfield store with an investigator. The investigator questioned the store director about "promising promotions" and contacting employees after hours, the filing states. The store director told the investigator about the discrimination complaint. After the interview, the complaint alleges, the district senior director privately told the store director he had "followed protocol."
The filing alleges the investigator did not interview the team member who originally called in the discrimination complaint and did not review the content of that April 7, 2025 call before Target decided to terminate the store director.
The store director became visibly distressed during and after the interview and requested a medical leave the same day, the complaint states. He has Generalized Anxiety Disorder, according to the filing. Target approved leave under the Family and Medical Leave Act from May 2 through July 27, 2025, with job-protected leave running through August 25, 2025.
Seven days after the leave request - and 32 days after the store director escalated the discrimination complaint - the company's human resources business partner sent a termination letter, the complaint alleges. The letter stated he had "engaged in gross misconduct" and that "once you have ended or exhausted any job-protected leave, your employment will be terminated," according to the filing. The complaint states the letter did not specify which communication, which team member, or which policy the store director had supposedly violated.
Target also demanded the return of his keys, laptop, and equipment while he was on approved leave, the filing states. His termination took effect August 25, 2025 - the end of his job-protected leave. Target did not restore him or offer an equivalent position, according to the complaint.
The filing argues the stated reason for the termination was a cover. Target did not discipline the store director he reported, the complaint alleges, and did not discipline that store director for communicating with the plaintiff about the team member's complaint while the team member was off the clock - the same conduct cited against the reporting store director. The filing further alleges Target did not terminate other store directors outside the plaintiff's protected class who communicated with team members about work matters while those employees were off the clock.
The complaint states that as a direct result of the termination, the store director suffered lost wages and benefits, career harm, emotional distress, and worsening of his anxiety disorder. The filing also alleges his wife, who was pregnant, went into pre-term labor within two days of receiving the termination letter.
The complaint brings five counts: race discrimination and retaliation under federal civil rights law, disability discrimination and failure to accommodate under the Americans with Disabilities Act, interference and retaliation under the Family and Medical Leave Act, and parallel claims under the Pennsylvania Human Relations Act. The store director seeks back pay, reinstatement or front pay, compensatory and punitive damages, and attorneys' fees.
He filed a charge with the Equal Employment Opportunity Commission on September 2, 2025, which was also filed with the Pennsylvania Human Relations Commission. The EEOC issued a right-to-sue notice on September 2, 2026.
None of the allegations have been tested, and no court has ruled on the claims.

Title: Reshoring Gains Ground in Defense and Advanced Manufacturing
Article_Text:
The reshoring momentum began more than 10 years ago, ignited by the 2012 presidential race between Barack Obama and Mitt Romney, during which both men criticized China for stealing American jobs, manipulating its currency, and committing human rights abuses. Reshoring experienced slow but steady growth over the next few years as companies began to consider bringing more manufacturing back to America. But the reshoring movement accelerated quickly after the COVID-19 pandemic exposed the enormous risks in global supply chains.
Since 2020, reshoring has been on the agenda in boardrooms across America, where rethinking global manufacturing has become a consistent topic of discussion. But even with all the executive attention, the question remains: Is manufacturing really coming back?
Yes and No
Reshoring is a popular idea and an obvious choice for American manufacturers, as long as businesses can make the economics work. That is, can a company compete on production costs with existing U.S. labor rates, which are often as much as 10 times higher than those in low-cost countries? In addition, companies must consider the complicated U.S. regulatory environment, environmental requirements and inconsistent government policy.
Companies that can automate production through capital equipment expenditures and reengineer their processes have a chance to make the economics work. But companies that depend on significant labor to build their products may not be able to compete. Reducing labor costs and automating production are key to successfully manufacturing in America.
While there has been slight and steady growth in manufacturing jobs over the past 15 years, various government policies, including tariffs and tax breaks, have not accelerated hiring as much as many had hoped. In the past two years, manufacturing job growth has been flat.
One Bright Spot: U.S. Defense Spending
One bright spot is manufacturing in the defense sector. The U.S. government is on track to spend $1.5 trillion on defense this year, and much of that will go to U.S. manufacturers or foreign companies that manufacture in the United States. Accelerated by the war with Iran, spending is expected to remain robust as the United States replenishes its weapons stockpiles.
Federal Acquisition Regulations require a certain percentage of each product purchased to be manufactured in the United States. Because of this, industrial manufacturing in America is expected to grow.
Other Made-in-USA Requirements Attracting FDI
Other U.S. government spending programs require products to be manufactured in America. The Infrastructure Investment and Jobs Act, the CHIPS and Science Act, and the Inflation Reduction Act all include requirements to buy raw materials, parts, subassemblies and other goods made, or at least partially made, in America. These funded programs have driven some manufacturing back to the United States, along with a significant amount of foreign direct investment from companies seeking to participate in government-funded programs.
For example, under the Infrastructure Investment and Jobs Act, specifically the Build America, Buy America Act, all iron, steel, manufactured products and construction materials used in federally funded public infrastructure projects must be produced in the United States.
The CHIPS and Science Act requires companies receiving federal subsidies, grants or tax credits to build, expand or modernize semiconductor manufacturing and research facilities in the United States. This has driven billions of dollars in foreign direct investment from Samsung and TSMC, both of which are building semiconductor fabrication facilities in the United States with partial funding from the federal government.
Foreign Direct Investment in U.S. Manufacturing
The three major government-funded acts have also generated strong interest from foreign investors. Foreign companies in the aerospace sector have invested heavily in U.S. manufacturing to sell products to the federal government and meet U.S.-made content requirements.
Major foreign aerospace and defense corporations investing in U.S. manufacturing include European companies such as Airbus, BAE Systems and Safran, which operate extensive U.S. subsidiaries and supplier networks. Semiconductors, which are essential components of aerospace and defense products, are also being manufactured in the United States for the first time in decades. This focus on U.S. manufacturing benefits both foreign companies and manufacturing employment in America.
Airbus, based in Europe, operates a major commercial aircraft final assembly and manufacturing facility in Mobile, Alabama, producing A320- and A220-family jets. The facility is supported by hundreds of millions of dollars in ongoing expansions.
BAE Systems, based in the United Kingdom, invested $135 million to upgrade and expand its defense and precision-guided munitions manufacturing facilities in Texas and New Hampshire. Safran, based in France, operates multiple U.S. production and maintenance sites. The company is expanding its aerospace electrical systems maintenance, repair and overhaul facilities in Sarasota, Florida, and has opened advanced manufacturing operations for space propulsion in Colorado.
Leonardo, based in Italy, manufactures helicopters through its U.S. subsidiary, Leonardo Helicopters, with substantial operations in Philadelphia.
Samsung, based in South Korea, has invested in a semiconductor fabrication plant in Taylor, Texas. The company has described the project as its largest-ever investment in the United States, with an initial value of $17 billion. Samsung said the facility would expand production of advanced logic chips and improve the supply of critical chips used in next-generation technologies.
Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Co. announced that the expansion of its Arizona site will include three new fabrication plants, two advanced packaging facilities and a major research and development center. TSMC’s total U.S. investment is expected to reach $165 billion, which the company has described as the largest foreign direct investment in U.S. history. The project received $6.6 billion in direct funding under the CHIPS Act.
The Outlook for U.S. Manufacturing
Momentum appears to be building for more foreign direct investment and domestic investment in advanced manufacturing in America. With the assistance of U.S. government funding, the attractiveness of manufacturing in the United States is at an all-time high. Efficiencies gained through automation, robotics and the deployment of artificial intelligence have also strengthened the case for manufacturing here.
Even though job growth is likely to remain slow because of increased automation, investment by U.S. and foreign companies should provide a boost to the American economy.

Title: Sean Kinney settling in at center for the Buffs
Article_Text:
The harshest review of Colorado football’s center position this year has come from Colorado’s center.
“I think I’ve got a long way to go before I really establish myself,” Buffaloes lineman Sean Kinney said Tuesday. “I have to play better than I did the first two games.”
He arrived in Boulder from Lafayette College, where he started all 12 games last season. The year prior, he was named to The Sports Network’s Freshman All-America team — playing right guard, left guard, and center across 11 starts.
At Georgia Tech, a bad snap got him benched. A second one went wrong in the fourth quarter. He was back on the field for the drive that won the game, and when asked Tuesday whether both snaps were his mistake, he did not look for anywhere else to pin them.
“Yeah, they were my fault,” Kinney said. “I mean, getting benched isn’t ideal. The bad snap, it sucks, it’s inexcusable. But I think just being a good teammate — my biggest goal in that game, even when I got benched, it didn’t matter to me, honestly, whether I was on the field or not. As long as we won the game. So being on the sidelines, staying locked in wasn’t that hard when the only goal was to win the game and get back on that plane with a W.”
The Buffaloes beat Georgia Tech 14-13 in Atlanta.
What he brought with him is somewhat unusual for a lineman. At Nazareth High School in Pennsylvania, Kinney won three individual state wrestling championships, was part of a team title, and had Division I wrestling offers waiting when it was time to choose.
It was not much of a choice.
“It probably should have been (hard) because I was ranked really highly in wrestling, not football,” Kinney said. “But I come from a football family. My dad played Division III, went to a national title game, and my brother played Division II and was all-league. So, full football family.”
The wrestling did not go to waste.
“A lot of it for me as a center is leverage,” he said. “It plays a big part into being able to stay low, and it’s something I’m trying to get back to. I’ve been doing a little bit more trying to focus on that. But naturally from wrestling, staying low — and it really helps with hands.”
Kinney has not been handed the job. He splits work with Demetrius Hunter, and both have taken reps at guard, as well.
“We push each other. We get graded every day. We see each other’s grades,” Kinney said. “It’s been a fun competition being able to go back and forth.”
Flanking him are Chauncey Gooden and Jayvon McFadden, both second-year players. Kinney did not undersell them.
“Those are probably two NFL guys as redshirt freshmen,” he said. “They go out there and dominate, and it makes my job a lot easier being next to both of them.”
Colorado (2-0) plays at Northwestern (1-0) on Saturday (5:30 p.m. MT, FOX), and Kinney offered the most specific scouting report anyone in the building had given publicly this week.
“They play really hard, and they’re a very smart football team. You’re not really going to get them with too much eye candy,” he said. “They’re going to be gap sound. The linebackers play hard. The safety comes down to the box sometimes. He can hit. It’s a little bit different from Georgia Tech, because Georgia Tech would get out of their gaps a little bit. They’re a very sound defense, and we have to communicate really well.”
Julian Lewis took the offensive line to dinner last week, a detail the quarterback mentioned after the Weber State win. Kinney supplied the rest of it.
“He took us to BJ’s,” Kinney said. “I did that at my last school, and I’m glad Julian kept it going. It really brings the O-line together. I wouldn’t say it makes you want to block more for the quarterback, but knowing the guy back there cares about you, it plays a factor.”

Title: Michigan needs to regulate the cameras reading your license plate
Article_Text:
More than 125 Michigan cities and counties now operate Automated License Plate Reader systems, yet Michigan has no law governing them. The lack of oversight is especially disconcerting given the facts that the data ALPRs collect is available to law enforcement agencies outside the state, the alerts they generate are frequently incorrect and officers use them for personal purposes. Due to the invasive nature of ALPRs, Michigan should regulate them.
Most of these cameras are operated by Flock Safety, a private company whose ALPRs scan each passing license plate and compare it against police department databases. Police departments run searches on behalf of U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement and Customs and Border Patrol, agencies that have brutalized and killed innocent civilians.
Officers have access to ALPRs, often without authorization. In April 2025, Wisconsin police tracked a driver using Flock’s camera network as he traveled into Michigan and back. The Wisconsin police already had a warrant for his arrest on an unrelated domestic violence charge but decided to search his movement history using ALPRs. The police inferred that he made the trip to purchase marijuana because the drug is legal in Michigan. He was stopped and charged with marijuana possession while the original charge was dismissed. Because neither Wisconsin nor Michigan law requires a judicial warrant for ALPR searches, Wisconsin deputies searched a nationwide database for the driver’s movements without it.
A judicial warrant would not have stopped them from arresting him on the charge they already had. Requiring a warrant, however, would have stopped the ALPR search that led the officers to suspect he was purchasing marijuana. A warrant forces an officer to state in advance what they are looking for and to convince a judge that they have a reason to look, which means an officer cannot search a person’s entire movements first and decide afterwards what the results could support. This protection matters in cases like this one, where the driver’s movements were tracked and a suspicion was formed without justification for searching all of his movements in the first place.
ALPRs also frequently produce inaccurate alerts. ALPRs read the characters on a plate without verifying which state issued it, so a stolen New Jersey plate can trigger an alert on an identically numbered Pennsylvania plate.
Other errors can arise from police databases that list vehicles as stolen even after their recovery. In California, it was found that 37% of alerts from fixed readers were misreads. When an alert wrongly flags a vehicle as being involved in a criminal case, officers approach the stop as a high-risk encounter. As a result, innocent drivers have been held at gunpoint, arrested or put in jail. The police department in Roseville, California has responded to this by implementing a policy to manually review every ALPR alert. Michigan does not require any official verification of ALPR alerts before initiating a search or arrest. Therefore, Michigan residents are put at risk any time they drive.
Though it is important to implement such a manual review system, it still does not address who is able to access and collect the ALPR data. Some officers have used their camera access beyond their professional capacities, utilizing the technology for personal motives. Earlier this year, a Milwaukee officer pleaded guilty after running nearly 200 searches to track a former partner and that partner’s ex. After this, Milwaukee imposed monthly audits on ALPRs, which ironically caught the internal affairs detective assigned to investigate the original violation. The officer was only caught because a victim searched their own plate out of curiosity on haveibeenflocked.com and reported it, prompting the investigation. Without private citizens choosing to audit the police, this internal misuse would have gone unnoticed.
However, ALPRs are not completely bad. For example, they can speed up investigations. Kalamazoo has used these systems since 2021 and reports that they aided in 23 homicide investigations, including a 2021 case where officers located a stolen vehicle and rescued the two children inside. Cases like these are why an outright ban would be shortsighted and why regulation is the best course of action. Regulating ALPRs would allow for successes to persist while cracking down on misuse.
Nineteen states have already passed laws regulating ALPRs. Virginia and Washington cap image retention at 21 days. Montana requires an officer to visually confirm a plate against the reader’s image before an automated match can justify a stop, along with daily updates to the alert databases that produce stale-record errors. These regulations would help solve key issues with ALPRs. Capping retention on databases helps protect against officer misuse by limiting the scope of data they can access; requiring officers to visually confirm a plate against the reader’s image reduces instances of traffic stops caused by false alerts.
Michigan House of Representative bills 5492 and 5493 have not been voted on by the Michigan House Judiciary Committee since April. Because the bills are tie-barred, one cannot pass without the other. The bills would require plate data to be destroyed after 14 days without a judicial order and mandate quarterly public reporting on plates scanned and matches that led to arrests. Michigan state representatives should vote in favor of these bills.
However, passing these bills would still leave the underlying problem unresolved, so the legislature should also consider adopting Montana’s manual oversight law and bar out-of-state and federal law enforcement agencies from accessing ALPR data without a warrant from a judge.
Michigan drivers shouldn’t have to suffer the consequences of an unregulated, unreliable camera monitoring system. By passing this legislation and continuing to enhance regulations, Michigan will take a necessary step toward protecting the privacy and safety of drivers without compromising the crime-fighting abilities of ALPRs.
Kai Farjo is an Opinion Columnist who writes about political economy, international politics and culture in his column “Material Matters.” He can be reached at kaifarjo@umich.edu.

Title: New album from Holy Pinto marks milestones with Milwaukee friends and strangers
Article_Text:
Aymen Saleh didn’t expect to fall in love with Milwaukee.
Hailing from Canterbury, England, he was touring the U.S. with his indie-pop project Holy Pinto when a friend invited Saleh to come stay with him in Wisconsin.
Saleh quickly connected with Milwaukee’s nightlife and music scene, and more than five years later, the city is still his adopted home.
Understanding Wisconsin, Together.
WPR’s “Wisconsin Today” newsletter keeps you connected to the state you love without feeling overwhelmed. No paywall. No agenda. No corporate filter.
“I think with English culture, through German-influenced Wisconsin culture, we have a lot of similar relaxed politeness mores,” Saleh said “I’m still here in a way that obviously I didn’t expect.”
Milwaukee became a major source of inspiration for Saleh’s music career and his new album called “Wedding Season.”
Much of the album was recorded in Milwaukee, including audio snippets from conversations he had with friends and strangers in bars and venues around the city.
Saleh joined WPR’s “Wisconsin Today” to discuss his path to Milwaukee, its influence on his music and the making of “Wedding Season.”
The following interview was edited for clarity and brevity.
Rob Ferrett: What brought you to Milwaukee, from your hometown of Canterbury, England?
Aymen Saleh: Essentially, when I got picked up by a couple of labels in America, and the music visa was signed off on, I was touring here as much as we could. Then my friend, Ryan, left. We started the band together. He wanted to do different stuff in life, because this lifestyle isn’t for a lot of people, as I now understand why. But it is for me, so no problems there. However, when he departed, it was like, “Oh, well, why don’t I stay in America?”
I was in Philadelphia a lot of the time, which was where my label was, and I was drifting a lot. I had a friend who was a musician in Milwaukee, who, in typical Wisconsin hospitality form, was like, “You can stay as long as you want, man.” When people in Philly say that, don’t trust them. When people in Wisconsin say that, it’s a bit more like, actually, I don’t think they mind. So that’s kind of how I end up settling here. It’s very wonderful. Obviously, it’s more affordable than a lot of the Brooklyn, New Yorks of the world.
Rob Ferrett: How would you describe the Milwaukee culture and music scene to your musical colleagues from around the country, or back in England, who haven’t experienced it?
AS: I get that a lot. A lot of people are like, “Milwaukee?” and I’m like, “It’s a really nice, affordable place to live.” There is a cool music community here. We actually have a lot of independent promoters still in Milwaukee and more independent venues than a lot of other places.
There’s actually a lot of music stuff going on here in a way that, like, when I grew up in Canterbury, there wasn’t much. That’s a tiny, antiquated … it’s not even really a city. We pretended it was, but it’s not really. [Milwaukee] is a significant upgrade in a lot of things. But it’s not as small as people might think. It’s not New York, but it’s a great city with a lot of good stuff going for it and a wonderful music scene.
RF: Back in 2020, you put out an EP called “Milwaukee: A Love Story of Truck Stops, Soccer Bars, and a Big Blue Van.” What inspired you to bring the city into your music?
AS: That is a little concept EP about my move here. It starts off with me in Texas at a truck stop around Christmas, and this gas station attendant was like, “Hi, are you OK? Do you have anywhere to go for Christmas?” And I was like, “Do I come across as that sad?” Like, I need to not be alone, right? So I think that’s when I reached out to my friend Alex in Milwaukee, and he’s like, “Just come down.”
So it kind of starts there in that story, and then it goes through settling here and being here for — I guess when I’d written that — maybe two years. I’ve drifted a lot in life, and two years felt like a long time at the time, so it’s kind of my story of being here. In terms of releasing that EP and that song, “Milwaukee,” it actually really got a lot of tension here. It turns out that if you write about Milwaukee, people in Milwaukee like you.
But also, it was weird hiding here as like the drifter who is here in between tours, to [become] like, “Am I a local band now?” After that, when COVID grounded everyone, it was like, “I guess I’m kind of a local artist now.” So I’m really proud of that one. That was a really special one for me.
RF: How did the new album “Wedding Season” come together?
AS: I started it around 2020, during COVID. I was playing a lot of piano and isolated in my apartment, and I’m not really a piano player, but it became the muse that was exciting me about the music. I love lyrics, and I feel like a songwriter, and that was helping get me out there. So I had a lot of piano, essentially like pop-adjacent songs, a lot of sadder stuff.
I started off with like 10 of those kinds of songs, and I realized that I felt like it was very self-indulgent. I don’t really like writing sad songs because it’s like, this is not like the kind of energy I love sharing in the world. It was all about me, and it felt kind of weird. So I started opening up to other people, and I think that’s where the concept came in. I would just ask friends or random people in bars to tell me about some of the stuff in the song.
Some of it was friends that I know are really charismatic, a lot of bartender friends, and they would tell some of the craziest stories I’ve heard in my life. I really had to trim it down because the stories are so compelling, they would overpower my own stories entirely. It wouldn’t be my record. So it was a lot of those late-night bar conversations, but not the kind of casual ones you have over like a NFL game at 8 p.m. on a Monday. I wanted to catch those 3 a.m. bar conversations, where, like, we should probably be in bed by now. So interspersed throughout the record are a lot of voices of friends and strangers in Milwaukee and bars.
RF: The album touches on a lot of relationships and life milestones like marriage, breakups and death. What message are you hoping it conveys?
AS: I think of it as a coming-of-age record, but not the “I’m going off to college” coming-of-age record. It’s more like, “Oh, people around me are like committing to each other.” It’s that kind of coming-of-age … And all these relationships aren’t just romantic. They’re also platonic. You can be singing about the dissolution of a marriage, this great, huge thing. But what about your best friend? What about someone you met in the bar that night that you had a deep conversation with? They’re all shades of the same thing.
So there’s moments in songs where it might sound like I’m singing about myself getting a divorce, which it’s not. I’m not divorced, but actually, it’s just about me growing apart from a friend. So I think it’s definitely a study of that, with the voice notes of a lot of people talking about these things. It’s all about expectations and how we relate to one another, and how we see ourselves comes into play. You can love someone but have very different values or direction or needs, and grow apart.

Title: Big Dave's Cheesesteaks making Washington DC debut
Article_Text:
September 16, 2026
Big Dave's Cheesesteaks has secured the site for its debut restaurant in the nation's capital, revealing its address at 730 7th St., NW in downtown Washington, D.C.
The location places the fast-casual concept in the Chinatown/Gallery Place corridor, near the Gallery Place-Chinatown Metro station and within walking distance of Capital One Arena and the National Portrait Gallery.
"We wanted our first D.C. location to be somewhere that already has energy," Derrick Hayes, founder and CEO of Big Dave's Cheesesteaks, said in a company press release. "This location puts us in the middle of a neighborhood where people come to eat, work, shop and experience the city. It felt like the right place for Big Dave's to establish itself in Washington."
The location choice aligns with the brand's national franchise strategy, which emphasizes high-visibility, accessible sites capable of building strong ties with local residents and visitors.
"When we look at a new market, the location has to make sense for the business and for the community we are entering," Shawna Snyder, chief operating officer of Big Dave's Cheesesteaks, said in the release. "This location gives us that foundation and creates a strong starting point for our development in the District."
The expansion is spearheaded by franchise group BIG DMV, which is leading the brand's rollout throughout the D.C. area.
The announcement comes during a period of accelerated growth for the brand. Big Dave's Cheesesteaks recently climbed to No. 4 on Fast Casual's Top 100 Movers & Shakers list, driven by rising franchise demand in major markets.
Founded by Hayes in a 700-square-foot gas station shop as a tribute to his late father, Big Dave's has expanded into a national fast-casual contender known for its Philadelphia-style cheesesteaks and community-focused mission.
Inspired to bring his West Philly roots to Georgia, Derrick Hayes launched Big Dave’s Cheesesteaks in honor of his late father. The brand gained buzz when Philly native actress Eve visited the original 700-sq-ft Dunwoody gas-station shop. Today Big Dave’s spans Atlanta, Mercedes-Benz Stadium, Orlando venues, a food truck and new SC franchises!

Title: Macklemore, Kraft exchange statements on Gaza donations as tour fallout continues
Article_Text:
Macklemore, Kraft exchange statements on Gaza donations as tour fallout continues
Kraft says Sheeran already asked him to commit $2M to 'fight this humanitarian crisis'
Rapper Macklemore and New England Patriots owner Robert Kraft exchanged statements Wednesday in the latest chapter of the saga involving the rapper's pro-Palestinian stance.
Ed Sheeran's tour of North and South America has been roiled by the decision this week to drop Macklemore as an opener on his tour because of his onstage pro-Palestinian comments.
Since then, all of Sheeran's other supporting acts have dropped out, including a group that performs with Sheeran during part of the show.
Sheeran, who is scheduled to perform in Philadelphia on Saturday, said the decision to cut Macklemore from the "Loop Tour" was the promoter's, not his own. The “Thrift Shop” rapper exclaimed “Free Palestine” during the Sept. 5 date in New Jersey.
Macklemore has said his removal was the result of an effort led by Robert Kraft, the billionaire owner of the New England Patriots. Kraft's involvement was implicitly cited in some of the statements from the supporting acts who left Sheeran's tour Tuesday, decrying the influence of money.
On Wednesday, Macklemore posted on Instagram that he would donate $1 million of his earnings from Sheeran's tour to organizations that are working to support the Palestinian people.
In the post, Macklemore also asked Kraft to match his donation, saying that the two could agree on protecting Palestinian lives.
"I will be donating the entire $1 million of my net earnings from Ed Sheeran's Loop Tour to six organizations working directly to support the Palestinian people," Macklemore wrote. "And I invite Robert Kraft to match my donation. Whatever we disagree about, perhaps we can agree on this: Palestinian lives are worth protecting. A Palestinian life is no less valuable than any other life on this earth."
Of the organizations that Macklemore is donating to, The Palestine Children’s Relief Fund has an active Boston chapter, and HEAL Palestine has also brought Gaza children injured in the war to Boston for surgery.
In response, Kraft noted that Ed Sheeran called him and "asked him to commit $2 million to match his donation to aid in the region to fight this humanitarian crisis."
The Associated Press contributed to this report.

The Washington Commanders placed linebacker Jordan Magee on injured reserve and signed veteran guard/center Lucas Patrick on Wednesday.
